96.title: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
96.content: Skill block-actions: Every block of a rendered document links back to where it can be changed: [edit] opens the block’s Markdown source in GitHub’s editor, and [feedback] opens a GitHub issue about that block, from the folio’s own issue form when it has one, listing the change-sets that already discuss the block. Use when a reader, reviewer or agent needs to propose a change to one block, when setting up a folio’s feedback issue form, or when a document site’s links point nowhere. Named by: Public comment on a review draft . A reader who finds something wrong in a block is one click from proposing the fix or saying what is wrong, and the click lands on the block, not on the repository. The links are per block, because a block is what a comment, a change-set and an edit are about. The code is folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts; the Tool is block-actions; the document build (build-document-site.ts) draws the links on every labelled block, and the public-comment overlay adds the issues that already discuss the block.

97.title: What each link does
97.content: | link | opens | what the person does next | . | ✎ edit | the block’s source (folio/<doc>/<chapter>/<root>.md, or its .ts if it has no .md) in GitHub’s editor, on main | edits and proposes the change; GitHub makes the branch and the pull request, which is reviewed like any content change (content-change-review.bpmn) | . | 📣 feedback | a new issue about the block | describes the problem; the issue is intake, and a public-comment folio triages it like any other comment (public-comment skill) | . | discussed in #n | the issue of each change-set the block’s comments are in | joins the existing discussion instead of opening a duplicate | .

98.title: Every issue is coded with its content
98.content: [feedback] codes the issue with the slug of the document it came from: the title reads Feedback [dpi-h-ra]: <section> — <block> and the body opens with **Content:** \dpi-h-ra``. A folio with several documents, or a repository that takes issues about more than one thing, can then sort feedback by what it is about without opening it. The code is in the title rather than only a label because GitHub silently drops a prefilled label when the reporter has no triage rights, and most public reviewers do not.

99.title: The issue form is the folio’s, and optional
99.content: With no form, [feedback] opens a blank issue whose body already says which block, which section, the source link and the block’s address on the site. It works on day one. A folio that wants structured feedback adds a GitHub issue form at .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/block-feedback.yml (start from the shared templates/issue-forms/block-feedback.yml, whose answers the drafting review sheet imports: skill review-sheet-script) (another name with --issue-template). The link then names the form and prefills only the fields the form declares, matched by id: . | field id | filled with | . | block | the block’s label (its anchor) | . | section | the heading the block is under | . | source | the block’s source path in the repository | . | page | the page it renders on | . | url | the block’s address on the published site (needs --site-url) | . | content | the document’s slug, the code the issue is triaged by | . A form may declare any subset, and fields it does not declare are not sent. Add the questions you want answered (what is wrong, a suggested wording, the reviewer’s organisation) as further fields; they are left for the person.

100.title: Where the repository comes from
100.content: GITHUB_REPOSITORY in CI, else the checkout’s origin when it is on GitHub, else --github <owner/repo>. No repository, no links: a page with no links is honest, a page with broken ones is not. --no-block-actions turns them off for a build that should have none.

101.title: Two forms of the same links
101.content: . | Full (blockActionsHtml): every href written into the page. Used on a one-page document and on index.hydrated.html, so the links work without JavaScript. | Compact (compactActionsHtml + compactActionsScript): the block’s facts as data attributes, and the hrefs built in the browser when a pointer or focus reaches them. Used on a lazy page’s shell, where a prefilled URL per block would bloat the page. The browser builder, BLOCK_URLS_JS, is held equal to editUrl and feedbackUrl by block-actions.test.ts; change both together or the test fails. | . The recipe lives in the harness, cat-harness-tools/src/core/edit-links.ts, so every layer can use it; this package re-exports it. It is published once as assets/js/edit-links.js (held equal to the code by a test). On a page, mark a link data-fa-link="edit|source|feedback" and either give its host the facts (data-src, optional data-repo, data-line, data-block, data-sec) or leave a GitHub blob/edit href, which the runtime reads the facts from. Generators that write Markdown use markdownEditLink. Three places keep their own link on purpose: the public-comment dashboard’s Discuss (it opens a change-set discussion, not feedback on a block), the bootstrap site’s Improve this page (bootstrap-tools may import nothing outside itself), and an IG page’s per-section ✎ / 📣 (SOURCE_LINKS_JS in build-ig-site.ts): a section’s heading can live in an included file, and its issue is titled after the section with the page apart. The IG page’s own Edit this page link does use the recipe. Any page that shows edit or feedback links uses these, not a URL of its own: one recipe, so a change to the issue form or the branch reaches every page at once.

102.title: In the library: edit opens the folio, never the source
102.content: A library entry is a frozen source: the version published for public comment stays in library/ exactly as circulated, and the changes the review asks for are made in folio/. So the library’s Document view (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts, drawn by the platform viewer and by build-library-site.ts on a folio’s site) shows: . | link | on | opens | . | source | the document, each section | the library’s own file on GitHub, read-only | . | 📣 feedback | the document, each section | an issue coded with the entry: Feedback [<entry>]: <section> | . | ✎ edit | each section, and its contents row | the FIRST folio block of the folio section MATERIALISED from it | . A section is matched to the folio by its number, else its title, through the folio-review-anchors/v1 file whose library names the entry. A section the folio has no counterpart for (a PDF’s front matter) gets no ✎ edit, because a guessed link would open the wrong block. The platform’s own library has no materialisation, so it shows source and feedback only. bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/build-library-site.ts --repo <folio> --out _site publishes a folio’s library at <out>/folio-assistant-core/<library dir>/<entry>/, the same <base>/<handler>/<kind>/<subject> route every viewer follows.

103.title: Using it as an agent
103.content: # one block's links, to hand a reader bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts --repo <folio> --block prose:1-1-4-a8e0b3 # every block's, as JSON bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts --repo <folio> . When someone in a chat says “this paragraph is wrong”, give them the block’s feedback link, not the repository’s issue page, and the edit link if they can propose the wording themselves.

104.title: What not to do
104.content: . | Do not point [edit] at the frozen review version under library/. Comments cite it, so it is never edited; the folio’s blocks are. | Do not point [edit] at the staging branch. An edit is a proposal to the published text, so it starts from main; a different branch is an explicit --edit-branch. | Do not hand-write issue URLs in a folio’s pages. They drift when a block is renamed; the build recomputes them from the manifests every time. | .

106.title: Relationship first, visualisation later
106.content: Skill board-diagram-interchange: A board is a DIAGRAM OF a folio, not a container of one. The OMG split between the semantic model and its layout, why the arrow runs one way, and what a note may never carry. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Treat a board like the OMG specifications treat BPMN layout: relationship first, visualisation later. BPMN separates the semantic model — bpmn:process, its tasks and its flows — from Diagram Interchange: BPMNDiagram, BPMNShape, BPMNEdge, which say where each of those was drawn. They are two documents about one subject, and the layout one points at the semantic one, never the other way. A folio board is the same shape: . semantic model notes, anchors, content nodes what is true diagram interchange board-positions.json where it was drawn .

107.title: What follows
107.content: A folio is complete with no board. Deleting every board loses layout and no content. That is the test to apply when you are unsure whether something belongs on the board or in the folio: if losing it would lose a fact, it is not layout. A note carries no x, no y, no board, no position — for the same reason a BPMN task carries no coordinates: layout lives on top of notes, not as data within them. One note may sit on several boards, at different places, without the note arbitrating between them. A coordinate on the note could not express that; a layer above it does so for free. An orphan is swept from the LAYER, which is the easy direction: one file, one pass, and nothing edited out of a note a person owns.

108.title: The arrow, and how it is kept
108.content: folio ──▶ board ──▶ position ──▶ note allowed note ──▶ position / board / folio REFUSED . This is a property a future edit can break silently, so it is checked rather than described. schemas/board-positions.test.ts asserts two things against the SOURCE: . | no field named x, y, board or position appears in todo.ts, carried-note.ts, landing-sticky.ts or note-anchor.ts; | board-positions.ts imports zod and nothing else — it names notes by id, and an id needs no type from the layer below. | . The first guards the failure that actually happens: somebody adding coordinates to a note “for convenience”, which makes a content node carry state and gives one note two answers on two boards.

109.title: Two graph typologies, because they are two things
109.content: | kind | holds | what it is | . | boards | content | what a board is and what it shows | . | board-positions | state | where each note was drawn | . content-context-and-state-graphs refuses a content node that carries state, which is the same rule one level up. And check:graph-typology-work asks a sharper question of the second: it is state, written by a running process every time somebody moves a note — but state that records a position in a PROCESS is work, and state that records a position on a CANVAS is not. Both kinds declare recordsWork: false.

110.title: A board declares what it SHOWS, and absent means everything
110.content: schemas/ui/board.ts: an optional filter over pages and kinds, OR within an axis and AND across them. Absent is the default and it means the whole folio — a query rather than a stored list, because a list of content nodes needs something to notice that a listed node was renamed and that a new one was never added, and a query has nothing to fall behind. Every harness above the floor has a board filled with all contents, which is the absent filter — so the minimal board and the total board are the same document.

111.title: Mergeability is the reason for the shape, and its limit is stated
111.content: Positions are the most concurrently-edited state a folio has: two sessions moving two notes is the ordinary case. So the document is sorted and indented, one note per line-block, and the sort is idempotent — a writer that reshuffled on save would conflict with every other save. It is a partial fix. Two notes that sort adjacent still conflict, because the inserted lines overlap. This removes the guaranteed conflict, not every conflict, and it should not be trusted further than that.

112.title: What this skill is NOT
112.content: Not the rendering. How a board draws, when a card becomes its avatar and what an open window does are board-windows. Not the tiles. Which boards and viewers a reader can reach is harness-tiles.

Semantic zoom is in here too and is deliberately not the same mechanism: the threshold is resolved from the kind and applies itself by SIZE, while opening and closing are a person’s acts. 120.title: Board: place a note
120.content: Process_BoardPlaceNote · advisory · 3 step(s) . 126.title: Board: relocate content to the trashcan
126.content: Process_BoardRelocate · strict · 5 step(s) . Moving open content to the trashcan from the board, with the reader’s confirmation in front of the move and not behind it. You are in this process when the fishbone is used on open content. The confirmation gateway has a real “nothing moved” end state, because a destructive action whose refusal is not drawn is a destructive action somebody performs by accident. The order of the two writes is the content of the diagram. The CONTENT relocates, and only then are its positions dropped and orphans swept — the folio carries what is true, the layout layer carries where it was drawn, and the arrow never runs the other way. 132.title: Start in the avatar, open into a window
132.content: Skill board-windows: Everything starts as its avatar; opening projects a window onto the board. The two mechanisms that must not be conflated, z-order, and the fixed chrome a content kind fills in. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Everything starts as its avatar, and [x] closes a window back to it. Opening projects a window onto the board; selecting any part of a window raises it. Each content kind controls its own avatar and rendering, and opens into a full-screen panel with fixed controls such as [x], [linksrc] or [edit].

133.title: TWO mechanisms, and conflating them is the defect
133.content: |   | trigger | who | . | semantic zoom | the card’s rendered width crosses a declared threshold | automatic | . | open / close | [x], or opening a card | a person | . An open window is not a zoom state: it is projected onto the board rather than being the card grown large, so it survives zooming out. Only [x] closes it. Collapsing the two gives a board where a card can close itself with no action taken, and where [x] and a zoom-out are indistinguishable. Semantic zoom is the GLASS’s, not the board’s . Every board slot — a landing sticky and a todo sticky alike — is one component: the same closed square tile (--fa-sticky-tile-size) with the theme’s faded art, and the same compact icon row underneath it. A slot is its closed tile at every width, so semantic zoom does not run on the board. It decides what a card shows on the folio glass, where a card is resized freely. Do not add a width observer to the board grid: it would be a zoom with nothing to change, and the next agent would read it as the card’s state.

134.title: One sticky, one icon row, in one order
134.content: Under every sticky, on every panel: view, edit, pin, send to fsh-guts, as icon buttons. An icon-only control carries aria-label (what a screen reader announces) AND title (the same words on hover); they are not interchangeable. No control sits inside the card body. The open window’s bar uses the same icons for the same acts. A link the sticky cannot serve is absent, never dead.

135.title: Pin is a toggle onto the FOLIO glass
135.content: There is one store answering “what is on my glass”: the folio. A second store holding a page-level copy of the card gets no glass tools, no folio geometry and no shelve, and has to be special-cased by the glass filter and count. | Pin makes the sticky a folio asset — todo/<id> (the key the glass’s own Todos panel pulls a todo out under, so the two ways onto the glass agree) or landing/<slot> — with shown: true, drawn by the glass’s own card path and placed by placeOnGlass. A landing sticky’s theme, picture URL and text travel in the entry as data, never as stored markup. | Unpin is shelveFromGlass — the middle of the three states below. The entry stays; the same pin puts it back, where the reader left it. | The pressed state is the store’s answer (folioStateOf(key) === "glass"), never the button’s memory. The glass’s own × shelves too, and the row’s pin follows it. | .

136.title: Send to fsh-guts asks first
136.content: A control a reader has to ask about has not said what it does, so discard is named for where it goes (Send to fsh-guts, the trashcan that is kept) and opens a confirmation that names the sticky, says it is restorable and per-browser, and says where it is restored from — the fish in the navbar’s icon row. Focus starts on Cancel; Cancel and Escape do nothing but close it. A dialog whose dismissal performs the act did not ask. The window bar’s send is the same act and takes the same confirmation. The inverse is Restore in fsh-guts.

137.title: The threshold is declared, inherited, and traceable
137.content: schemas/kg/semantic-zoom.ts (instance data: semantic-zoom.json): a folio default (belowPx) with a per-kind override (byKind) — the repository’s inheritance rule (inherit everything, override anything; a variant states only what it CHANGES). So: . | the folio always has a number, and every kind resolves to one; | a kind that states nothing is complete, not invalid — requiredness is checked after resolution, never on the declaration; | an override carries a required because, and the resolver returns the source alongside the value, so a reviewer can tell a deliberate override from a folio default that does not fit. | . The boundary is stated once. Strictly below the number, so the declared width is the last one that still shows words. A boundary written one way in a comment and the other way in the renderer makes a card flicker.

138.title: Z-order: selecting any part raises
138.content: Windows stack, and selecting any part of one raises it — not a title bar, any part, because a reader who clicks into a window’s content has already said which one they mean. Z-order is session-only. The DI layer carries no z: a committed stacking order would make every raise a file write and every two sessions a conflict, on the most concurrently-edited state a folio has. If that proves wrong, z is one optional field in the positions document.

139.title: The chrome is fixed; the kind fills it in
139.content: A content kind declares which controls it offers, and the platform fixes the frame: . | [x] is always present and always in the same place, so a reader learns the frame once; | a declared control that names nothing known is a finding, not a missing button; | a control the environment cannot perform is hidden, and the reason reported — a dead [edit] 404s for exactly the reader who cannot edit, which reads as “this page is broken” rather than “you cannot do this”. | .

140.title: Closing must have a reachable inverse
140.content: An action whose inverse is not reachable is not a toggle. On an overlay, close may set hidden, because the launcher tile re-opens it. On a board that IS page content, hidden removes a section of the page, so the inline board collapses to a control in its own position, and focus follows it — left alone, focus lands on <body> and the keyboard position is gone. A control two clicks deep inside a collapsed launcher does not count as reachable. A default of “hidden” is allowed only with the inverse on screen. The glass’s tile strip starts slid away; its “Show tiles (N)” tab stays in view, in the strip’s own position, and the same tab hides the tiles again. See harness-tiles §”The glass strip”.

141.title: The floor, which is not negotiable
141.content: This instance’s declared interaction profile is low-dexterity. Every board action is keyboard-operable; drag is an accelerator and never the only way in. Targets are at least the tile size. And the board is ALWAYS collapsible to a linear, tile-based listing — a board that cannot be read linearly cannot be read by a screen reader, printed, or translated. The listing is the ARTEFACT and the board is the overlay . The board is an extra laid over a simple tile-based listing. So the floor must be correct with no JavaScript at all, not merely when the board is toggled off: notes built only by docs-ui.js from a fetch of assets/todos/index.json give a reader with JavaScript off no note, no count, and no hint that notes exist. Three checks follow: . Document order, never the board’s order. The board may stack by BPMN subprocess depth; the floor does not, because document order is what a screen reader and a printout depend on, and a floor that reordered would be a second answer to “what comes next”. Collapsed, never removed. When the board mounts it moves the listing into a disclosure so the page does not show the same notes twice. It does not delete it, hide it from assistive technology, or display: none it: a listing the board removed would have no way back while the board is open. Assert against the SERVED HTML. A test that reads the DOM passes because the board built that DOM. The assertion is on bytes the server sent — a browser context with javaScriptEnabled: false over the same renderer the generator writes with.

142.title: The folio belongs to the HARNESS, not to the library
142.content: A content library is something a reader browses — a replica, a published instance, any folio published as a site. A folio is the reader’s own surface: their notes, the assets they have materialised, the documents they created or linked. So the folio visualisation is cat-harness’s, available by convention on any harness, and a library never implements its own. A library may have its own landing page and its own harness; neither is licence to build a second folio. Consistency is the requirement: a reader moving between libraries must find the same folio, because the point of carrying a folio is that it does not change underneath them. A note or a todo MAY reference nodes in another KG library. The folio is not scoped to the library it is pulled down over, so a renderer must not assume local resolution.

143.title: A tile, or an avatar?
143.content: A tile is what the HARNESS declares, an avatar is what the FOLIO holds, and a theme is how either one looks rather than a third kind. The test is in harness-tiles §”A tile, or an avatar?”, and only there, because one rule with two homes is free to drift.

144.title: An asset has THREE states, not two
144.content: Pulling the folio down gives a glass — a surface over whatever is being browsed, carrying sticky notes and the avatars of materialised assets, including materialised KG like cat-bootstrap or cat-harness themselves. | state | where the asset is | how it got there | . | in the library | not the reader’s at all | the default | . | in the folio, not displayed | materialised into the folio’s own reproduce directories — library/ for the bytes, uploads/ for a source — off the glass | the reader closed it, “back in library” | . | on the glass | displayed in the pulled-down folio | the reader pulled it out of the library | . “In the folio” is not folio/. The folio is the reader’s REPOSITORY, of which library/ and uploads/ are declared parts — both carry dependents: "reproduce". folio/ is a different graph typology: renderable authored content. corpus-grep searches library/ only, so a node materialised anywhere else reads as ABSENT to every consumer. Closing returns an asset to the middle state and NEVER to the first. Only its display goes. Putting it back on the glass is a separate act performed from the library, not from the glass it just left. A two-state model would make closing a sticky and un-materialising an asset the same gesture, and a reader tidying their glass would silently discard work; the middle state is what makes closing cheap enough to do freely. When you implement close, check that the library offers the way back — not that the glass does. Close says where the way back is, at the moment of closing. The glass’s [x] opens a confirm that names the instance’s library and links it; Escape and Cancel leave the card where it is, and only the confirm shelves it — after which the glass says, with the same link, where the asset went. Naming the library matters because a reader holding assets from several libraries would otherwise have to remember which one each came from. The place is the card’s own, so there are three. A library card goes back to its instance’s library, a todo to the Todos board, and a landing sticky pinned to the glass to the page it was pinned from; calling a sticky “your Todos” would send the reader to a list it was never on. One function answers “where does this card go back to”, and the confirm, the status after it and the [x] button’s own label all read it, so the three cannot disagree. The confirm is the page’s one confirm dialog, shared with sending a sticky to fsh-guts, so focus-on-Cancel and Escape-cancels are stated once. Opening a library card goes to the asset’s visualizer when its index entry declares one, else to its entry page; resizing is a corner drag, with +/− in move mode and the move bar’s buttons as the non-drag path.

145.title: Two settings panels, two names, each points to the other
145.content: The glass has its own settings (theme, avatars, opacity, blur), and the page has its own under ▦ Actions (scheme, reading preferences, the Discarded fish, Declared kinds). They are named “Glass settings” and “Page settings”, so a screen reader does not read two controls identically, and each panel opens with a link to the other, as its first control, because a reader who opens the wrong panel needs a pointer to the right one. Site chrome and board state are unrelated settings but they are neighbouring places, and a reader moves between places. | The names are declared once (SETTINGS_NAMES in docs-ui.js), because each panel’s link prints the OTHER panel’s name; a panel renamed in one place only would leave the other panel’s link naming something that no longer exists. | The link must OPEN its target, not toggle it, and not open it underneath. The glass’s openPanel closes a panel that is already open, and the open glass covers the sidebar where Page settings lives. So the glass-to-page link shuts the glass first, and the page-to-glass link shuts the launcher first. In both cases focus lands on the target panel’s heading. | No link to nothing. A page with a glass and no sidebar has no launcher. Each panel registers an opener, and the link is drawn only when its target registered one. | . The same holds for any future pair of panels that share a word: name each one for what it acts on, and point each one at the other. scripts/tests/settings-labels-distinct.test.ts checks the source; test/settings-crosslinks.e2e.ts checks the rendered page at 1280×800 and 390×844, by mouse and keyboard.

146.title: Lazy window content fetch and render safety
146.content: Rendering the board with N cards makes 0 per-card detail fetches up front: each board slot (todoSlot / renderBoardTiles) renders only its summary tile/avatar. When a card carries a per-card detail or artifact URL (detailHref, bodyHref, artifactHref, or a non-inlined jsonldHref), opening its window (openCard / createLazyWindowLoader.openWindow) fetches that card’s content lazily on open, caches the result by card id (so re-opening uses the cached result and never pre-fetches the other N - 1 cards), and renders any body or tool/skill output through the declared renderToolOutput (RENDER_AS: text, url, markdown, json) and safeHref boundary (schemas/ui/render-output.ts, site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js). A refused URL scheme (such as javascript:) is never fetched and is shown as escaped text.

147.title: Not this skill
147.content: The layout layer and why a note carries no coordinates: board-diagram-interchange. Relocating content out of a folio is deletion-requires-confirmation, applied by the content core’s processes/ui/board-relocate.bpmn.

148.title: board-windows (skill)
148.content: The skill board-windows as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/board-windows.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

149.title: Reading a knowledge graph before you have anything
149.content: Skill bootstrap-kg-navigation: Read and navigate a knowledge graph with nothing installed — no MCP server, no tools, no harness. Named bootstrap- so it cannot be confused with a navigation Skill of a Harness that is installed. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . This skill assumes a text editor and nothing else. No MCP server, no skill-fetching tool, no work-plan store, no build. If those exist they are not yours to rely on yet — see AGENTS.md.

150.title: A graph is files that declare what they are
150.content: Three facts carry the whole model, and every one of them is checkable by reading: . | An instance declares the directories it scans, in its declaration at its root. Each entry is an id, a path, and the kinds of graph found there. | A directory is a place to look, not a type. One may hold more than one part of a graph, so the directory does not say what its files are — the files do, in their own front matter or $schema. | Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. An override matches on an entry’s id, never its path. Matching on path turns one relocated graph into two, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | . Two more words you will meet in a declaration. A field this skill does not describe is an Extension: a Harness added it, and you ignore it. A Harness’s own kind of declaration, which requires everything bootstrap’s does and adds Extensions, is a Subkind of bootstrap’s: read it as bootstrap’s, and it still means what it says. Versions and addresses. A declaration may state its version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and an iriBase. Every identifier it mints, and every page meant for a person, is then <iriBase>v<major>/…: the address carries the major alone, so only a breaking release moves it. The exact release you read is fixed by the pin that brought this repository to you, not by the address. Bootstrap’s own are in its declaration; read them there rather than trusting a copy.

151.title: Do this, in order
151.content: . | Read the repository’s declaration. If there is none, this repository is not an instance yet, and that is the case bootstrap exists for. | Find the entry whose graphTypologies name the kind you want. In bootstrap they are named for what they hold: skills, processes, scenarios (the Roles), schemas and models. The entry’s path is relative to the declaration. | Read the files in that directory. A markdown file declaring name: and description: in front matter is a skill — its body is the instruction you were looking for. A file declaring $schema: is stating that it is something else, and is not a skill however it is named. | Follow a reference by id, not by path. A node that names another names it by id; resolve it through the declaration rather than guessing a filename. | .

152.title: What “I could not determine” means here
152.content: An absent declaration and an unreadable one are different: . | what you found | what it means | what to do | . | no declaration | not an instance yet | this is bootstrap’s case — continue | . | a declaration that will not parse | an instance asserting something broken | stop and say so; do not fall back | . | a declared directory that is not there | the declaration is wrong | stop and say so — scanning nothing and reporting a clean run is the defect | . | no declaration for a kind you want | this instance has none of it | that is an answer, not a failure | .

153.title: What this skill is NOT
153.content: It does not describe what a Harness above bootstrap holds, such as its content or its checks: those belong to the Harness you have not loaded yet. If you need one of them to finish bootstrap, the boundary is in the wrong place — say so rather than importing the definition.

155.title: bpmn-authoring
155.content: Named by: Review task, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, SWOT situation analysis, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: place a note . Skill id: bpmn-authoring · Package: workflow · Named by l2-dak-authoring.bpmn (Business processes · BPMN 2.0, Business analyst lane) and crdm-requirements.bpmn (Phase 2: Map current workflow (BPA), Agent lane). Author BPMN 2.0 business process diagrams — both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn.

156.title: Inputs and outputs
156.content: schemas/skills/bpmn-authoring/: . | in — processName (required), sourceWorkflow, existingBpmn, participants | out — bpmnFile, diagramFile, taskCount, gatewayCount, participantCount | . graphviz is a declared capability with degradation: skip — layout help degrades, authoring does not stop.

157.title: Diagram Interchange is not optional
157.content: A .bpmn with no DI section — no explicit x/y on its shapes — parses and renders blank, although the XML looks complete. bun run cat render:bpmn renders every diagram to docs/assets/img/workflows/ with bpmn-js in headless Chromium; bun run cat render:bpmn:check fails when an SVG is stale. Run the renderer and look at the SVG before you call a diagram done.

158.title: Readable at 100%: check it before and after (author check)
158.content: Every diagram you write or touch must, when you are done: . | fit 1400 × 900 in diagram units, so its 16px text reads at about 14px in a 1200px band without zooming; every task a fixed 120 × 120 square: boxes never grow to fit their names, and a name that does not fit is shortened (TASK_SIZE in the tools layer); | have no label on another label, on a flow (its own included), on a box or across a lane line: a gateway’s question above the diamond, its answers beside their flows, every label inside one lane; | have right-angled flows and every name inside its box, pool and lane names inside their strips; | have no crossing flows, and the lane order that keeps flows between lanes shortest. | . bun run cat bpmn:detangle <file> reports all of it, and --write fixes what it can (lane order, right angles, box and lane sizes, label places). Run it before and after, and put both counts in the PR. Zero findings on every diagram you touch, or it does not merge (owner, 2026-11-02, after 63 of 80 harness diagrams were found with findings: “improve bpmn authoring process/skills so doesnt happen again”). A report nobody has to act on is how they piled up. Run bpmn:detangle <file> --check last; a finding you leave needs a reason in the PR, and only diagram-too-wide / lane-order may be left that way. Then look at the render: the check cannot yet see a box drawn across a lane line or outside its own lane, two flows drawn on top of each other, or a flow that wanders through a lane it does not stop in. Those are found only by looking. The same findings are in render:bpmn’s warnings and the process’s QA report, so a reviewer sees what the author left. The procedure, and why the budget is 1400 × 900, is bpmn-detangle.

159.title: In this repository, a diagram is executable
159.content: processes/**/*.bpmn are not pictures. workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete run them, and workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. That has consequences for how you author: . | Every activity carries <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="…"/> naming the skill that implements it, and <cat-harness.processes:bean store="beans/"/> where it touches the work plan. bun run cat check:workflow-refs fails on a ref that resolves to nothing, and bun run cat kg:audit additionally fails when the named skill exists but no package can serve it. | Every lane names a role. Declare the role once as a top-level <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> (before the collaboration and the process), and set partitionElementRef="<role id>" on the lane; the id is the role’s in scenarios/roles.json, verbatim. Lane names are free text; an explicit ref is the join that does not depend on spelling. <bootstrap.processes:role ref> is the deprecated form. A diagram using any bootstrap.processes: element declares the namespace as the first child of <bpmn:definitions>: <bpmn:import namespace="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns/" location="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns.jsonld" importType="http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld"/>. | A store is not a lane. Lanes are for people and agents, the roles that act. A place where things are kept, such as the work plan (work items), a corpus, a session record, an activity log or a published bucket, is a <bpmn:dataStoreReference>. The tasks that read or write it point at it with data associations, and each task sits in the lane of whoever does it. A “Work plan — beans” lane holding “Open the bean” says the store does the work, when the agent does. | The process’s own bpmn:documentation opens with what it is for. Its first sentence is the diagram’s row on the publication-workflow page. kg-export carries it on the Process node as summary (the whole text as description), the page reads it from the published named-subgraph JSON-LD (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) rather than from anything written by hand, and check:process-index fails when a declared diagram’s node has none. So that sentence says what the process does or answers — not who asked for it, which work item or issue it came from, or where the work got to. Those belong later in the documentation, or in the work item. | A gateway may be computed rather than chosen — see dmn-authoring. | Policy is declared on the process. <cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement="strict"/> means workflow_gate refuses a step that is not enabled; absent policy means strict. Steps marked relaxable="false" may never be relaxed by any package. | .

160.title: Readable diagrams: what the research supports
160.content: These rules are what holds up from the BPMN comprehension research, checked mechanically. kg:audit reports each rule below per process (src/workflow/diagram-quality.ts in the tools layer). The sources, and how strong each rule’s evidence is, are in the process-model-quality methodology. | Separate routing from work. A task never has two outgoing flows: put an exclusive or parallel gateway after it, or a reader must guess fork vs choice (activity-implicit-split, major). A loop-back INTO a task is fine. A gateway either joins or splits, not both (gateway-mixed). A question is a gateway, never a task: a box named “Should it leave now?” or “Separate this graph?” is a decision drawn as work. If someone must judge first, draw that as a task (“Judge whether it should leave”) or a call to Process_AskThePerson, then the question on the gateway after it. | Keep it small. Split by phase into call activities past 20 flow nodes (process-size). That 20 is house style. The only threshold with evidence is 7PMG’s 50 (process-decompose, major), and it predicts modelling errors such as deadlocks, not reading speed. | One start event per process level (process-single-start). Several named end events are fine, and the work item CLOSE pattern needs them. | A decision is a question, its branches are the answers (decision-label-question). | Label activities verb-object: imperative verb, then its object (Review the draft, not Draft review) (activity-label-verb-first). The evidence is one study of how ambiguous labels felt (29 students), so this is reported, never gated. | A name says the step, nothing else. No trailing [skill] slug: the skill is in <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>, and the page links it from there. No step numbers (“1 ·”, “Phase 2:”, “P1.1”): the flows already give the order, and a number in front breaks verb-first. A number that cites a section of a source document goes in the task’s documentation. A list of numbered steps is a sign the diagram copies a document’s outline; group the steps into phases instead. | . Split by phase: how . A diagram can be right in every step and still unreadable on its page. When process-size fires, or a diagram has a start event per lane, split it like this: . | The top-level process shows the phases. Each phase is a <bpmn:callActivity calledElement="…"> to its own process. Keep at the top only what moves the work between phases: who hands off to whom, and the decisions that send it back (rejected → revise). A loop that crosses phases is drawn at the top; a loop inside a phase stays in that phase. | A phase lives in its own file, <parent>-<phase>.bpmn, next to the parent, with its own process id (Process_<Parent><Phase>) and a first documentation sentence that says what the phase does. It becomes the phase’s row on the publication-workflow page like any other diagram’s. | A phase that ends two ways ends in two named end events, and the caller’s gateway right after the call reads which one it reached, as GW_BeanYours reads Process_BeanOpen’s. | Keep the node ids when you move nodes into a phase. A test, a schema or a skill that points at Task_X then changes only its file and process, not its id. | Open and close the work item at the top, once. A process that is only ever called runs on its caller’s work item, so a phase calls neither Process_BeanOpen nor Process_BeanClose (check:bean-calls). “Once” holds for the top as well: a process with several outcomes routes them all into one Process_BeanClose call, which decides itself whether the work item is completed, scrapped or blocked, and only then branches to its named end events. One close per outcome repeats the same box and makes the diagram wide. | A caller’s adjudication accepts looks one level down. If the judgement moves into a phase, put accepts on the call to that phase, and take it off any caller further up. | Name a call activity for the phase, verb-object like any activity (“Review the change”), not for its file. | . A phase that only one parent calls is still worth its own file: the point is the page a reader opens, not reuse. Untangle every diagram you touch . The same discipline as ArchiMate views (archimate-models §”Untangle every view you touch”), and the same geometry: a change never adds a tangle. Run bun run cat kg:audit before and after, and compare edge-crossing, edge-through-node and edge-rectilinear for the diagram. Say both counts in the PR. Route loop-backs in the channel below the lane (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”), then look at the rendered SVG. What the evidence does NOT support . Do not import these from style guides or model output; each was checked: . | Mandatory left-to-right flow. Figl & Strembeck 2015 (44 people) found no significant difference in accuracy or time across four directions. Lay out left-to-right for consistency, not because it reads faster. | A word cap on labels, a gateway fan-out cap of 4, and a fixed colour palette. No study behind them. Colouring matching split and join gateways made novices more accurate and experts faster, not more accurate (Reijers et al. 2011). | OR-gateways need no rule: the process model refuses inclusive gateways at load. | .

161.title: If it has actors, activities and a control flow, it is BPMN
161.content: Not a Mermaid fence. Mermaid stays for the things that are not processes — component maps, lattices, navigation graphs. The audit of which is which is on the publication workflow page, which the content core authors.

162.title: Why this skill is in a platform package
162.content: It covers both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn, and platform processes such as crdm-requirements.bpmn name it, so it cannot live in a content-type package: a platform process depending on a content-type package crosses the boundary the platform-boundary-guard subagent keeps. Its DAK material stays here rather than in a second skill, because a generic skill naming a domain worked example is ordinary, and two skills that must be read together to author one diagram are not.

163.title: When a layer above transforms it
163.content: A layer built on this one may transform an authored business process into another artefact — FHIR Shorthand, for instance — and then the BPMN is a source artefact rather than documentation of one. Author it knowing it will be transformed: names and ids you choose here appear in what is generated. That layer’s own tooling skill has the mechanics; this one names no layer above it.

165.title: Code node review
165.content: Skill code-node-review: Review the knowledge graph’s CODE nodes — Tool definitions in the tools graph and schema definition nodes under schemas/ — for the joins a reader cannot see: that a node declares what it is, that what it names resolves, and that the mechanism it describes is the one that actually runs. Named by: Code node review .

166.title: What you are reviewing, and why it is not ordinary code review
166.content: Two node kinds: . | node kind | lives in | declared by | says | . | Tool | tools/<id>/<id>.json (the tools graph) | "$schema": "tool-definition/v1" | one concrete mechanism that exercises a skill | . | Schema definition | Zod modules under the tools layer’s schemas/; their generated JSON Schemas under schemas/kinds/ here | the module and its exported types | the shape of a content object, and its own place in the KG | . They are graph nodes that happen to be code. Ordinary review asks whether the code is correct; this asks whether the node is correct — whether it declares what it is, whether its references resolve, and whether the mechanism it advertises is the one that runs. A file can compile, pass its tests, and still be a broken node.

167.title: Tool nodes
167.content: A skill states a capability generically; a Tool carries the concrete mechanism (skills-and-tools). Review a Tool node for: . | It names the skills it satisfies, and they exist. A Tool naming no skill is unreachable from the capability it implements; a Tool naming a skill that does not exist is a dangling edge check-tools can catch but a reader cannot. | The mechanism is the one that runs. A vendor, CLI, binary or endpoint in a Tool must be the one the pipeline actually invokes. A Tool describing an aspiration is worse than no Tool: it answers “how is this done here?” wrongly and with authority. | IRIs are minted, not written out. toolTypeIri forms I/O type IRIs against the instance’s canonicalUrl at load. A hardcoded IRI silently breaks when the publication base moves, and nothing fails at build time. | Coverage is a finding, not a score. Not every skill has a Tool node. A skill with no Tool is a gap worth naming in review; it is not a defect in the skill. | .

168.title: Schema definition nodes
168.content: Reviewed as nodes, the recurring defect is a file that does not say what it is: . | The node declares its own kind. kg (skill front matter), bean-defs (work item front matter) and workflow-state ($schema) declare themselves. schemas/*.ts largely does not — @module names the path rather than the node type, some files carry none, and *.test.ts files sit in the declared directory without being schema nodes at all. A consumer then tells them apart by filename, which is a coincidence of the current layout rather than a contract. | A widened type is a widened contract. Adding a field to a shared schema changes every instance of it, including in downstream folios. Ask what happens to a folio that does not set it, and whether the mirror (JSON Schema, the Python side, the interchange schema under tools/) moves with it. | A REMOVED field needs a reason in the file. The tools layer’s schemas/content/translation.ts carries a comment where roundTripQA used to be, saying what it held and why it went. Without that, the next author re-adds it in good faith. | Defaults are policy. profiles defaults to every profile while adapters narrows — because narrowing silently stops criteria running and a wrong pass is believed where a wrong fail is argued with. When you review a default, review which way it fails. | .

169.title: The audits to run, and what they cannot tell you
169.content: bun run cat check:tools # Tool nodes: declared skills resolve bun run cat kg:audit # the KG joins, per node, into kg-qa/ sidecars bun run typecheck # a malformed schema module fails here by design . kg:audit writes a sidecar per node rather than printing and exiting, so “this has been broken since it was drawn” and “this broke in the change under review” are distinguishable. Read the sidecar, not just the summary. What no audit can tell you: whether the mechanism a Tool describes is the one that runs, and whether a schema field means what its name suggests. Those are the two things a human or agent reviewer is for, and why this is a skill rather than a check script alone.

170.title: Where this runs in a process
170.content: review-code.bpmn (Process_CodeReview) is this skill’s subprocess. It is called, not inherited: an actor already acting as a reviewer descends into it and takes on the code-reviewer lane for that call path only, so the skills are the union along the path rather than a permanent widening of the outer role. review-task.bpmn is the generic entry that routes a change to this subprocess, to the narrative one, or to both. The feature-request process calls it too — crdm-requirements.bpmn audits the code nodes an implementation adds before an MVP goes to staging, because a Tool or schema node shipped in an MVP is the version stakeholders start building expectations on.

171.title: Do not
171.content: . | Do not review a Tool node without checking what it claims to invoke. The failure this catches is a node that documents a mechanism nobody wired. | Do not approve a schema widening whose mirrors you have not looked at. | Do not treat a clean check:tools as coverage. It verifies the Tools that exist; it says nothing about the skills that have none. | .

173.title: The language you communicate in
173.content: Skill communication-language: Determine the language an agent SPEAKS IN — the language of a turn, as against the language of content. Covers the four inputs and their order, why a model’s own languages are never the answer, the boundary between speaking to the person and writing durable artefacts, where the determination is recorded so a sibling session does not re-ask, and when to re-ask. Named by: Hand back to the discussion .

174.title: Why this exists
174.content: The language of a turn is a determination to make, not a default. The skills and the corpus are in English; an agent that answers in English without asking has let a default stand in for a decision. Content language is a separate question, owned by translation-manager. Determine it regardless of context. Mirroring the language of the request fails for the person who writes a terse instruction in one language and wants the report in another, or who can type a language more easily than they can read a wall of it.

175.title: Make the determination before the first substantive turn
175.content: Beside the other opening steps — the session-start sweep and opening-brief. The sweep prints the interaction preferences first, before the work plan.

176.title: Four inputs, and the order is not negotiable
176.content: | rank | input | where it lives | . | 1 | the person’s stated preference | cat-harness/memory/interaction.json, per user | . | 2 | the language of their own turns | the conversation | . | 3 | the model’s declared languages | bootstrap/models/models.json | . | 4 | the instance’s defaultLocale | its translation-sources declaration (defaultLocale, default en) | . A stated preference wins outright. It is the only input that is a decision rather than a signal, and a person who has said it once must not be asked again (WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7, Redundant Entry); for a user who types with difficulty, asking again is not a small cost. Their own turns rank above the model’s languages. The model’s languages are an INPUT, never the determination: a model strong in a language the person cannot read is worse than the fallback. Rank 3 can only suggest that a pairing may be better served by something other than the corpus’s language; it never selects one on its own. Only human-validated entries are read at all. validatedLanguages() in bootstrap-tools/schemas/model-registry.ts returns nothing for self-reported or unverified, because a model’s own claim about which languages it handles well is a generated assertion about a generated system. self-reported is not a weaker human-validated; it is a different kind of claim.

177.title: The boundary: SPEAKING versus WRITING
177.content: The rule above governs what you say to the person. It does not govern what you write into the repository. | artefact | language | . | chat replies, questions, status reports | the determination | . | commit messages, PR bodies, issue comments | the instance’s source language | . | code comments, skills, work items, schemas | the instance’s source language | . | folio CONTENT | translation-manager, not this skill | . The reason is the reader: a commit message or issue comment is read by reviewers and later agents, not only by the person in this session, and one person’s preferred language would narrow who can read the record.

178.title: Record it where a sibling session reads it
178.content: cat-harness/memory/interaction.json, in the user’s entry, beside profiles: . "someone@example.org": { "profiles": ["low-dexterity"], "language": "fr", "note": "…", "source": "stated by the user" } . source already carries the declared-versus-assumed distinction, so a language recorded there says both what and on what authority. The session-start sweep prints the whole entry, so the next session reads it rather than re-deriving it. Never write a preference the person did not state. The file is context — read at session start, never written by a process. An inferred language recorded as though stated is worse than no record, because the next session will not re-ask.

179.title: When to re-ask
179.content: . | Never, on a recorded preference, unless the person changes it. | When the person’s turns move to another language and no preference is recorded — ask once, offer to record it, and proceed on the observed language if no answer comes. | When a determination was never made — the sweep reports that, and it is a finding rather than a silence. | .

180.title: What “could not determine” looks like
180.content: defaultLocale, said out loud. An agent that falls through to rank 4 says so once rather than presenting the fallback as a choice, because an unknown rendered as a determination is indistinguishable from a real one.

181.title: Related
181.content: . | interaction-modality — the FORM a question takes; this is the LANGUAGE it takes. Both are read from the same file. | translation-manager — the language of content, which this skill does not govern. | bootstrap-tools/schemas/model-registry.ts — why a model’s own word is not evidence. | .

183.title: Compiled Artefact Cache
183.content: Skill compiled-artefact-cache: The general pattern for caching expensive compiled artefacts (Lean .oleans, FHIR ASTs) across builds. Defines branch-based storage, validity checking, exit code protocol, safety guards, and the restore→build→contribute loop. Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Human Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . This skill documents the generalisable pattern for caching compiled artefacts (such as Lean caches and FHIR ASTs). It is the shared contract that specific implementations (e.g. lean-cache-restore and ig-ast-delta) adhere to.

184.title: The restore→build→contribute loop
184.content: The cache is not a maintenance chore but the output of every authoring session. Every session should leave the cache warmer than it found it: . restore ──▶ draft / edit ──▶ build ──▶ contribute ▲ │ └───────── next agent starts here ─────────────┘ .

185.title: Branch-based storage
185.content: Artefacts are stored on orphan branches named for their package and toolchain (e.g. lake-cache/<package>-<toolchain>). This keeps the repository clean while persisting large derived outputs across builds.

186.title: Validity checking (3-valued)
186.content: The validity of a cache is not a simple boolean. It relies on the CompiledInputsSchema defined in the content core’s schemas/materialization.ts. Validity is checked BEFORE use via compiledValidity() and returns one of three states: . | valid: The cache matches the current inputs (e.g. toolchain, source revision, input digest). Restore and build. | stale-inputs: Identifies exactly which input changed. The cache cannot be used as-is; restore for the current toolchain instead, or build cold. | cannot-tell: The cache record lacks required input fields. Never a pass. Build cold or find the missing inputs first. | .

187.title: Exit code protocol
187.content: Scripts managing the cache must adhere to a standard exit code protocol. Branch on these codes rather than grepping the output: . | Code | Meaning | Next | . | 0 | present / restored / published | proceed | . | 1 | miss — no such branch | build cold, then contribute | . | 2 | usage or environment error | stop the run, read the message, do not fallback to full build | . | 3 | found but unusable (corrupt, won’t link, wrong toolchain) | repair or reseed | .

188.title: Safety guards
188.content: When contributing a build back to the cache, it must be safe to run unconditionally. The contribution is refused unless it passes these guards: . | Non-empty: There must actually be artefacts to cache. | Own-package: Artefacts must belong to the package itself, not just its dependencies. | Trace coverage: There must be sufficient metadata (e.g. >90% traced) for the build tool to use the cache effectively. | No-shrink: The new result must not be materially smaller than the incumbent cache, preventing partial builds from destroying a fuller cache. | . For cold starts, seeding the cache uses a test-branch staging approach: the cache is seeded to a -test branch, and a restore is verified from a clean clone before touching production.

189.title: The warm-start principle: Cache the intermediates, not just the output
189.content: The core value of the cache is that an expensive step’s intermediate outputs survive across builds. The pattern is: a cache branch carries not just the final output but also the intermediate build artifacts that prevent the build system from re-deriving them: . | cache type | final output | intermediate artifacts | what they prevent | . | Lean | .olean files | .trace files | Lake rebuild + eviction | . | FHIR AST | AST JSON + edges | txcache/ (tx.fhir.org expansions) | Publisher re-hitting tx.fhir.org for every ValueSet | . input-cache/txcache/ goes on the fhir-ast branch alongside the AST files. Preserving these intermediates is what makes subsequent incremental builds (such as those in ig-incremental-build.bpmn) fast: a warm build with cached packages and terminology runs several times faster than a cold one.

190.title: Instantiations
190.content: | Aspect | Lean Cache (lean-cache-restore) | FHIR AST (ig-ast-delta) | . | Artefacts | .olean files, .trace files | Per-resource AST JSON, dependencies.json, txcache/ | . | Inputs Schema | CompiledInputsSchema | CompiledInputsSchema | . | Key Inputs | toolchain (Lean version), sourceRevision | toolchain (Publisher version), sourceRevision, inputDigest | . | Storage Branch | lake-cache/<package>-<toolchain> | fhir-ast/<ig-package-id> | . | Service Script | lake-cache.sh (9 verbs) | ig-cache.sh (7 verbs) | . | Refreshed by | an agent’s lake-cache.sh contribute | a reusable workflow of the IG layer, on a runner (the Publisher needs Java and a 10 GB heap), which each IG repository dispatches; a site build refuses an AST that is not valid | . | Cone Engine | Lake’s .trace-based dependency graph | SUSHI’s fsh-index.json (forward: file → resource) + fsh-cone.ts (reverse: who uses this file) + AstPlanCli | . | Incremental | lake build (only stale modules) | IncrementalBuildCli (cone rebuild loop) | .

191.title: The file-to-resource mapping comes from the toolchain, not from us
191.content: Do not reimplement what the compiler already knows. SUSHI already writes fsh-generated/data/fsh-index.json on every run — the authoritative mapping from source .fsh file to output FHIR resource, with source locations. The AST exporter copies it into the AST directory; the incremental planner reads it there. No modification to SUSHI is needed. fsh-cone (a Tool node, declared by the FHIR IG layer) provides the reverse half — who depends on a file — so a changed RuleSet- or Alias-only file (which produces no resource itself) can be traced to the resources it affects. These two maps together give the planner a complete cone. Without fsh-index.json the planner can only plan a full build; with it, a single-file change rebuilds only the resources in its cone, which is a small fraction of an IG.

193.title: Complete initialization
193.content: Process_CompleteInitialization · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . A SUB-PROCESS of initialize-harness, called after a harness is installed and also when the location turns out to be an instance of the chosen harness already. It is how an agent — the one that installed the harness, or one dispatched for exactly this with nothing but this diagram and the declaration — makes sure EVERY initialization step is done. THE STEPS ARE NOT LISTED HERE. They are named by the declarations: the instance’s <name>.json and every declaration it needs, read from the sibling checkouts. A declared directory is a step (it exists); a declared asset is a step (the file is there); a dependency’s <name>/docs/bootstrap/initialization.md is a step (it was followed); the root README and the sections it opts into are steps; the repository a declaration names makes the site steps — a Pages workflow, a gh-pages branch, Pages switched on, the address answering. A harness above bootstrap names more in the same way — a work-plan store it declares as a directory is a directory step — and bootstrap does not need to know which. The skill initialization-steps has the table. IDEMPOTENT BY CONSTRUCTION. Every step is CHECKED before anything is done, and a done step is left alone, so running this twice changes nothing the second time. Nothing is replaced: a step that would overwrite what somebody wrote is a step for a person, not for the agent. FOUR STATES, NOT TWO. done; not done; could not determine — the check could not run (no forge CLI, no network), which is NEVER reported as done; and stated — the declarations name it but nothing can observe it (reading and following instructions), exactly as a stated precondition is never reported as satisfied. THE PRIMARY STEP IS DRAWN, not left in the list: A_CheckDocuments, the harness’s JSON Schemas and JSON-LD at the IRIs they name, checked first after the declarations are read. Everything after it — directories, README, the site — is either how those documents are reached or how a person reads about them. WHERE TOOLS ARE AVAILABLE, a toolset may perform the same checks (initialization-steps); otherwise the agent reads files. The diagram is the same either way. NO work-plan element on any activity, and isExecutable is false, for the reasons initialize-harness gives. i i i i i i i i i

199.title: Which harness, and where
199.content: Skill confirm-harness: Narrow the harnesses and locations this could be, then have the Requestor settle it. Takes a list; returns at most ONE harness. It needs a person: the Requestor settles it, never the agent. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . You are the Bootstrapping Agent. You may narrow; only the Requestor may decide.

200.title: The contract
200.content: |   |   | . | in, from the Bootstrapping Agent | 0 or more harnesses · 0 or more locations | . | out, from the Requestor | 0 or 1 harness · 0 or more locations | . At most one. A list of two harnesses is not an answer, and you may not break the tie yourself. Zero is a real outcome, not a failure to try again: it ends the process, logged.

201.title: Building the list you go in with
201.content: Harnesses. The default is bootstrap itself. Add any the context already names: “please set up <owner>/<repo> here” in a discussion names one, and so does any Harness built on bootstrap that the Requestor mentions. Locations. Is this already a git repository? Were one or more URLs to repositories supplied? Both are Knowledge Graph Data Stores and the difference is only how you reach them — the git CLI, or a forge’s API. Assume a remote repository is read-only (read-from). Having push access to a remote git repository is never evidence that you are meant to modify it, and never makes it written-to. When a remote Knowledge Graph is supplied, two modes are open — and the Requestor chooses which: . | keep it here (read-from) — build and render from the remote Knowledge Graph in this repository, with whether to materialize its content locally or reference it in place asked as its own question; or | put a harness on the remote repository (written-to) — instantiate the harness in that remote repository itself. Nothing is written to a remote repository without the Requestor’s explicit permission for that repository. | .

202.title: Asking
202.content: Before you ask, say where you are — Initialize a harness, determining the harness and repositories, as the Bootstrapping Agent, asking the Requestor — and if you cannot tell that the person in front of you is the Requestor, ask that first (human-agent-discussion). Ask through human-agent-discussion: context, the candidates as options, your recommendation, and, said before the question, that there is no default: with no answer, the process stops. Ask once, with what you found, and make it answerable by picking: . What should this become? I can see (list). If it is none of those, name the repository — owner/name. If they answer with a kind — “a paper”, “a guideline” — that is not an answer yet: tell them which harnesses you know of and ask them to pick one. A kind is a property of the harness they name, and you read it from that harness rather than asking for it separately.

203.title: Do not guess
203.content: A wrong harness does not fail. It succeeds at being the wrong thing, and every consumer that reads the declaration believes it. So when you cannot get an answer: say the process needs one harness, log the failure, and stop.

205.title: A confirmation can be waived — by the person who is owed it
205.content: Skill confirmation-waiver: A human may waive a confirmation they are owed — for a session, for a process run, or until a stated time. Covers what a waiver is made of, where it is recorded (the context graph, never the work plan), the gates that can be waived and the rules that cannot, why every waiver carries an expiry, and the one thing an agent may never do: grant itself one. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Several rules here stop an agent and hand a decision back: merging to main, removing a durable artefact, spawning a swarm, closing a work item whose evidence the session could not re-derive, re-entering a process it fell out of. The person who is owed a confirmation may give it in advance, for a stated scope. That is the same decision, made earlier, by the same person — never an agent making an exception for itself.

206.title: A waiver is five fields, and none is optional
206.content: | field | what it carries | why it cannot be omitted | . | granted_by | the person, by the identity the repository already knows them by | a waiver with no grantor is an agent’s own decision wearing a hat | . | quote | the grantor’s own words, verbatim | the agent’s paraphrase is the thing under suspicion; a summary can widen a scope without anyone noticing | . | gate | which gate class is waived (below) — never “everything” | a blanket waiver is indistinguishable from no rule, and nobody can audit what it covered | . | scope | session:<id>, process:<instance-id>, or until:<ISO-8601> | an unscoped waiver outlives the situation that justified it | . | expires | a timestamp, always | same argument bean-blocking.md makes for a block: a waiver with no expiry cannot be told from one nobody remembered to withdraw | . A waiver missing any field is not a waiver, and the gate stands. An agent that finds a malformed one asks, exactly as if none existed.

207.title: The gates that can be waived, and the rules that cannot
207.content: A waiver relaxes a rule whose text is ask first. It can never relax a rule whose text is never. Never delete a work item is such a prohibition: no waiver reaches it, and the non-destructive move (scrapped, with reasons) is always available. | gate class | the rule it relaxes | waivable | . | merge-to-main | merge-to-main — the owner’s authorisation for each merge (and crdm-requirements-workflow §Phase 6) | yes, for green heads only: a head in a repository with no CI is never covered | . | bean-close | bean-coordination §”When you cannot re-derive it yourself” — the ready-to-close batch | yes | . | deletion | deletion-requires-confirmation — report and wait | yes, per artefact class, never blanket | . | swarm-spawn | swarm-management — asked every time, per swarm | yes, with the agent count and model level named in the quote | . | process-reentry | process-state — confirm before re-entering | yes | . | issue-close | issue-working — an agent never closes an issue on its own say-so | yes; the waiver names the issues | . | agent permission grants | agent-permissions — a person grants what a coding agent may do | no — never self-granted, and granted per permission | . | hand-edited agent config | harness-projections — consent per change to .claude/settings.json and the like | no — consent is per change | . | work item deletion | todo-manager, never delete a work item | no — a prohibition, not a gate | . | fabricating evidence | anywhere a rule says re-derive rather than quote | no | . A never that somebody wants waived is a change to the skill that owns it — not a waiver.

208.title: Where a waiver lives — the context graph, never the work plan
208.content: A waiver is context: read at the start of a turn, consulted by whatever gate is about to fire, and never produced by the work it governs. That is the context layer as content-context-and-state-graphs defines it, so a waiver is a node under memory/waivers/ — the same graph an agent’s durable memory lives in. Not beans/. The work plan is state: it records what is being worked on and where it got to. A waiver is not work, has no Done-when, and must be readable by a gate that fires before any work item is opened. The work plan is also branch-local, so a session-scoped waiver filed there could be invisible to the session it was granted for. Not the interaction node (memory/interaction.json) either: that is read at session start and never written by a process, and a waiver is granted mid-session.

209.title: Consulting one — the three-state read, as everywhere else
209.content: Before a gate fires, look for a waiver in scope. There are three answers: . | A valid waiver covers this gate, in scope, unexpired → proceed, and say in the turn report which waiver you are acting under, quoting its words. A waived action is still an announced one. | No waiver → ask, exactly as the gate’s own skill says. | Could not determine — memory/waivers/ unreadable, a malformed node, a clock you cannot trust → ask. A gate that cannot read its waivers has not been waived. | . An expired waiver is kept, never deleted, as a scrapped work item is: the record of what was permitted, to whom and when, makes the next grant reviewable.

210.title: What an agent may never do
210.content: . | Grant itself a waiver. A waiver whose quote is not the grantor’s own words does not exist. If you are composing the sentence, you are the grantor, and you may not be. | Widen one. session: does not reach the next session; process: does not reach a sibling instance; deletion for build artefacts does not reach content. When the scope does not plainly cover the case in front of you, it does not cover it. | Infer one from tone. “go ahead”, “yes”, “do it” discharge the gate they were said to — that is an ordinary confirmation, and it needs no waiver node. A waiver is a standing grant over future gates, and it is recorded only when the owner says something that plainly is one. | Treat a waiver as a reason to skip the work. merge-to-main waived still means green CI and no conflict; bean-close waived still means the evidence is quoted in the work item. A waiver removes the asking, never the doing. | .

211.title: Checked, not trusted
211.content: bun run cat check:waivers reads every node under memory/waivers/ and fails on a missing field, a gate outside the table above, a scope that names a non-existent session or instance, and a waiver over a non-waivable rule. It reports expired waivers as inert, never as findings — they are history. The check reads the same table this skill publishes, so a gate class without a row is refused and the vocabulary cannot drift into “everything”.
