733.title: Harness projections: CI writes them, the owner consents to every hand edit
733.content: Skill harness-projections: Who may write under .claude/, and when. The generated projections of the knowledge graph (.claude/commands/*.md from skill:commands, the assembled agent memory under .claude/agents/ and .claude/agent-memory/) are written by CI, which commits them to the PR branch, and never by an agent. A hand-edited .claude/ file (settings.json, its hooks, a hand-written command or agent definition) changes only with the owner’s explicit consent to that change: the agent shows the exact diff and the reason, asks first, and records the consent. Read before staging any path under .claude/. Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Human Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release .claude/ is what the Claude Code harness reads before any skill is loaded: the slash commands a person can type, the memory injected into a subagent, and the hooks and permissions every session runs under. An edit there changes how every later session behaves, including sessions that never see the commit.claude/ is one instance of a general rule. Every coding-agent Tool has config files, and some of them are projections of the graph: CI writes the projections, and a person consents to each hand edit.claude/ is named here because it is the agent-host directory the generators write. Which files a Tool reads, and which of them are generated, belongs to that Tool’s adapter. Securing what the agent may do at all is agent-permissions.

734.title: Two kinds of file, two writers
734.content: | kind | examples | source of truth | who writes the .claude/ file | . | projection (generated) | .claude/commands/<name>.md carrying a generated: key (skill:commands); the marked region of .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md (agent-memory); .claude/agents/* where the memory assembler writes them; .claude/skills/ synced from packages | the skill’s front matter, the memory nodes under memory/, the package | CI only. A workflow step runs the generator and commits the result to the PR branch. | . | hand-edited | .claude/settings.json and its hooks, a hand-written command (no generated: key), an agent definition’s hand-written body, a memory file’s ## Session log | the file itself | an agent, only with the owner’s consent to that exact change | . The rule for a projection: edit the source, not the projection. To change a slash command, change the skill’s user_invocable or description. To change what a subagent remembers, add or edit a node under memory/ (agent-memory). Push the source change and let CI write the projection. You may run a generator locally in its --check form, or into a scratch tree, to see what it would write. Do not stage or commit anything it writes under .claude/. This applies inside skill-registration too. skill:register runs skill:commands, which writes .claude/commands/ in a composed checkout. Commit what it writes everywhere else, and leave .claude/ to CI. Why CI and not the agent. A projection is correct only if it was generated from the tree that lands. An agent’s local run reflects the tree it had, and a hand-merged projection drifts from its source; the CI step runs on the PR head, so the projection on the branch is the one the merge will carry, from one writer.

735.title: Hand-edited files: consent per change
735.content: Before you write a hand-edited .claude/ file: . | Show the exact diff. Paste the unified diff itself, not a description of it. | Give the reason: what breaks or is missing without the change, and what the change does to every later session (a hook that runs on every tool call; a permission that stops a prompt). | Ask, and wait. The order is context, diff, recommendation, question (interaction-modality §4.1). “Go ahead” discharges this question, for this diff only. | Record the consent in the commit that makes the change, and as a comment on the PR: . claude-config-consent: by: <owner's login> on: <ISO-8601 date-time> file: .claude/settings.json diff: <sha256 of the diff shown> evidence: "<the owner's words, verbatim>" (<session link or comment permalink>) . | . A standing waiver does not reach this. Consent is per change, so there is no gate class for it in confirmation-waiver’s table, and a waiver that claims one is not a waiver. A broad instruction such as “fix the hooks” or “make the session start work” authorises the investigation. It does not authorise the edit. Bring the diff back. When a hook or setting gets in your way, report it; do not edit it. This is the same rule as prepare-merge §Guardrails (“fix the tool” rather than delete the branch), with one extra step: here, fixing the tool is itself a change that needs consent.

736.title: Where it sits in the process
736.content: merge-to-main.bpmn runs Task_RegenProjections in its build-pipeline lane before it reads any evidence. CI regenerates the projections on the head and commits them to the PR branch, and the evidence is then read on that new head. A PR whose projections are stale therefore cannot reach the merge gate looking green (merge-to-main).

737.title: What this does not do yet
737.content: . | The CI step is declared here, not built. In the platform repository, merge-main.yml runs regen (which includes skill:commands and agent-memory) and pushes to the PR branch, but only for PRs labelled merge-main when main moves. code-quality-gates.yml runs skill:commands:check and agent-memory:check and fails, but commits nothing. A step that regenerates the projections on every PR head and commits them is a workflow change in the repositories that carry .github/. That change is not made here. | No check refuses an agent-authored commit under .claude/. Telling a CI-written commit from an agent’s needs a committer convention (the bot identity the workflow pushes as), and a gate that reads it. | skill:register still writes .claude/commands/. Restricting it to --check for that one step would be a change to skill-register.ts. | .

738.title: harness-projections (skill)
738.content: The skill harness-projections as its source file cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/harness-projections.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

739.title: A tile is the harness’s, not the node’s
739.content: Skill harness-tiles: A tile is a function of the harness watching a directory, not of nodes. Where the tile set comes from, what a tile opens, and the two gaps it reports rather than hides. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . A tile is a function of a harness watching a directory, not of nodes. If a harness declares visualisers, each one gets a tile; a tile defaults to the theme, and a harness can declare one or more visualisations, each with a title. The tile set is not a new registry — it is the visualiser obligation made reachable. A harness declares its visualisers in its <instance>.json visualisers (HarnessVisualiserSchema), and kg:audit reports which directories owe one. A graph that owes a visualiser owes a tile, so the audit needs no second list free to disagree with it.

740.title: Where a tile goes — the declared route, and nothing else
740.content: Each visualiser is ONE declaration in the harness that owns it: . "visualisers": [ { "id": "library", "renderedBy": "library-viewer", "coversKinds": ["library"], "subgraphs": "instance" }, { "id": "todos", "renderedBy": "state-viewer", "covers": ["todos"], "alias": "todos" }, { "id": "fsh-guts", "renderedBy": "staging-graph-viewer", "covers": ["fsh-guts"], "publish": "staging-only", "writer": ["scripts/gen-fsh-guts-viz.ts"] } ] . | id is the URL segment; renderedBy names a Tool node (the implementation may live anywhere); covers names this harness’s own directory ids, coversKinds graph typologies, over every declared directory of them in the checkout. A harness never names another instance’s directory — that would be a lower layer naming a higher one. | The URL is computed, never chosen. visualiserRoute in schemas/kg/visualiser-route.ts is the ONE function every generator and reader uses: <harness>/<id>/ for the full KG, <harness>/<id>/<sub-graph>/ for one sub-graph (subgraphs: "instance" — one per covered instance — or "directory", nested under subgraphUnder[kind] where the visualiser declares one), and an asset path below either. Every page is written to that route under the site’s docs layer, so the file and the URL cannot disagree. A tile opens the sub-graph view when it exists, else the full one. | A page claims nothing. A page carries only rendered-by: <Tool>, as provenance; it carries no renders: or <meta name="renders">. A directory’s coverage.visualiser is filled IN MEMORY by withViewers from the declarations, never from disk. | Collisions are declaration errors. bun run cat check:visualiser-routes refuses two declarations resolving to one route (or one inside another’s subtree), a page drawn by a Tool outside every route that Tool is declared to render, a page under a route that names a different Tool, a visualiser covering a kind its Tool does not renders, and any renders: or coverage.visualiser on disk. | The short URL is an opt-in alias. alias: "todos" makes <base>/todos/ a redirect to <base>/cat-harness/todos/, composed by compose-docs.ts for every page under the route. An alias that names another alias, a harness, or anything the site already carries at its top level is refused by the gate before a build and by the composer during one. A tile always links the canonical route. | publish: "staging-only": compose-docs withholds the route (and its alias) from a canonical deploy. | .

741.title: Instantiated is a different fact from declared
741.content: Only the harnesses instantiated in the folio get tiles, not every dependency. Which instances are instantiated here is answered by the root index.config.json (instances[]), or without an index by each root <name>.config.json. That rule is index-config’s; the tiles only consume it, because the navbar cannot be derived from the declarations alone and a directory listing is not the question a reader is asking. Dependencies keep a group of their own rather than disappearing, so a reader looking for one is not answered with silence. A harness a KG subscription chose is instantiated by the same file, with no local declaration: its declaration is the substrate snapshot kg:subscribe cached at the pin. bun run cat kg:instantiate <subscription> <harness> writes the config and the harness’s state directories (and, under an index, the harness’s instances[] entry), and refuses a harness that was not chosen, not declared at the pin, or whose needs nothing here holds. The tile is drawn from the snapshot (scripts/subscribed-harnesses.ts): it links nowhere, because nothing of it is published here, and a snapshot that cannot be read is a finding on the tile rather than an empty one.

742.title: Which harness / is — the landing is index-config’s rule
742.content: The site’s landing page is one of the instantiated harnesses. It is never the instance the generator happens to live in, and never the repository’s name. Which one it is — site.landing in the root index.config.json (an instance name or "hub"), or the per-config site.landing flag without an index — is index-config’s rule. resolveLandingInstance in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts reads both, and check:landing-instance is the gate. When the landing is the neutral hub, / is the harness listing (harness_details.html, these tiles) and the todo panel — the landing sticky panel, not a second board.

743.title: “Harness” carries TWO senses, and only one of them is this rule
743.content: | sense | what it means | how you tell | . | 1 — instantiated here | this checkout runs it | an entry in the root index.config.json instances[] — or, in a folio with no index, a root <name>.config.json (index-config). Read the file, not a number quoted here | . | 2 — a layer others instantiate | a base a downstream repo stands up | nothing in this checkout. It is a statement about the layer’s role in the stack | . The rules on this page are about sense 1. Sense 2 is correct usage too: a layer can be declared, not instantiated, and declare no visualiser — so it owes no tile — while being exactly what a downstream repository instantiates. No count is given for either sense, because a count in prose is a claim nothing checks; ask the filesystem. Do not write a checker for this. A predicate on the word cannot separate its two senses, so it is an adjudication, not a check (adjudication). When the word is load-bearing, say which sense — “instantiated here” or “a layer downstream repos instantiate”.

744.title: A tile opens the INSTANCE, not a kind handler’s view of it
744.content: A viewer page is a RENDERING with its own IRI, separate from the asset it shows; see kg-viewer §”The asset and its rendering are two resources with two IRIs”. scripts/mount-instance-docs.ts carries the two routes: . | route | handler | what it is | . | /<kind>/<instance>/ | the kind’s, cat-harness’s | the default rendering any instance declaring that kind gets | . | /<instance>/ | the instance itself | its own themed root | . The tile’s target is the instance’s own themed root when it has one, and a handler’s viewer only when it does not. The viewers stay reachable, listed beneath. An instance has that root when it has its own site directory, read from its own declaration — never by probing the BUILT site, where an instance whose pages are generated at build time has none until its generator runs.

745.title: Order is the declared dependency stack, reversed
745.content: Bottom to top, computed from the declared needs, never written out as names: a name list is a rule true only for the instances somebody remembered. The spine’s head keeps the top and its floor keeps the bottom. An instance whose layer nobody declared is undetermined — placed below the head, alphabetically, carrying a finding that says its place is not derived. Absent is not []: one is nobody having said, the other is an instance asserting it sits on nothing. A broken graph does not blank the navbar. flattenDependencies returns an empty order on a cycle, which is right for a pipeline and wrong for a sidebar, where showing nothing hides every instance over one typo. The problems are reported and the list falls back to alphabetical.

746.title: Two gaps, reported rather than hidden
746.content: Both are the third state, and they are DIFFERENT findings: . | declared and not rendered — a graph the instance declares with no published page. Not linked (a dead link reads as “this site is broken”), and reported. | rendered and not declared — a page published under a kind the instance does not declare. Also not linked, because the declaration decides what a tile may claim to show — and reported, because staying silent would hide a working viewer behind a rule, and the remedy is one line in a declaration. | .

747.title: An inert row SAYS why, and “no viewer” is four answers
747.content: A declared graph with no published viewer appears in the navbar as a row that does not open. Drawing it grey is not saying it: . | A title on a non-focusable element is a label for a pointer and for nothing else — no keyboard path, and not reliably announced. | Dimming alone is state carried by contrast, and can pass the contrast ratio while saying nothing. | . The reason is content: real text in the row. It is in the accessibility tree, survives a stylesheet that does not load, and cannot disagree with a second signal. Do not use aria-disabled — nothing is a control, and marking a <span> disabled announces a widget that does not exist. “No viewer” is four states, told apart by inertNote (harness-tiles.ts): . | state | the row says | is it a gap? | . | declared publish: "staging-only" | staging only | no — withheld on purpose | . | instance declares renderExemption.of: ["visualiser"] | no viewer by design | no | . | a viewer exists off the conventional path | viewer not published | yes, and a different one | . | nothing declares a viewer | no viewer yet | yes | . One wording for all four would label an intended state a gap, which is as wrong as hiding a real gap. Neither navbar picks the words. They render what the generator gave them, which keeps them one navbar rather than two that agree by maintenance. A kind the generator said nothing about renders with no claim about why.

748.title: A tile, or an avatar? WHO DECLARED IT
748.content: A tile is what the HARNESS declares. An avatar is what the FOLIO holds. | the thing | renders as | because | . | a declared visualiser (the harness’s visualisers) — over a directory or sub-graph | tile, functional | the harness declares it; §”A tile is the harness’s” above | . | a set of schema instances — todos | tile, content | the harness declares the set; the instances are the folio’s | . | a note, a document, a materialised asset in the folio’s reproduce directories (library/, uploads/) | avatar | the folio holds it; it is the reader’s, not the harness’s | . A TILE IS ONE OF TWO KINDS, and they bind to different things . |   | functional tile | content tile | . | subject | a directory or sub-graph | a set of schema instances | . | bound to | a SKILL | a SCHEMA | . | resolved when opened | a tool that implements the skill | the instances | . | what empty means | a gap to report — a skill nothing implements is unreachable | a real state — “nothing outstanding” is not “broken” | . A functional tile names the SKILL, never the tool. schemas/tools/tool-types.ts makes tools that satisfy one skill interchangeable, so a tile bound to a tool breaks the moment another tool is chosen. Likewise VisualiserDeclarationSchema takes “one path, or several visualisations”: a sub-graph may be rendered more than one way. Empty is asymmetric. A content tile opening on zero instances is CORRECT and must not be hidden — an empty board and a person with nothing outstanding are opposite facts. A functional tile whose skill has no tool is a gap to report. THEME IS NOT A THIRD KIND. A theme is a palette and its art; a tile takes the avatar’s declared hue. Theme is how either one looks, never an alternative to being a tile. Size does not decide it . A whole materialised knowledge graph (such as cat-bootstrap or cat-harness) on the glass renders as an avatar. So these two tempting rules are wrong: . | “Many behind it → tile, one → avatar” — a materialised graph is many things and is an avatar. | “Opens a viewer over a set → tile” — opening that avatar opens a viewer over a set, and it is still an avatar. | . Declaration ownership decides: a materialised asset is in the reader’s folio however big it is. The same subject can be both. todos is a content tile in the strip and an individual todo is an avatar on the glass: the tile is bound to the SCHEMA and the avatar is one INSTANCE of it. What is checkable here, and what is not . Tile-vs-avatar is not. Nothing classifies a folio item; the rule governs authoring, and the renderer reads the graph an item came from, so a gate would be a declared property whose check cannot answer its own claim. “A functional tile names the skill, never the tool” IS: a declared visualisation naming a tool id where a skill name belongs is decidable against knownSkills() and the Tool graph. No such tile exists yet, so nothing is gated today.

749.title: The navbar icon row is DECLARED, and three states is not two
749.content: navbarIcons on the instance declaration. A closed set — close, todos, beans, processes, kg, fsh-guts, qr, launcher — because a free string lets an instance name an icon nothing draws. Seven is the cap and it is refused, never truncated: silently dropping an eighth entry would overrule the instance’s decision. fsh-guts is a control, like launcher: a button that opens the discarded-items list and carries its live count, not a link. It is also the way back the discard confirmation names, so that dialog says “the fish in the icon row” only when this icon is on the page, and points at Page settings otherwise (board-windows §”Send to fsh-guts asks first”). | declared | means | . | absent | inherit — walk needs, site owner as the floor | . | [] | show none | . | a list | this instance’s own answer | . Absent and [] must not collapse. The guard is !== undefined, never a truthiness test: a truthiness test turns “nobody has said” into “nothing to show”, and makes an instance that has not declared the field indistinguishable from one that wants a bare navbar. The distinction is kept at every layer: resolveNavbarIcons returns undefined for undetermined, harness-tiles.ts omits the field rather than writing [], sync-docs-harness.ts emits null, and the client draws no row and says so once. The walk is needs, not a second traversal. Nearest declaration wins, breadth-first toward the foundation — the direction resolveSkillDirs already composes. A new walk would be a second answer to “what is this instance built on”, free to disagree with the first. Destinations are looked up, never written down. They come from the instance’s own declared visualisations plus siteLinks, so an icon whose graph this instance does not publish gets no href and renders as a non-link. close and launcher carry no href on purpose: they drive controls on the page, and an href would make them look like navigation.

750.title: The theme avatar: the assignment is theme-mediated
750.content: The navbar’s mark is the instance’s theme card art, clipped — not its icon. The chain: . instance → its sticky contribution → the sticky’s theme → the theme’s imageRole → the instance’s images carrying that role → the card layout → its avatarRegion . resolveThemeBackdrop is the join and returns the DeclaredImage, so the crop comes with it. An indirection is not an absence: look through the theme before concluding no assignment exists. Take the card layout, not laptop or mobile. KgImageSchema refuses a non-square avatarRegion in pixels, and only the square crop can satisfy that: equal fractions on a landscape image give a box wider than tall, and the clip scales width and height separately. A card with no declared crop is a finding, not an avatar: the whole composition squeezed into a small frame is unreadable. Report it and fall back to the mark.

751.title: Where a tile lives, and what it must not eat
751.content: Tiles render in the navbar and on the glass: one declaration, per-surface visibility, never two registries. The sticky board carries NO tiles. | Removing a surface loses nothing only if the others still carry it. Every tile this repository declares names navbar and glass, so each stays reachable. A tile that named ONLY a surface that is not mounted would vanish silently — report it, do not re-route it on the author’s behalf. | board stays a legal value in TILE_SURFACES, and nothing mounts it, so existing declarations that name it stay valid (the “every field but ref is optional” rule in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts). A declaration saying ["board"] alone is valid and renders no tile; the graph-tiles e2e asserts both halves. | . They are collapsible, with the count on the summary so a collapsed list still says how much is behind it — a fixed-height sidebar of tiles must not push the page nav off the top. Theming comes from the avatar’s declared hue: one hue, both schemes derived, so no tile can be legible in one mode and invisible in the other. A per-instance palette would be a second colour vocabulary beside theme.ts.

752.title: On a folio’s own site, a tile describes the FOLIO
752.content: A page’s tiles describe the instance whose site the page is on. A folio’s own Pages site (an IG repository’s folio-site.yml, a document folio’s folio-staging.yml) wears the platform’s chrome, and the platform’s _data/harness.json comes with it: tiles, counts, icon row, rail scopes and title, every path root-relative to the platform’s site. Unscoped, the folio’s badges show the platform’s counts and its links 404. cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/foreign-site-scope.ts applies the rule to the data, once, for both passes (compose-docs --shell --instance, and rail-standalone-pages --foreign-site): . | the link points at | on a folio’s site it | count | . | the folio’s own root (/<instance>/…) | resolves inside the folio’s baseurl | kept | . | a page the folio’s declaration publishes at its site’s root (/beans/), when the folio IS the checkout’s root (rootOwnPages) | stays root-relative, on the folio’s own site | kept | . | another instance’s state graph (work items, todos, QA, health, uploads …) | is not linked; the icon says why in words | none | . | a platform content, context or derived graph (skills, processes, tools, schemas, docs …) | is re-based, absolute, onto DOCS_SITE_BASE, with its qualifier shown | none | . | a kind nothing classifies | is treated as state | none | . The state row is unlinked rather than shown at zero or re-based. Per schemas/ui/tile-count.ts, absent is a third state, never 0: a folio that declares no beans graph has said nothing about work items. Showing 0 would be a claim, and showing the platform’s number answers the folio’s question with somebody else’s. The icon keeps its place and its accessible name says, for example, *“ declares no beans graph"* (§"An inert row SAYS why"). Ownership is decided by where the link points, never by a kind of the same name. A folio that declares a qa directory does not borrow the platform’s QA tile and its count; borrowing it because the word matched would put the platform’s number back on the folio’s page. A count beside a borrowed link is dropped too: the link is accurate, but the number would still sit on the folio’s page next to the folio’s own. The qualifier is shown instead, so the tile reads as the platform’s. The host’s count projections are not chrome. compose-docs --shell leaves out every assets/**.json that declares a headline tile count, as it does _includes/generated/. A badge whose file 404s renders as ABSENT, with no number. A figure that is not a tile follows the same rule: . | figure | it came from | on a folio’s site it | count | . | the translation sweep badge | _data/translation-qa.json, the platform’s | the shell leaves the file out; the badge stays, inert, reading “QA: not published”, and says why: *“ publishes no translation QA sweep on this site"* | none, and not “not run”, which would be a claim about the folio | . | the navbar’s locale swap | _data/translations.json, the platform’s index of its own pages | the shell leaves the file out; the index reads as null, “could not determine”, and the navbar stays as built | n/a | . | the fsh-guts fish | a button whose count is fetched from this site’s /fsh-guts.json | the button is drawn only when the folio links its OWN fsh-guts; otherwise the fish is the row’s re-based link, named *“the platform’s: declares no fsh-guts graph"*, or an inert icon with the note | none, never ”?”: ? means the read failed | . A folio that publishes its own sweep or fsh-guts document gets its own figure back with no further change: foreignSite.absent (written by scopeHarnessData) only supplies the words for when the site carries nothing. The two _data/ files are named in HOST_DATA_PROJECTIONS, since neither declares what it describes. foreign-site-scope.test.ts fails on a shell that carries a _data/ file nobody has classified as chrome or projection. A folio that IS the root of its own site (for example one whose site is generated rather than a Jekyll tree) needs four more things: . | Its declared pages are its own. Its visualisers under its own site directory publish at the site root, by the same ownsSite || isRepoRoot rule siteDirMount gives its icon (harness-tiles.ts), and the scope keeps them (ForeignScope.ownPages). | The icon row’s own paths and counts resolve on the folio’s site. After scoping, every root-relative href left in the row is the folio’s, and so is the count.json its badge fetches. rail-standalone-pages --foreign-site writes the row’s data-fa-root as the page’s own site root (rowRoot), while its script and style still load from the platform (assetRoot). | Its mark loads from its own site (ownsCheckout). | An image mark can sit on the rail itself. The rail draws the instance’s tone square behind every avatar; a declared image with ground: "none" (KgImageSchema) is drawn with no tone. | . The pinned rail reserves its width. Hover and focus open the bar over the page, as a peek; pinning keeps it open, so .main moves over (docs-ui.css). The gate is foreign-site-scope.test.ts. It runs both foreign-site passes over a folio and asserts (a) no tile carries another instance’s count or links its state graph, (b) no href is left root-relative unless it is the folio’s own path, (c) the platform’s translation sweep and index are not shipped and the rendered head_custom.html hands the badge its words, and (d) the fish fetches no count from a site that has no fsh-guts. The client halves are in translation-badges.e2e.ts and navbar-row.e2e.ts. A check of a page’s chrome has to run on a site that is not the platform’s, because on the platform’s own site the platform’s tiles are right by construction.

753.title: The glass strip — pinned first, and “+N more” counts the rest
753.content: No tile may be silently off-screen: a reader cannot tell a tile scrolled out of view from a tile that does not exist. | The pinned set is DECLARED, never written into a surface. glassStrip on the instance’s declaration lists the pins in order: { "chrome": … } for the glass’s own controls (todos, filter, settings) and { "kind": … } for a graph typology. It is inherited along needs like navbarIcons, so absent inherits and [] pins nothing. sync-docs-harness.ts resolves each kind to ONE tile (resolveGlassStrip): the directory named for the kind, else the first glass tile that holds it. A kind several harnesses publish gets one slot, and the others wait in More, where their qualifiers tell them apart. A pinned kind that no tile holds is reported in glassStrip.unmatched and never skipped silently. | Fit, not scroll. The strip shows as many pins as fit at the current width, in declared order, and refits whenever its box changes. It never scrolls sideways (scrollWidth <= clientWidth is asserted at 1280×800 and 390×844). | The last tile says “+N more”, and N is exact. N counts every tile not on screen: pins with no room at this width, plus everything the reader keeps in More. Shown + N is always the total. The tile is a button named “N more tiles”; it opens More and moves focus into it. Pins that did not fit come first in More, marked as pinned. | The reader may still arrange. A strip the reader has arranged, by dragging or with the Strip and More buttons, overrides the declared default in that browser. The fit and the count apply to their arrangement too. | It starts HIDDEN. With no stored choice, the folio opens with the strip slid away. Only its tab shows, reading “Show tiles (N)”. The tab is the one control both ways (board-windows) and carries aria-expanded. The reader’s choice is remembered in this browser as 1 or 0, and storage that cannot be read counts as no choice: hidden. | . glass-strip-fit.e2e.ts holds the four fit assertions and glass-strip-default-hidden.e2e.ts the default.

754.title: summary and alsoWritten — what a reader sees, kept apart from why it was named
754.content: A harness section on the landing page shows the declaration’s summary, a one-line gloss, and lists alsoWritten, the other spellings of the name. A description made to carry them shows the reader a naming rationale or spellings that render as one line. Authoring notes belong in description or a _comment. The reader-facing line goes in summary, and alternative spellings go in alsoWritten as a list, never inline. A harness’s sticky shows the same text as the landing page. A sticky contribution declares bodyFrom: "summary", and the card’s words are readerText in schemas/content/sticky-contribution.ts: the summary (else the description), then the alsoWritten spellings after “Also written:”. That is the rule docs/_includes/harness_details.html applies, read from the same two declaration fields, so there is no copy of the text to keep in step. bodyFrom: "description" still parses, because the pinned bootstrap/bootstrap.json declares it. bun run cat landing:sticky:check fails when a card built from its declaration does not open with that text. A bodyAppend may follow the reader’s text, and a card with a literal body is not compared.

755.title: harness-tiles (skill)

756.title: Asking a person, in one reusable way
756.content: Skill human-agent-discussion: Ask a person (or a sibling agent) for what no file holds. First determine where you are — the context, the Role you act as and theirs, the Process and task (or that you are idle) — and ask about whichever you cannot determine before anything else. Then context, the options, a recommendation and what happens with no answer, then ONE question. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Human–agent discussion, Initialize a harness . You are the agent that needs something only a person can supply: a choice, a judgement, or a step only they have the rights to perform. Every diagram in bootstrap that needs one calls processes/human-agent-discussion.bpmn as a call activity rather than drawing its own asking.

757.title: Before you ask: determine where you are
757.content: The diagram’s first three tasks come before any question, and each is declared as a precondition of the first one (bootstrap.processes:precondition … before="A_GiveContext"): . | determine | what you must be able to say | why it comes first | . | the context (A_DetermineContext) | what is already known, each fact with where it came from; which declaration governs it (the instance’s <name>.json, the diagram you are in, the Skill its task names); and whether the question has already been decided — earlier in the conversation, or in a declaration that quotes the person’s ruling | a settled question asked again reopens a decision and spends the person’s attention twice. Cite what you read, not what you remember | . | the Roles (A_DetermineRoles) | which Role you are acting as — the lane of the task that called this discussion — and which Role the person you ask holds | an Actor performs a task in a Process as a Role; nothing is a Role by nature. Who holds the decision decides whom you may ask: only the Requestor chooses a harness | . | the Process and task (A_DetermineProcess) | the Process, the lane and the task the question belongs to — “Process: Initialize a harness, at Determine the harness and repositories, as the Bootstrapping Agent” — or that you are in none: you are idle, classifying a request to find the Process it belongs to | a reader who does not know which Process you are in assumes the last one’s rules still hold | . Say all three in the message, as the first part of the context. A caller that already determined them hands them in; you check them rather than re-derive them. You are out of process — the Process is undetermined — when you cannot name it, when two candidates fit, when the step you believed was next is not the one the diagram enables, or when the work in hand is not what you said you would do. Do not infer your way back in. What cannot be determined is asked first . When any of the three cannot be determined, that becomes the first question of this same discussion (A_AskUndeterminedFirst), and the caller’s question waits, counted. Ask about the outermost first — the Process, then the Role, then the context — since the outer answer usually settles the inner. It goes through the same order as every question below, and it allows no default: a Process or a Role assumed rather than confirmed is an authority nobody gave you. Its answer is recorded, the three are determined again, and only then is the caller’s question put. If it is declined or met with silence, record what is still open and stop: a step completed in the wrong Process records an authority that was never given. I am in Initialize a harness, at Determine the harness and repositories, acting as the Bootstrapping Agent. I cannot tell whether you are the person who wants this repository set up, or relaying for someone: the request came from another agent’s message. If you are, I will ask you which harness next; if not, I will stop and record that the Requestor is unknown, since only the Requestor chooses. Are you the person who wants it set up? (One more question after this one.) .

758.title: The order is the rule
758.content: . | Context. Where you are (the three determinations above), what is being decided, what depends on it, and what you already know, each fact with where it came from. In the message itself: a link is where somebody goes for more, never where the terms are defined. | Options. Every option still open after you narrowed from context, each with what it costs and what it makes hard to undo. An option you could have ruled out yourself wastes the reader’s attention. | Recommendation. The option you would take, marked, and why. | What happens with no answer. Said before the question, so silence has a meaning both sides agreed to before it happened: the default, when the caller allows one, or “the question stays open and the work stops”. | One question, answerable by picking. With several decisions open, ask one in full and give a count for the rest. | . The test before you send it: can the reader answer without opening anything? If not, the question is not ready.

759.title: What can come back, and where each ends
759.content: | what came back | what you do | end | . | an answer that settles it | record it, and who gave it (a person or an agent) | Answered — or, when it answered a question about where you are, determine again and put the caller’s question | . | an answer that does not settle it (a kind instead of an option; two options) | follow up once, narrower, naming what is still open | back to the answer | . | a refusal | record what was asked and what is still open | Still open | . | nothing | apply the default only if the caller allows one, and say so; otherwise record what is still open | Default applied or Still open | . A default is the caller’s to allow, never yours. A caller allows one only when the decision is reversible and its own instructions name the default. It is recorded as assumed, with the default named, never as the person’s answer, and the next message tells them it was applied so they can reverse it. Which harness a repository becomes allows none: a wrong answer does not fail, it succeeds at being the wrong thing (confirm-harness).

760.title: The record
760.content: In the form the caller asks for. For bootstrap’s harness question that is a document conforming to discussion.output.schema.json (discussion). For a step only the person can perform (complete-initialization), it is the step with the person’s word beside it. A person saying “done” is recorded as their word, and the next check decides whether it holds.

761.title: Symmetric in its participants
761.content: The answering lane is a person or a sibling agent that already holds the answer. The record says which, because the two are evidence of different weight. Neither is refused, and they are not conflated.

769.title: Human Translation Workflow
769.content: Process_HumanTranslation · advisory · 16 step(s) . The human half of translation: a coordinator assigns a locale to a qualified translator, the translator works in their own tool, a subject-matter expert judges accuracy, and only then is the result official. You are in this process when a person is doing the translating. translation-workflow is the machine half — extraction, injection, staleness — and it hands off to this one at exactly the point a judgement is needed. The two are separate because completeness is mechanical and accuracy is not: the coordinator’s gate asks whether enough strings are filled, the reviewer’s asks whether they are right, and no amount of the first substitutes for the second. What makes a translation OFFICIAL is the reviewer’s sign-off, never the file being complete. i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i

775.title: Incremental render — the cache is easy, the cascade is the work
775.content: Skill incremental-render: Rendering only what changed — seeding a build from a previous render, the two edges that decide what must re-run, why a step declares GRAPH TYPOLOGIES rather than paths, and the rule that could-not-determine always re-renders rather than serving a stale page. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Three steps. Only the third is hard, and it is the one that fails quietly: . | Seed — start from a previous render rather than from nothing. | Re-render what changed — the steps whose inputs moved. | Re-render what DEPENDS on them. | . A page that was not re-rendered looks exactly like a page that was, so an incremental render that gets the dependency graph wrong ships wrong pages and reports a clean build.

776.title: The two edges, one mechanism
776.content: | edge | example | one change means | . | projection | <page>.html ← <source>.md | one source file → one page | . | index | community-list.html ← every catalogue node | one member → the whole index | . The index edge is the one people forget: an index is derived from a SET, so it goes stale when a member changes even though the index file itself did not. The runner treats both alike: if any declared input changed, the step re-runs, and the step’s own --check decides which outputs actually differ. The downstream half uses needs, which already orders the pipeline: a step whose dependency re-ran re-runs too.

777.title: A step declares GRAPH TYPOLOGIES, not paths
777.content: RenderStep carries two ways to say what it reads, and the second is the one to use: . | field | what it names | when | . | inputs | repository-relative files or directories | a path that is not a declared graph — a config file, a script’s own fixtures | . | inputGraphs | graph kinds from <name>.json — cat-harness, beans, schemas, … | anything the declaration already locates | . check:declared-paths rejects a literal path to a declared graph. A second answer to where do the skills live goes stale the moment a directory moves, and the render then hashes a path that is not there, finds nothing, and reports the step unchanged. The subprocess, and why there is one . render-pipeline.ts is in the harness layer. Resolving a graph typology means readDeclaration, which validates every kind in the declaration — and this repository declares a folio directory whose kind is registered by core, on the argument (written on schemas/kg/folio-graph-typology.ts) that a layer which cannot render must not own the renderable kind. So the harness layer cannot resolve any kind in-process without importing core, which check:partition rejects. So it asks across the boundary the way the pipeline asks every renderer it runs — by spawning one. cat-harness-tools/scripts/declared-dirs.ts is core-layer and prints one line of JSON on stdout, {graph: [dirs]}. A failure prints nothing to stdout and exits non-zero, so the caller cannot read could not resolve as declares nothing — the distinction this whole skill turns on. The pipeline reports it: . Graph typologies could not be resolved here, so every step that declared only graphs re-rendered: <reason> . and every graph-declared step becomes undeclared, which always re-renders. Safe direction, said out loud: a silent fall-back to a full render leaves the cache inert with nothing in the output saying why. The cost: a graph is coarser than a file list . kg-current declares the whole cat-harness graph, and everything needs its way back to kg-current, so editing one skill re-renders every step. That is the right trade: over-declaring costs needless runs, under-declaring ships stale pages that look fresh. A finer declaration is available whenever a step’s reads can be expressed without spelling a declared path.

778.title: Hash content, never mtime
778.content: mtime is the obvious shortcut and it is wrong twice: a fresh checkout rewrites every mtime, so CI would re-render everything; and a file touched but unchanged re-renders for nothing. Hash the content, and hash the path alongside it — moving a file is a change, and an index keyed on filenames notices. Sort before hashing, by codepoint. readdirSync order is not stable across machines, and localeCompare is ICU-dependent — a seed written on one machine would mismatch on another. byCodepoint in render-selection.ts is the comparator.

779.title: Could-not-determine always re-renders
779.content: Four states send a step to the “run it” pile, and none of them is an error: . | state | why it runs | . | inputs changed | the obvious one | . | something it needs re-ran | the cascade | . | the seed’s manifest does not mention it | absent is not fresh — it may never have run | . | it declares no inputs | it has not said what it reads, so nothing can be concluded | . And three at the build level: no manifest at all is a full render; a manifest that is unparseable or carries the wrong schema tag is treated as absent; and graph typologies that could not be resolved turn every graph-declared step into the fourth row above. A corrupt manifest is never partially believed — half a cache is worse than none, because the half that is wrong is invisible. This is the repository’s standing rule applied to rendering: could-not-check is never green. Here it costs a re-render, which is the cheap direction.

780.title: Under-declaring is the dangerous direction
780.content: A step whose real input is not listed keeps a stale output and looks exactly like one that re-rendered. A step that over-declares costs one needless run. So when unsure, list it. bun run cat render:order names every step that declares no inputs, because those are the ceiling on how incremental a build can be — and a step that always re-renders should be a decision (alwaysRun, with a reason) rather than an omission nobody noticed.

781.title: Steps that always run
781.content: A narrower graph buys more caching: beans reaches only docs-pages and state-dashboards. The two that always run are bootstrap (pending — nothing to cache yet) and kg-dynamic (alwaysRun: it exports the running workflows’ state, whose stuck states are measured against the clock, so no source hash could make caching it correct). Report the cached steps as cached, never as a pass. In this pipeline a “skip” already means its input never rendered, so a served-from-seed step gets its own mark (=). The counts must add up: a cached step returns no error, so it must not also be counted as having run. A build report that sums to more than its own steps is one nobody trusts the rest of.

782.title: Usage
782.content: bun run cat render # full bun run cat render:order # order + which steps are cacheable bun run cat render --write-manifest <path> # full, and record the inputs bun run cat render --seed <path> # incremental against that record bun run cat render --seed <old> --write-manifest <new> .

783.title: Not built
783.content: Seeding from the published render. The manifest and the selection are here; copying a previous build’s OUTPUT into place before the run is a deployment step and belongs with feature-staging.yml. Until it exists, a seeded run skips steps whose inputs are unchanged but has nothing to serve — so use --seed only where the previous output is already in place.

786.title: index.config.json: what this checkout instantiates
786.content: Skill index-config: index.config.json at an instantiation root says which harnesses the checkout instantiates, where each one comes from (local, or a remote mount pinned to a SHA), each instance’s config INLINE in its entry (a legacy <name>.config.json is only imported until --inline retires it), and which harness / is. Covers instantiated against declared, landing resolution and its error case, index.lock.json and its legacy fallback, the reserved index stem, the generated .gitignore block and its gate, and index-config:migrate (with --inline) for separated repositories. Named by: Remote-mount a dependency, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph . The schema is folio-index-config/v1 in cat-harness/schemas/kg/index-config.ts. The index is the ONE config. Each instance’s config is written inline in its instances[] entry. A <name>.config.json is a legacy file: imported only as a migration step, then retired with index-config:migrate --inline --write. Never create one — not to make a tool find a recipe, not for a new instance. If a reader only finds config in the file, that reader is the bug; fix it to read the index entry first. index.config.json holds three facts about how a checkout is instantiated: which harnesses are instantiated, which one is / (a checkout has one <base>/index.html), and where each one comes from, so each is stated once rather than spread across every root config. When it exists at the root it is authoritative. When it is absent, readers fall back to the root *.config.json files, their site.landing flags, and remoteMounts on the root declaration. { "$schema": "folio-index-config/v1", "instances": [ { "name": "folio-assistant", "source": { "local": { "at": "." } } }, { "name": "cat-harness" }, { "name": "my-ig", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "owner/my-ig", "ref": "<40-char sha>", "overrides": { "my-ig": { "whole": true } }, "trust": { "consent": { "...": "..." } } } } }, { "name": "my-guide", "contentType": "document", "site": { "build": { "sourceSteps": ["site:document"] } } } ], "site": { "landing": "cat-harness" } } .

787.title: Instantiated is a different fact from declared
787.content: A declaration (<name>.json) says what an instance declares. It travels with the harness into every checkout that uses the harness. An index.config.json entry says the instance is instantiated in this checkout. Without an index, a <name>.config.json at the root says the same thing. Tiles, the landing and the hub listing are all drawn from the instantiated set, which instantiatedHarnessNames(root) returns. Never derive that set from declarations or from a directory listing. The dependencies of an instantiated harness are not instantiated just because a mount’s closure brought them in. They keep a group of their own rather than disappearing. A harness that a KG subscription chose is instantiated the same way: kg:instantiate adds its entry, with its config inline, when the checkout has an index (and only without one writes a root <name>.config.json).

788.title: Inline, over a legacy import while one remains
788.content: Each entry’s effective config is built like this: . | Start from a legacy imported file, while one remains. That is import when it is given, else <name>.config.json, and only if the file exists. The target state is that no such file exists. | Overlay every other key of the entry (everything except name, import, source and _comment) as an inline HarnessConfig field. Objects merge key by key, and arrays and scalars are replaced. Inline fields win. | . effectiveInstanceConfig(root, name) computes it. readHarnessConfig(dir) returns it for any instance that an index lists, walking outward from the instance root and stopping at the first directory that holds either the index or the instance’s own config. An instance the index does not list is read from its own config file. Readers that are handed a root and a name (the site recipe in build-instance-site.ts) use readInstanceConfig in cat-harness-tools/scripts/instance-config.ts, which reads the same way and REPORTS every legacy file it reads. Retiring the files is index-config:migrate --inline --write: each imported file is folded into its entry by exactly the overlay above, so no effective config changes, and the file is deleted. index-config:inline:check fails while one remains.

789.title: Local or remote
789.content: . | source absent: local, at <name>/. | source.local.at: local, at that path. Use . for the instance declared at the root. | source.remote: a remote mount. It is a remoteMounts entry minus harness, which is the entry’s name. It reuses RemoteMountSchema instead of restating it, so it has ref (not pin), overrides.<name>.whole and .path, note, trust.consent and track, and every field added to RemoteMountSchema arrives with no edit here. | . There is one read path and one write path for remote mounts: . | Read: readDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot) returns the index’s remote entries when an index exists, else the declaration’s remoteMounts. If both carry mounts it throws and names both files. It never picks one. | Write: writeDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot, mounts) always writes index.config.json, seeding the index from the checkout first if there is none. It refuses while the declaration still carries remoteMounts. Nothing writes remoteMounts on a declaration. | .

790.title: Which harness / is
790.content: resolveLandingInstance(root) is the only reader. It applies these rules in order: . | condition | / is | . | the index is unreadable | invalid: the gate fails. There is no fallback to the flags, because the index was written to override them | . | the index’s site.landing names an instance it lists | that instance (by: "index") | . | the index’s site.landing is "hub" | the neutral hub: the harness listing and the todo panel | . | the index’s site.landing names an instance it does not list | invalid: the gate fails, and it is never a silent fallback | . | no site.landing (or no index), one instance | that instance (sole) | . | no site.landing, several instances, exactly one config flags site.landing: true | the flagged one | . | several flagged | the hub | . | none flagged | ambiguous: check:landing-instance fails, because the answer is never guessed | . | nothing instantiated | none: a state of its own, not a default | . gen-landing-data.ts and sync-docs-harness.ts ask this resolver. They do not use their own location. check:landing-instance also checks that the index and the root *.config.json files agree: . | A root config that the index does not import fails the check: without the index it would instantiate a harness, with it it does not, and nothing picks between them silently. | An import that names a missing file also fails the check. | An entry with no config file at all is the target state, and passes. | A legacy file an entry still imports is reported every time. It passes while it is a pending migration (every key it holds is either not inline or inline with the same value). It fails when the entry overrides one of its keys with a different value: the file’s value is then dead text that a reader of the file alone takes for the config. | .

791.title: A harnessed repository runs its checks on its own pull requests
791.content: Instantiating a harness in a repository includes turning its checks on there, through one reusable workflow the harness owns, never a copy per repository, so a layer is judged on its own pull requests and not only when an index re-pins it. Switching off a repository’s builds must not switch off its gates. The workflow is the tools layer’s .github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml. A repository calls it from a workflow of about fifteen lines that runs on pull_request: . jobs: checks: uses: <owner>/<tools-layer>/.github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml@main with: mode: layer # or `index`: the repository is its own index instance: <instance> # layer mode: its directory in the folio-assistant index path-in-repo: <instance> # where the instance sits in the repository ('.' at the root) . | layer mode is for a repository that an index mounts, such as cat-harness or the DAK layer. The workflow checks out folio-assistant and puts the PR in place of the locked mount. | index mode is for a repository that is its own index: an IG repository over the DAK layer, smart-ra, or a folio. Its own index.lock.json is replayed. | The gates are the harness’s graph checks over the repository’s own instance, plus every check:* / *:check script of that instance and its whole dependency harness (its transitive needs). Each is named <owning-instance>:<script>. | A PR fails only on what it newly breaks. Each gate and test runs on main and on the PR. Anything already red on main is listed, never hidden, and never counted against the PR. | . A layer PR that declares a new directory is red on two index gates it cannot clear. The index README lists every declared directory, so the PR leaves index:render:check and readme:sync:root:check stale, and only the index re-pin that takes the PR regenerates the README. Read those two as expected when they are the only new failures, and run them green in the index re-pin instead. Disabling a repository’s automatic builds is not disabling its checks. When an IG repository’s automatic gh-pages or IG Publisher triggers are switched off (the onboarding question in the FHIR IG layer’s ig-build-pipeline), the harness caller stays on.

792.title: The exemptions of the index’s own workflows
792.content: .github/workflows/ belongs to the index, so the steps CI runs there that the local gate set does not are exempted HERE, under gateExemptions.steps, each with a kind and a reason (GateExemptionsSchema, the same shape an instance declaration carries). They land in the same change as the workflow step, never ahead of it in a layer: an exemption for a step CI does not yet run matches nothing, and gates-workflows.test.ts refuses a stale exemption as it refuses an unclassified step. "gateExemptions": { "steps": [ { "match": "bun run cat state:push -- --id health", "kind": "ci-only", "reason": "…" } ] } . An instance still exempts its OWN scripts and steps in its own declaration.

793.title: index.lock.json, and the legacy name
793.content: The lock records what the declared mounts resolved to. It is generated by mount:remote and kept as a separate file. The legacy name is <root-instance>.mount-lock.json. The rules for each reader and writer: . | Writers write index.lock.json. mount:remote first renames a legacy lock onto the new name, so the old file is moved, never dropped. | Readers take index.lock.json first, then fall back to the legacy *.mount-lock.json, so downstream folios and old branches still replay. The readers are: . | mount-from-lock.ts | mountedInstanceRoots | mountedUnder in git-corpus.ts | mount:remote:check | . | Both files present is an error that names both. Two locks are never merged. | . mount-from-lock.ts imports only node:*, so it restates the rule inline and its test holds it to lockFilesIn.

794.title: The reserved index stem
794.content: index.config.json ends in .config.json, so a scan that treats “each root *.config.json is a harness” would find a harness called index. The index stem is therefore reserved across the board: . | rootConfigStems skips every index.* file. It is the one root scan; every other reader calls it or instantiatedHarnessNames. | findDeclarationFile skips every index.* file too. | The index schema refuses an instance named index, and hub, because that is the landing keyword. | . Do not add another copy of the scan: a new copy is how the reserved name leaks back in.

795.title: The generated .gitignore block
795.content: # BEGIN index mounts (generated from index.config.json — do not edit) /my-ig/ # END index mounts . The block holds one /<path>/ line per remote instance in the index, where the path is overrides.<name>.path, else <name>/. After those it lists every further instance root the lock records, because a mount’s closure can land instances that the index never names. Three things write the block: . | mount:remote | writeDeclaredMounts | index-config:migrate --write | . check:index-ignores fails when the block is missing or disagrees with the index. When an index exists, mount:remote does not append to .git/info/exclude: a local exclude rule is invisible to every other clone, so a path the committed block does not cover is reported as not ignored. Without an index, it still appends there.

796.title: Converting a checkout: index-config:migrate
796.content: bun run cat index-config:migrate # print the index it would write, and its findings bun run cat index-config:migrate --write # write it; move remoteMounts; write the block; rename the lock bun run cat index-config:migrate --check # exit 1 when --write would change anything (a gate here) bun run cat index-config:migrate --inline --write # also fold each <name>.config.json into its entry, and delete it bun run cat index-config:inline:check # exit 1 while any imported <name>.config.json remains bun run cat index-config:migrate --root <clone> # a separated repository's standalone checkout . The converter reads only the files under --root, so it runs on a standalone clone of any separated repository. | Which root configs it imports: a root <name>.config.json is imported only when name is an instance the checkout declares (at the root or one level down) or mounts. Anything else becomes an unmatched-config finding and is not imported. A repository cut from a fork, for example, can carry the fork’s own <fork>.config.json; importing it would instantiate a harness the repository does not hold. | Re-runs: it is idempotent. A re-run moves only the remoteMounts entries that the declaration has gained since the last run. An entry the index already holds identically is dropped from the declaration. An entry the index holds differently throws, and you reconcile it by hand. | .

Scroll horizontally to see all columns → . | locale | catalogues / templatesQ1: availability | entriesQ2: strings | translated | fuzzy | untranslated | officialQ3: signed off | . | ar Arabic | 6 / 3716.2% · view files → | 361 | 361100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | es Spanish | 6 / 3716.2% · view files → | 346 | 346100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | fr French | 6 / 3716.2% · view files → | 346 | 346100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | ru Russian | 6 / 3716.2% · view files → | 346 | 346100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | zh Chinese | 6 / 3716.2% · view files → | 361 | 35999.4% | 2 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

1196.title: Glossary
1196.content: Derived: every term this instance's swimlanes define — the role's title and description, the lane names that bind it, and whether the term has been retired. This is an index, not the documentation. It says what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a process is for, when you would be in it, and what it is not, is authored beside it and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. Filter this table | Artefact | What it declares about itself | . | Activity logglossary-ledger.json | The agent activity log. A MECHANICAL role: it is written to at task start and task end, and emptied by an actor — one entry, all of them, or on a periodic sweep — and it decides nothing. Modelled on work-plan and corpus, the two existing stores; its skill is the contract it is held to. Its entries are held in the instance's unpublished store and never reach a published graph; the activity-log skill names the location, which is deliberately not repeated here because a role description IS published.notation role/logfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Actorbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_LogMessage/lane/Lane_Actorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Adjudicatorglossary-ledger.json | Settles a criterion whose reviewer entries disagree, and records WHY. Inherits reviewer because an adjudicator is a reviewer with one added entitlement — the adjudication permission — and the separation is the point: a reviewer reports, an adjudicator settles, and a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. The KNOWLEDGE spreads (several roles carry the adjudication skill, because each has to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint); the ENTITLEMENT does not, and lives on the actor as a permission.notation role/adjudicatorfirst seen 2026-09-22status current | . | Administratorglossary-ledger.json | Administers the role graph itself: who exists, what they may act as, and what they may do. The ONE lane whose activities change the substrate every other diagram's lanes bind to — which is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit. Declared 2026-09-20 on the owner's answer that administration is a swimlane; role-model.md's rule is that a role is never invented to make a diagram drawable, so it waited for that.notation role/administratorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_HumanAgentDiscussion/lane/Lane_Agentfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | Archimateglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/archimatefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Attestation serviceglossary-ledger.json | Signs a QA report's run hashes over an API. A MECHANICAL role, and the one that DISAPPEARS when the actor performing it cannot reach out — which is why the signing process carries a second, human lane rather than a retry.notation role/attestation-servicefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Attestationsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/attestationsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Authorglossary-ledger.json | Writes and revises folio content. The position, not the person: an editor and a guideline developer both act as author when they are changing a block.notation role/authorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | The session agent doing the work. The broadest skill set here, and the one whose membership most needs auditing.notation role/authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring Committeeglossary-ledger.json | The people writing a document with its editor, while it is still a working draft: contributors who give feedback through the Contributor Feedback sheet, one change set per row, in their own Blue column. They recommend; an Editor decides, through the sheet's Ready columns. Added 2026-10-31 by the owner, so the drafting sheet names a process role rather than a job title, as the public-comment sheet names the Feedback Review Committee. 1272.title: auto-docs index
1272.content: Derived documentation over a declared sub-graph. Each entry below is generated from the repository on every build, so it is what the tree actually holds rather than what anybody remembered. These are indexes, not the documentation. They say what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a thing is for, when you would reach for it, and what it is not, is authored beside them and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. | Decisions …every DMN decision table a declared `processes` graph holds, with the decision's own name | Docs …every AUTHORED documentation page an instance publishes, with the title and description its own front matter declares | Processes …every BPMN process, with its own documentation, its lanes, and the skills its activities name | Roles …every role a declared `scenarios` graph defines, with the description it declares | Schemas …every schema module a declared `schemas` directory holds, with the first sentence of its module docblock | Skills …every skill markdown file, with the description it declares in its own front matter | Tasks …every named activity in a declared `processes` graph — task, user, service, manual, script and call activities | Tools …every Tool module a declared `tools` directory holds, with the first sentence of its module docblock | .

1276.doc: The catalogue, as a graph — who-iris
1276.title: The catalogue, as a graph
1276.content: The replica pages show what IRIS looks like. This one shows what this catalogue knows — and, more usefully, what it records that it does not know. The gap is the point, not a backlog. This instance models 235 node(s) against 273,559 items across 1,057,223 files upstream. Cataloguing by reference means recording that something exists without holding it, so a small number here is the design rather than a shortfall.

1281.title: Verifiable AI Guideline Evaluation: Multi-Measurement Debiased Inference, Peer Councils, and Hybrid Bounds
1281.content: Adopted 2026-10-08 (work item folio-assistant-tn3d, issue #2513). Expanded with UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) public health benchmark evidence and recommendation discrepancy analysis. All eight foundational sources were ingested into library/ and verified before this methodology was adopted.

1282.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1282.title: 1. The Load-Bearing Idea, in One Sentence
1282.content: Clinical AI cannot be verified by uncalibrated model self-grading or exhaustive expert inspection: rigorous evaluation without gold standards requires decomposing multi-model error covariances, conditioning on document complexity, anchoring against known benchmark fragments, verifying decision logic on-manifold, and gating recommendation discrepancies through structured DAK decision models before executable code generation.

1283.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1283.title: 2. The Methodological Quadriad
1283.content:
Traditional evaluation paradigms fail in healthcare guidelines: . | Naive Gold Standards do not exist for newly authored guidelines (e.g. HIV PrEP L2/L3), while historical guidelines (e.g. Immunization) contain real-world conflicting statements across publication years. | Uncalibrated LLM-as-a-Judge suffers from cardinal rating drift (one rater’s “8” is another’s “6”), peer collusion, and shared prompt/inductive biases. | The Recognition vs Generation Illusion: UKHSA’s PubHealthBench (arXiv:2505.06046v4) demonstrates that while frontier models achieve >90% on Multiple Choice Question Answering (MCQA), their generative accuracy collapses to 57–74% in free-form clinical guidance advice. Direct generative authoring from narrative L1 prose into executable L3 logic is therefore inherently hazardous. | Exhaustive Human SME Review is economically impossible: WHO clinical panels cannot manually verify thousands of generated CQL lines, FHIR StructureDefinitions, and decision logic rows. | . This methodology combines four rigorous statistical and empirical pillars into an integrated evaluation engine: . flowchart TD subgraph "Pillar I: Information Limits & Noise Disentanglement" CRB["CRB Upper Bounds
