2986.title: NPM Knowledge Graph Distribution
2986.content: Skill npm-kg-distribution: Package, release, distribute, and retrieve Knowledge Graphs using npm tooling and tarballs: declare package.json as an authored pre-packaging asset in the Knowledge Graph, build .tgz packages via bun pm pack, record publications as folio-binary-release/v1 state documents hosted on GitHub binary releases, and retrieve remote Knowledge Graphs using npm install for both unhydrated source graph and hydrated materialized graph views. Named by: Mount a declared subgraph . Knowledge Graphs in the folio ecosystem can be distributed and consumed as npm packages — packaged tarballs (.tgz) containing either the authored source graphs, pre-compiled hydrated graph views, or both. |   | where | . | the packaging tool | pack-tarball (bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts) | . | the retrieval tool | kg-retrieve-npm (bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts) | . | the release schema | schemas/sdlc/binary-release.ts (folio-binary-release/v1) | . | asset verification | cat-harness-tools/scripts/check-declared-assets.ts | . | related skills | remote-mount, kg-export, package-release, kg-subscription | .

2987.title: 1. package.json as an authored pre-packaging asset in the KG
2987.content: A file that is not declared in <instance>.json is a file no check verifies, so package.json is declared as an authored Knowledge Graph asset that defines package identity, exports, dependencies, scripts, and the tarball inclusion whitelist (files array). Each instance that publishes an npm package declares package.json under assets in its <instance>.json: . { "id": "npm-manifest", "src": "package.json", "role": "package-manifest", "title": "package.json", "description": "The npm pre-packaging source manifest declaring package identity, exports, dependencies, scripts, and tarball whitelist." } . Why declare it under assets . | Verification at commit and mount time: check:declared-assets verifies that every declared asset exists on disk. | Remote mount resolution: remote-mount.ts and mount-from-lock.ts check out, lay down, and verify declared instance assets so that mounted dependencies carry their package identity. | Single source of packaging truth: package.json’s files field acts as the authoritative whitelist for what is bundled into the distribution tarball. | .

2988.title: 2. Packaging via bun pm pack & folio-binary-release/v1
2988.content: An npm package is built as a compressed tarball (.tgz) using bun pm pack: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts --root <instance-root> --destination <out-dir> . The packaging process: . | Reads the authored package.json to verify package identity (name and version). | Invokes bun pm pack --destination <dir>, which respects .npmignore and the files array in package.json. | Computes the exact file size in bytes and the SHA-256 digest of the .tgz tarball. | Generates and validates a folio-binary-release/v1 state node recording the release event. | . The folio-binary-release/v1 state node . A published tarball is represented in the Knowledge Graph as a folio-binary-release/v1 document (schemas/sdlc/binary-release.ts). A release record captures the publication event, never the binary payload itself: . { "$schema": "folio-binary-release/v1", "release": { "id": "cat-harness-v1.0.0", "version": "1.0.0", "tag": "v1.0.0", "publishedAt": "2026-10-08T18:30:00.000Z", "url": "https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/releases/tag/v1.0.0" }, "origin": { "kind": "github-release", "repository": "litlfred/cat-harness" }, "assets": [ { "name": "cat-harness-1.0.0.tgz", "bytes": 524288, "digest": { "algorithm": "sha256", "digest": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855", "verifiedAt": "2026-10-08T18:30:00.000Z" }, "fetchedFrom": "https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/releases/download/v1.0.0/cat-harness-1.0.0.tgz", "contentType": "application/gzip", "disposition": "published" } ] } . Key invariants: . | Never the bytes: The schema is .strict(). Content and blobs are rejected. | Verifiable fixity: SHA-256 digests and byte counts are required. | Provenance: fetchedFrom must state where the binary can be retrieved. | Dispositions: An asset’s state after publication is tracked (published, superseded, deleted-before-deploy). Any deliberate removal must provide a dispositionReason. | .

2989.title: 3. GitHub binary releases hosting .tgz tarballs
2989.content: Published Knowledge Graph tarballs are hosted on GitHub Releases: . | The git tag (v<version>) marks the exact source commit in the repository. | The .tgz package is uploaded as a release asset attached to the GitHub release. | The release URL follows the canonical scheme: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/v<version>/<package>-<version>.tgz | . This provides: . | High availability via CDN. | Immutability tied to the release tag. | Checkable fixity against the folio-binary-release/v1 document. | .

2990.title: 4. npm install as an alternative retrieval Tool for remote KGs
2990.content: Remote Knowledge Graphs can be retrieved into a workspace or consumer environment through three distinct mechanisms, each serving a specific architectural need: . | tool / mechanism | transport | granularity | best when | . | remote-mount | Git shallow blobless fetch at 40-char SHA | Transitive dependency closure of declared directories | Developing against dependencies whose TypeScript/code is imported directly | . | kg:subscribe | Substrate snapshot via HTTP | Selective subgraphs and on-demand assets through 5 gates | Consuming large external reference datasets (WHO IRIS, FHIR) | . | kg-retrieve-npm (npm install) | NPM package tarball (.tgz) via registry or GitHub release | Pre-packaged bundle with whitelisted files and optional pre-built views | Distributing versioned Knowledge Graph packages with immediate consumption | . Unhydrated source graph vs. Hydrated materialized graph views . When an npm package distributes a Knowledge Graph, it can provide two distinct graph views: . 1. Unhydrated source graph view . The authored source files as they exist in the repository: . | package.json pre-packaging manifest. | <instance>.json instance declaration. | Authored source directories: skills/ (markdown instructions), schemas/ (Zod/TS definitions), processes/ (BPMN diagrams), methodologies/, text-based metadata. | Binary media assets excluded: PNGs, JPGs, PDFs and figures under library/ and uploads/ are excluded via .npmignore during unhydrated packaging, keeping the base package compact (~2-5 MB). | Packaged as <package>-<version>.tgz. | Ideal for agents and developers authoring new knowledge, extending skills, or compiling the graph locally. | . 2. Hydrated materialized graph view . The complete, materialized Knowledge Graph artifacts and binary assets: . | Binary media assets included: Losslessly optimized library PNGs, figures, and covers. | Named subgraph JSON-LD (docs/subgraph/<instance>/<path>/index.jsonld). | Fully dereferenced hydrated JSON-LD (index.hydrated.jsonld). | Metadata indexes, RDF N-Quads, and pre-computed search indices. | Packaged via pack-tarball --hydrated as <package>-<version>.hydrated.tgz. | Ideal for read-only consumers, visualizers, semantic search engines, and portal deployments that require immediate access without installing compilation toolchains or running offline export pipelines. | . 3. The subgraph index package — one per pin . A third, narrow package carries a pin’s subgraph index files and nothing else: <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>, built by the subgraph-index-package Tool through pack-tarball and released as subgraph-index-<sha> on every push to main. A hydrated remote mount reads it; see remote-mount §”Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package”. Using kg-retrieve-npm . To retrieve and inspect a remote Knowledge Graph tarball or package: . # Retrieve and inspect both graph views from a tarball bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz # Retrieve and verify integrity against a folio-binary-release/v1 document bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --release path/to/release.json # Retrieve only the unhydrated source graph view into a target directory bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --view unhydrated --destination ./deps/my-kg # Retrieve only the hydrated materialized graph view bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --view hydrated --destination ./static-kg . When verified against a folio-binary-release/v1 document, any mismatch in byte size or SHA-256 digest immediately refuses the package, preventing corrupted or tampered graph data from entering the consumer environment.

2992.title: W3C N-Quads Dataset Packaging & Subgraph Distribution
2992.content: Skill nquads-distribution: How to compile, partition by named subgraphs, and distribute W3C N-Quads datasets beside pre-compiled SPARQL 1.1 named queries for static edge and client-side querying. Enforces upstream skolemization for zero blank nodes, partition size budgets, and single-source-of-truth publishing via declared served directories. Named by: Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . This skill governs the compilation, subgraph partitioning, packaging, and distribution of RDF datasets formatted as W3C N-Quads (application/n-quads) paired with audited, pre-compiled SPARQL 1.1 named queries. It provides a single source of truth across CLI, MCP tools, and static client-side web applications, enabling sub-second multi-graph query evaluation without running dynamic database servers.

2993.title: 1. Architectural Principles
2993.content: 1.1 W3C N-Quads Standards Conformance . | Specification: Conforms strictly to W3C RDF 1.1 N-Quads (w3c-n-quads). | Format: Line-based statement serialization: subject predicate object graphLabel? . | Zero Engine Lock-in: Oxigraph is the execution engine; the data format is strictly vendor-neutral W3C RDF. Any conforming triplestore/quadstore (Jena, Comunica, GraphDB) can consume these files directly. | . 1.2 Upstream Skolemization (Zero Blank Nodes) . | Blank nodes (_:b0) clobber each other across distributed documents and cannot be referenced across partitions. | Rule: Every compound node (e.g. Dublin Core qualified statements, MeSH authorities, work item notes) must be deterministically skolemized at intake into a stable URI: https://<domain>/entity/<id>#<property>_<index>. | Invariant: The dataset contains zero blank nodes (_:). | . 1.3 2-Tier Subgraph Partitioning . To prevent browser V8 heap exhaustion on edge devices, datasets are never delivered as a single monolithic multi-gigabyte dump. They are partitioned into two tiers: . | Tier 1: Global Routing Spine (<dataset>/spine): . | Contains the top-level hierarchy, IDs, titles, primary categories, and access gate verdicts. | Target payload: < 50 KB gzipped. Loaded instantly on application bootstrap. | . | Tier 2: Subgraph Partitions (<dataset>/subgraph/<id>): . | Contains detailed entity graphs (e.g. full Dublin Core metadata per DSpace community, or historical task audit logs). | Loaded additively and on demand when an agent or user accesses that domain. | . | . 1.4 Partition Size Budget . | Budget Ceiling: No partition may exceed 50,000 quads or 5 MB gzipped (enforced by MAX_RECOMMENDED_PARTITION_BYTES in schemas/kg/nquads-distribution.ts). | Protects mobile Safari and Chromium from OOM crashes during WASM decompression. | . 1.5 Git Hygiene: No Binaries in Repo . | Compiled .nq and .nq.gz files are never committed to Git. | They are generated during CI build or local execution into an ephemeral output directory, and served to GitHub Pages via mount-instance-docs through "served": true. | .

2994.title: 2. Checkable Requirements
2994.content: | # | Requirement | Why, in one line | . | NQ-1 | Strict W3C N-Quads Compliance | Prevents proprietary dialect lock-in; interoperable with any RDF store | . | NQ-2 | Zero Blank Nodes via Deterministic Minting | Blank nodes collide across document boundaries; stable URIs join cleanly | . | NQ-3 | Zero Binary Bytes in Quads | Keeps the graph lightweight; PDFs/images live in static CDN storage | . | NQ-4 | Partition Budget Cap (< 5 MB gzipped / 50k quads) | Prevents V8 heap exhaustion on mobile and edge devices | . | NQ-5 | Topology Manifest (subgraph-manifest.json) | Informs clients of partition quad counts, item counts, and relative URLs | . | NQ-6 | Pre-compiled Named Queries (queries.json) | Replaces arbitrary runtime queries with audited, injection-proof SPARQL | . | NQ-7 | Served via Instance Declaration (served: true) | mount-instance-docs.ts publishes files to _site/ without manual copy steps | . | NQ-8 | Single Source of Truth | CLI, MCP tools, and web browsers consume the exact same .nq.gz files | .

2995.title: 3. Concrete Implementations
2995.content: Implementation A: Document Repository Library Catalogue . | Compiler: scripts/build-oxigraph.ts | Spine Graph: <https://example.org/graph/spine> $\to$ catalogue-spine.nq.gz (communities, collections, handles, titles, copyright gates). | Subgraph Partitions: <https://example.org/graph/community/{id}> $\to$ community_{id}.nq.gz (Qualified Dublin Core, descriptors, spatial coverage). | Queries: search_by_mesh, filter_by_community, licensed_bitstreams. | Declared Served Directory: dist/oxigraph/ with "served": true in instance configuration. | . Implementation B: Folio Assistant Beans Work Plan . | Compiler: cat-harness-tools/scripts/beans-query.ts | Spine Graph: <https://folio-assistant.org/graph/beans> $\to$ beans-spine.nq.gz (every work item with its ID, status, parents, and dependency edges). | Subgraph Partitions: <https://folio-assistant.org/graph/beans/claims> $\to$ claims.nq.gz (session claims, burndown history, and audit records). | Queries: safe_drain_candidates, actionable_leaves, critical_path_blockers, rollup_invariant_violations, circular_blockers. | Declared Served Directory: beans/dist/ with "served": true in beans.json. | .

2997.content: Process_NQuadsDistribution · strict · 7 step(s) . Extract, partition, package, and distribute knowledge graph datasets as W3C RDF 1.1 N-Quads with pre-compiled named SPARQL queries. Governed by skills nquads-distribution and named-query-execution, grounded in schemas/kg/nquads-distribution.ts. CRITICAL INVARIANTS: . | 2-TIER SUBGRAPH ARCHITECTURE: A lightweight Spine backbone partition is loaded on startup, while bulky subgraphs (communities, workflow domains) are lazily fetched on demand. | UPSTREAM SKOLEMIZATION: Zero blank nodes across all partitions. Every node must carry a deterministic minted IRI. | PARTITION BUDGET CEILING: Partitions must strictly stay under 5 MB gzipped / 50k quads to protect browser heap and memory allocations. | GRAPH AVAILABILITY GUARD: Queries declare requiredSubgraphs; execution fails fast with MissingPartitionError rather than silently returning partial query results. | NO COMMITTED BINARY PAYLOADS: .nq.gz distribution payloads are gitignored, generated on demand or in CI, and served to Pages via ‘served: true’. | . i i i i i i i

3008.title: Inline PDF viewer — a pinned pdf.js, installed at build time
3008.content: Skill pdf-inline-viewer: Show a published PDF inside a generated page — search, scroll, jump to page, print and download — with the pinned pdf.js viewer the site build installs. Which two Tools do it, the publication-gate rule that decides whether a page may embed a document at all, why the viewer opens only allowlisted hosts, and the three pdf.js behaviours that were measured rather than assumed. Read before putting a PDF on a page, before bumping the pdf.js pin, and when an embedded viewer shows an empty frame. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Skill id: pdf-inline-viewer · Package: ui-core · Tools pdf-viewer-install, pdf-viewer-embed · Code cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-viewer.ts . A lightweight inline viewer for PDFs on a CDN: search, scroll, jump to page, print and download. pdf.js is copied onto the built site (not loaded from a CDN) and loaded lazily.

3009.title: The two acts, and which Tool does each
3009.content: | act | who does it | Tool | . | put the viewer into a built site | the site workflow, once per build | pdf-viewer-install | . | show one PDF on one page | a page generator, once per page | pdf-viewer-embed (TypeScript: embed() from pdf-viewer.ts) | . docs-site.yml and feature-staging.yml both run the install right after mount-instance-docs.ts, passing --allow for the repository owner’s cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/<owner>/ and raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/. Nothing of pdf.js is committed. The viewer lives at <site root>/assets/vendor/pdfjs/ in the built site only.

3010.title: May this page embed this document? The publication gate decides, not you
3010.content: An embed is a link that also renders. So it follows the same rule as the download link: if the bitstream’s publication gates (copyright, restrictions) are not permitted, the page gets no viewer: the embed returns nothing whenever the download link would be withheld, and the page says only “held here, not published”. Never embed a document to “just preview” it. A preview is publication.

3011.title: Why the viewer opens only allowlisted hosts
3011.content: The pdf.js generic viewer refuses a cross-origin ?file=. That is validateFileURL, whose error is “file origin does not match viewer’s”. It refuses so that a hosted viewer cannot be pointed at any document and lend it the host’s address. Our PDFs are on a CDN, not on Pages, so the build adds a shim (folio-open.js) that opens ?src= instead. It opens a URL only when the URL starts with an --allow prefix, or is on the viewer’s own origin. Anything else is refused on screen and never fetched. | A prefix is a prefix, not a substring. https://evil.example/cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/<owner>/x.pdf is refused, and a unit test pins that. | An empty allowlist is a usage error, not a default. Forgetting --allow would otherwise ship a viewer that refuses every CDN document while the build reports success. Write --allow same-origin-only when that really is what you want. | .

3012.title: Three things measured rather than assumed (pdf.js 6.4.299)
3012.content: All three are listed under binds in the pdfjs entry of upstream-pins.json, so a version bump re-checks them. | The modern build needs a very new browser. It calls Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed. Chromium 140 lacks it, threw during startup and never opened the document. The install uses the legacy build, which carries its own polyfills. | webviewerloaded fires on parent.document when the viewer is framed by a same-origin page, and on its own document only otherwise. An embed on this site is the same-origin case, so a listener on document alone never fires and the frame stays empty. The shim listens on both, and checks detail.source. | defaultUrl is the tracemonkey sample paper. The shim sets it to empty, so a missing or refused ?src= shows an empty viewer rather than somebody else’s document. | .

3013.title: The embed, and what it does when it cannot work
3013.content: . | Site root from the browser. One generated page is served at several depths (/<folio>/, /folio-assistant/<folio>/, /branches/<branch>/<folio>/). The caller passes the route pattern, using the folio-mount.ts convention (group 1 is the root), and the inlined client applies it. A page off the route gets a frame saying so, never a 404 inside the frame. | Lazy. The frame is pointed at the viewer only when it comes within 200px of the viewport. This uses an IntersectionObserver, because how engines treat loading="lazy" on a script-set src varies. A reader who never scrolls there downloads nothing. | Plain links always. “Open the PDF on its own” and “Download” sit under the frame whether or not the viewer works. They are not a fallback that appears on failure. | .

3014.title: Caching: why the frame’s address carries a version tag
3014.content: GitHub Pages serves every file with max-age=600 through a CDN, so a hard reload can still be answered from a copy up to ten minutes old. | The frame’s address ends &v=<rev>.<deploy>. <rev> is VIEWER_REV, a hash of the pinned release, the shim and the patch. <deploy> comes from the host page’s document.lastModified, which Pages sets at deploy time. So the frame is exactly as fresh as the page around it. A reader who sees the new page gets the new viewer. | The shim is fetched as folio-open.js?v=<rev>, so a change to it cannot be masked by a cached copy. | Where a server sends no Last-Modified (a local preview), the browser reports the current time, so the frame is simply never cached there. That is correct, just slower. | . The outer page itself is outside this. If the green staging banner shows an older commit than the deploy, the whole page is a cached copy. Wait out the ten minutes, or use a private window.

3015.title: The site’s own post-build passes leave the viewer alone
3015.content: viewer.html is Mozilla’s markup with one <script> added. minify-site.ts skips it (rewriting it would ship bytes no pdf.js release contains), and check:duplicate-ids and publish-verify’s html-unique-ids count it out of scope, not passed. It declares id="buttons" twice upstream. That finding is real, and nobody here can fix it without forking pdf.js. They ask isVendoredViewer(), so there is one answer to “is this ours”. The two passes that INJECT into every page skip it too. These are the staging banner and the standalone navigation rail; otherwise both draw inside the PDF frame. Any new pass that writes into every *.html in _site owes the same exclusion. standalone-rail.test.ts and pdf-viewer.test.ts each assert it for the existing two.

3016.title: Cost
3016.content: About a 7 MB download per build, adding about 12 MB (404 files) to the built site. The size matters most for staging previews, each of which carries its own copy on gh-pages. bun run cat health reports the size of gh-pages. Nothing is added to a clone.

3017.title: Verifying a change here
3017.content: Unit tests (cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/pdf-viewer.test.ts) run the shipped shim and client against stubs: the allowlist, the parent-document listener, the root derivation at three depths, and lazy loading. They cannot check that pdf.js opens, searches and prints. For that, install into a scratch site with --zip, serve it, and drive it in a browser (see rendered-verification). Check, and screenshot for the author: the page count shows, a search finds matches, the page box jumps, print and download are present, and a narrow viewport does not load the viewer until it is scrolled to.

3018.title: pdf-inline-viewer (skill)
3018.content: The skill pdf-inline-viewer as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/pdf-inline-viewer.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

3019.title: Placement — decide where it goes before you write it
3019.content: Skill placement: Establish where a new node belongs BEFORE you create it — which instance, which declared graph, which kind of node, and which of the two “stub” conventions applies. Read before adding a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision table, schema, tool or content object, and before writing any literal that names one folio. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Code node review, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . One question, answered before the first file exists: . Which instance owns this, which of its declared graphs does it go in, and what kind of node is it? . An agent that starts writing and works the answer out afterwards produces a node in the wrong repository, under a hardcoded path, named by a composed string. All three are silent: the tests pass, and the damage lands on the next consumer. This is a decision procedure. Four steps and a stop. Run it in order; the later steps are meaningless if an earlier one is a guess.

3020.title: Step 1 — which instance?
3020.content: folio-assistant is the platform, not the content. It holds skills, schemas, the pipeline and the MCP server an agent uses to author a folio — a paper, a WHO SMART Guideline, an IG — and the folio lives in a separate repository. Ask of the thing you are about to write: . Does this name, assume, or default to one folio? . A paper directory, a document title, a badge URL, an owner/repo, a Lake library prefix, a workflow filename, a simulator path, a licence block, a vocabulary, a constant with a subject-matter value. If the answer is yes, it does not belong in platform code. There are three destinations, not two, and collapsing the third is the common mistake: . | destination | what goes there | test | . | the platform | the mechanism, parameterised | the same code is correct for every folio | . | the folio’s tree | the subject matter itself | a reader of that folio would look for it | . | the folio’s config | the value the mechanism reads | it varies per folio but platform code needs it | . A value that varies per folio and is consumed by platform code is a config field — <name>.config.json, <name>.json, lakefile.toml — never a literal in a script and never a file the platform has to go and find. A Lake prefix, for example, is read from lakefile.toml, and left unprefixed when no lakefile names one, because a wrong namespace is worse than none. Do not infer the instance from the directory you are standing in. Read the declaration at the repository root, carrying name, stub and directories. basename($PWD) is not an identity — a repo cloned into a differently-named directory resolves to nothing, and reports no config rather than an error.

3021.title: Step 2 — which declared graph, and where does that instance put it?
3021.content: A node’s location is not a path you memorise. Every instance declares the directories it scans in <name>.json, and each entry names the kind of graph it holds — cat-harness (skills, roles, workflows, decisions, requirements, permissions), schemas, tools, qa, beans, folio and the rest. The vocabulary is open. | Ask for a skill, do not open a file. skill_list for what exists here, skill_fetch to load one, work_plan_prime for the work plan. With no MCP, resolve the graph from the declaration (readDeclaration in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) and read the directory it names. | In this repository the skills graph’s path is skills/. That is a fact about this instance, not a convention you may carry to another one. Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. | Overrides match on the entry’s id, never on its path. An instance that sites its knowledge graph elsewhere redeclares the same id with a different path. Matching on path makes two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | Declare only what exists. A declared-but-absent directory is worse than an undeclared one: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. | . Full rules, inheritance order and the three read states: directory-conventions.md. The docs graph, and the filing question it answers . docs is an authorable destination like the others, and the one an agent most often forgets to consider when it derives a destination list: deriving the list is not enough if the derivation drops a declared graph. What goes there: a design-memory asset — something produced while BUILDING, rather than the thing built. kg-contribution-offer carries the one question that identifies the class and why fsh-guts is the tempting wrong answer (its content may be thrown away; a design record’s value is that it survives). WHOSE docs/ comes first, and it is Step 1’s question again. Detailed information, design and planning for a harness, feature or tool go into that harness’s docs/: docs is a declared graph, and the instance that owns the feature owns the record of why it is shaped that way. A feature’s reasoning filed in the wrong instance’s docs/ reads fine and is unreachable from the place that needs it. Then where inside it, which is this skill’s question and not kg-contribution-offer’s: . | the asset is | it files under | . | why a subsystem is shaped as it is — requirements, options, rulings | <instance>/docs/architecture/, with parent: Architecture in the front matter | . | options for a decision not yet taken, with what each costs | <instance>/docs/proposals/, kind: proposal, and a row in its index.md | . | what was FOUND — prior art, a survey, a measurement, a comparison — that informs a decision without proposing one | <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/, kind: research, and a row in its index.md | . | how a person does a task with it | <instance>/docs/guides/ | . | how to REACH a data source the content describes — endpoints, shapes, quirks | <instance>/docs/, beside the subject it serves | . | what a declared thing IS, generated from source | <instance>/docs/reference/ — never hand-edited | . Three rules that catch the usual mistakes: . | A design record is dated and says what it was true OF. It is history, so it carries the commit, PR or issue it describes. A record written in the present tense becomes a claim about today, and goes stale invisibly. | It states what it could NOT establish. A requirement referenced but never defined, a measurement not taken: named as such. A design record that reads complete when it is not is worse than a short one. | It is prose for a person, not instructions for an agent. If you find yourself writing “the agent SHALL”, it is a skill and it is in the wrong graph. | . The line between the two, stated as a test: . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls: real, worth keeping, and none of it needed to act. Both directions fail silently — a skill that swallows them makes every agent read a chapter to find a rule, and a rule filed in docs/ because it arrived with context is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Inheritance . An instance inherits its dependencies’ directories and skills, deepest dependency first and root last so the root wins: declarationChain + resolveDirectories for directories, and resolveSkillDirs in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts for the cross-instance skill overlay. So a skill placed in the platform reaches a downstream folio through its declaration; never copy a skill into the folio, which mints a second copy free to drift.

3022.title: Step 3 — which KIND of node?
3022.content: The axes below are distinct. Ask the separating question; do not pattern-match on what the thing resembles. | you are about to write | ask | the two answers | . | a new content type | does it need different code, or only different rules? | different code → an adapter; only rules → a profile plus a subclass | . | something a participant is or does | must the performer know it, or may the participant do it? | know → a skill, on the lane’s role; do → a permission, on the actor | . | a participant | does it persist across processes, or is it a position inside one? | persists → an actor; a position → a role, which is the BPMN swimlane | . | a sequence of steps | does it have actors, activities and a control flow? | yes → BPMN under the workflows directory, not a Mermaid fence and not prose | . | a branch at a gateway | is the answer computed from facts, or chosen by a person? | computed → a DMN table plus a <cat-harness.processes:decision/> ref; chosen → an ordinary gateway | . | a durable fact for one agent | does it govern, or summarise what governs? | governs → a skill; summarises → a memory entry under the memory nodes | . | subject matter | would a reader of one folio look for it? | yes → the folio, as data — never the platform | . Adapter vs profile is the expensive one. Adapters (paper, dak) partition block kinds into disjoint namespaces, and adapterForKind — what QA-criterion scoping reads — must stay total and unambiguous. Profiles (document, paper) nest: every document kind is also a paper kind. Making document a third adapter would make adapterForKind ambiguous on every shared kind. Actor / role / skill / permission. One sentence carries the model — an actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Permissions stay on the actor: moving them onto Role, which looks right, conflicts wherever a permission is held by some but not all actors sharing a role. Resolution rules, how to bind a lane, and how to add a role: role-model.md. Do not re-derive them here. A .md under the cat-harness path that declares its own $schema is not a skill. The audit walks that directory recursively; declaration beats location, the same contract part-of: carries. Adding a graph typology is a registry change, not a new top-level directory. If nothing in the open vocabulary fits, that is a decision to hand over (Step 5), not one to settle by creating a folder.

3023.title: Step 4 — which stub? There are two, and they are unrelated
3023.content: This is the step most often skipped, because “stub” reads as one word. The agent-file stub — a pointer, never a home . AGENTS.md is the agent-generic source of truth. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are thin stubs whose entire content is a pointer to it; scripts/init-folio.ts writes all three for a new folio. | Never put guidance in a stub. It reaches one tool’s agents and nobody else, and the other two stubs are then quietly wrong. | And prefer not to put it in AGENTS.md either. That file’s own banner says it: it is a bootstrap pointer, and the discipline lives in the skills graph. A rule that exists only in AGENTS.md is not in the generated reference, not in the published skill docs, and not found by an agent that went looking for the skill first. | . So: new guidance is a skill. Add a pointer from AGENTS.md if it needs one, and register the skill in its package manifest. The artefact stub — resolve it, never compose it . The declaration carries stub, the filename stem of every artefact this instance publishes. artefactStub() is the one function that answers it (stub when declared, otherwise name), and renderingPath() / siteDir() derive the published paths from it: . <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld <base>/<name>/<stub>.json <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json <base>/<stub>/ docs/<stub>/ . The graph document is under the instance’s own directory, the host’s included: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document (instance-publication §”Which base an @id is minted against”). Compose nothing; resolve everything. A hand-written path such as /kg/ 404s, because the real path comes out of renderingPath. A naive guess is not merely fragile, it is wrong on real instances. WHO’s SMART Base IG publishes under a stub shorter than its repository name, so “the stub is the repo name” fails on the reference implementation the convention was modelled on. The declaration file itself is NOT stub-named: it is <name>.json, found by findDeclarationFile() matching a file’s stem to its own name. Everything it describes is named after the stub, because by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration that names them.

3024.title: Step 5 — when you cannot tell, stop and ask
3024.content: Placement has three states, like everything else here: determined, determined-empty (this instance genuinely has no such directory — a real answer), and could-not-determine. The third is never to be rendered as the first. Do not guess and do not pick the repository you happen to be standing in. A misplaced node is not a typo: it is a second copy of something, free to drift, that a later agent will find and believe. Hand the decision over the way interaction-modality.md §4.1 requires — context → options with what each costs → your recommendation, marked → what happens if they say nothing → the question. The test is one pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . Every identifier expanded on first use. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. I need to place <thing>, which <one sentence on what it does>. Two candidates: A. <instance/graph> — costs <what this makes harder, concretely> B. <instance/graph> — costs <…> Recommend B, because <the property that decides it>. If you say nothing I will do B and note it in the PR body. A or B? .

3025.title: The worked failure this skill exists to prevent
3025.content: A platform script that writes a whole README holding one folio’s title, badges and licence destroys the README of every other folio it runs in, because prose about a folio belongs to that folio. Every step above catches it: Step 1, the content names one folio; Step 2, a helper path is composed rather than resolved; Step 4, published paths are built by convention and checked against nothing. The pattern that replaces it: the folio owns the file; the platform owns the markers, and writes a section only where the README carries its marker pair (readme-sections).

3026.title: Checklist
3026.content: Before you create a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision, schema, tool or content object: . | Instance — platform, folio, or the folio’s config? Does anything in it name one folio? | Graph — which declared entry, resolved from <name>.json by id? Not a path you remember. | Kind — which side of the separating question in Step 3, and can you say why in one sentence? | Stub — if it is guidance, is it a skill rather than a stub or AGENTS.md? If it publishes, does every path come from artefactStub() / renderingPath()? | Registered — bun run cat skill:register (skill-registration), and bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts run, so the published mirror is not stale. | Could not determine? Stop. Ask in the Step 5 frame. Do not default to the repo you are in. | .

3027.title: placement (skill)
3027.content: The skill placement as its source file cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/placement.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

3028.title: Process state — the task you are in, inside the process you are running
3028.content: Skill process-state: Track where you are inside a running process — which task, in which swimlane, under which role — and recover deliberately when you find yourself outside it. Read before completing a workflow step, and whenever something unexpected interrupts one. Covers what to do about notes and stickies you re-anchored while off-process, which leave no trace in the artefact. Named by: Hand back to the discussion . An agent working a BPMN process holds nested state: a task, inside a process instance, under a role that owns a swimlane. Losing track of the outer level while still acting on the inner one looks like ordinary work and produces changes nobody authorised.

3029.title: The three levels, and what each one answers
3029.content: | level | answers | where it lives | . | process instance | which run of which process is this? | beans/workflows/ (workflow-state graph in work-plan-store) | . | swimlane / role | am I the actor who may do this? | the lane on the activity; checked by the executor (task-authorization) | . | task | which step am I on, and is it enabled? | workflow_next | . workflow_next reports what is enabled now, which lane owns it, and which skill implements it. workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. Those two are the ground truth; your memory of where you were is not. Name yourself when you complete a step. Pass actor as a declared actor id, not a free-text name: workflow_complete checks that actor against the lane’s role and the ODRL policies before recording anything, refuses a role mismatch or a deny, and writes the verdict into the history. An actor you type is recorded as asserted, not authenticated. Say so rather than presenting it as identity. workflow_gate takes the same actor and target, so ask it before doing the work (task-authorization). The history is checked again afterwards. bun run cat prov:qaqc turns every instance’s history into a W3C PROV-O log and re-runs the same check on each step; claude or a login in actor, rather than a declared actor id, shows up there as undeclared-actor. It is advisory: the findings are listed on the /prov-qaqc/ page, and CI fails only when that page is stale (task-authorization §”The after-check”).

3030.title: Say which process you are in — every turn
3030.content: Claiming a work item says what you are working on. This says where in the process you are working, which is the question a reader cannot answer from an id. Name the process, the lane and the task, and say when you switch: . Process: crdm-requirements, Agent lane · Phase 6 — implement. Completed A_Implement; next is A_Summary. The engine’s “what is enabled now” call (workflow_next) reports the enabled step, the lane that owns it, and the skill that implements it. Say which permission you are acting under. Entering a task in a lane means performing it as that lane’s role, and that needs an ODRL rule that permits it there (permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts: the actor, the action, and the process, task and role as scope). If the answer is unknown or deny, you are out of process for that task: route it to a lane whose actor holds the permission, or stop and ask. The engine enforces this before the task at the deterministic end of the spectrum; at the agentic end nothing stops you, and the QA/QC report over the PROV-O record finds it afterwards (agentic-harness.html#bpmn-execution). Switching processes is the case that matters. Moving between processes changes who is accountable for the next step and which gates apply, and a reader who does not know you switched will assume the old lane’s rules still hold. Naming it is not the same as recording it (advisory) . A turn that is in a process has an INSTANCE under the declared workflow-state graph. Naming the process in prose is the report; the recorded instance in the work-plan store is the evidence. Without recorded instances, a reviewer sweeping a window of merged work cannot classify a single session by lane. workflow_start creates it, workflow_next and workflow_complete advance it, and the state lives in the work-plan store precisely so a sibling session reads the same position — workflow-state.md §”Where running instances live”. Opening or claiming a work item for a process step means starting or resuming its workflow instance: . | Claiming or starting work in a process (code-change-review, merge-train, crdm-requirements, etc.): start an instance with workflow_start passing bean: "<id>" (CLI: bun run cat workflow:start --process <process> --subject <subject> --bean <id>), or resume the running instance that already names that work item. workflow_start writes the process:<Process_Id> tag and Workflow: backlink onto the work item so the visualiser can place the work item on its current BPMN step. | Advancing through tasks: call workflow_complete (bun run cat workflow:complete --id <instance> --task <node> --actor <actor>) as each step finishes so the token moves with the work. | Closing the work item: complete the final step so the workflow instance reaches status: "completed". If a work item is closed (completed or scrapped) while its workflow instance still sits running, run bun run cat workflow:instances --sweep to close stale instances while preserving their history and PROV-O trail (cat-harness#988). | . The session-start sweep reads the work-plan store and reports “no instance recorded” as a FINDING, not as silence, when the directory holds none. A finding is not a failure — plenty of turns are legitimately outside any process — it is the prompt to say which. This rule is ADVISORY: nothing gates on it. Record the instance when the turn is in a process, but no check refuses a merge without one, and none should be added without a new ruling from the owner. It is labelled advisory because a rule called STRICT that nothing enforces teaches readers that the word is decoration, including where it is enforced. The gap is computed, never quoted, because a count written down goes stale with nothing to say so. bun run cat workflow:instances prints today’s count: instances recorded, instances started since the rule, first-parent merges in the same window, running instances whose work item is closed or missing from the store (staleInstances), in-progress work items carrying a process:<id> tag with no running instance (untrackedProcessBeans), and the CI workflows that read the graph. Merges are an upper bound on the instances owed, since a steward’s train, a docs-only fix or a revert may have none. The command reports the gap and exits 0 by default (--strict exits 1 on stale or untracked process work items; --sweep closes running instances whose work item is completed, scrapped, or missing); only a count it cannot make (store unmounted, shallow clone, an undatable instance) exits 2. Arriving without the sweep — a mid-session clone, a project thread . A session that clones a harness repository after it started has no route to this skill: . | the sweep above runs from .claude/hooks/session-start.sh, and a hook runs only when the repository is there at session start; | the workflow_* and skill_fetch tools come from the folio-assistant MCP server (.mcp.json), which starts with the session, so a mid-session clone has neither; | the repository’s CLAUDE.md reaches the agent only once the clone is registered. | . So, when you clone a harness repository after the session started: . | Register it if the platform offers that (Claude Code on the web: register_repo_root), so its CLAUDE.md and skills load. | Run the sweep by hand, from the checkout root: bash .claude/hooks/session-start.sh. It lays the mounts down and prints ## Running processes, the prompt this section depends on. | Name the process before the first edit. A code fix in a layer is sdlc/code-change-review; a repin is sdlc/upstream-version-adoption; a preview is sdlc/feature-staging. A delivery is delivery-summary plus the deep-link rule in staging-review. | With no workflow_* tools, say so. “Process X, not recorded: this session has no workflow engine” is the true third state. Never write it as recorded, and never leave it out. | . A coordinator that briefs a thread (a project’s coordinator session, a swarm lead, anything that spawns an agent) puts the process, or “none”, the governing skill and the repository in the brief. A spawned thread starts with nothing else that would tell it, and the coordinator’s own memory holds no process rules by design. When the brief is written during a live discussion with a person, it also names the discussion: who is talking with the person, how to reach them, the standing card rules, and any feedback channel in play (a review sheet’s id and tab, an issue). That is definitions.discussion of the hand-back-to-discussion input schema, and it is what lets the thread hand its cards, questions and results back instead of leaving them in its own channel.

3031.title: How to tell you are out of process
3031.content: You are outside the process if any of these is true, and each is cheap to check: . | workflow_complete refused a step you believed was next. The refusal is not an obstacle to route around — it is the detector working. | You are about to change a corpus file and cannot name the instance that authorised it. scripts/check-corpus-gate.ts refuses exactly this at the commit boundary; discovering it there is late. | workflow_next returns a step in a lane whose role you are not playing. | You cannot say which process instance you are in without looking it up — and looking it up returns nothing, or more than one candidate. | The work you are doing was not in the brief you opened the turn with. An unplanned detour is the most common way this happens, and the least likely to be noticed from inside it. | .

3032.title: Recovering
3032.content: When one of the five fires, stop making changes and recover in this order: . | Re-read the instance. work_plan_prime reports every instance’s position next to its work item. State is committed, so a sibling session’s progress is visible too. | Reconstruct from context what you were doing and which task it belongs to. You usually can: the branch name, the claimed work item, and the opening brief together pin it. | Say what you concluded, and confirm it with the user before resuming: . I completed the QA sweep but never completed Task_ReviewFindings, so the instance is still sitting before the editor decision. I believe I am in content-lifecycle instance cl-2f9, in the editor lane, at Gateway_EditorDecision. Confirm before I proceed? . This confirmation is not optional and not a formality. An agent that silently re-enters a process it inferred its way back into is asserting authorisation nobody gave it. The whole point of the swimlane guardrail is that the actor is assigned, not self-declared. The person owed the confirmation may give it in advance for a stated scope — see confirmation-waiver.md. | If you cannot reconstruct it, say so and stop. A wrong instance is worse than none: completing a step in the wrong run records an authorisation that did not happen. | .

3033.title: What you MOVED while you were out of process
3033.content: Steps 1–3 reconstruct where you were. They do not reconstruct what you changed position of, and for notes and stickies that is a separate problem with a sharper edge: . A move is not self-documenting. moveNote (schemas/ui/note-anchor.ts) returns the note with its new anchor and nothing about the old one. A note that has been moved cannot say where it was. So a sticky re-anchored during an off-process detour leaves no trace in the artefact. There is no field to read back, no diff that distinguishes “moved deliberately” from “moved by an agent that had lost the thread”, and — because a move keeps the id — nothing that even looks unusual. The only possible record is what was written to a work item at the time. Work items carry no anchor: a work item is not a thing pinned to a block, it is the record that a pinning changed. workflow/bean-link.ts has the note op that writes it. So, as part of recovery, before step 3’s confirmation: . | Name every note or sticky you re-anchored during the detour, with its anchor before and after. Read them off the work item’s note trail — not off the notes, which no longer know. | If the trail is silent and you moved things, say that. A gap is a finding. “I moved stickies and did not record where from” is recoverable by a person who remembers; “everything is fine” is not. | Do not move anything back on your own judgement. Re-anchoring to undo is another unlogged move, and it is a durable change made to cover one — see deletion-requires-confirmation.md, which is the same rule about a different verb. | . A note carries no movedFrom history. History kept in the artefact being moved is lost when the note is deleted, or moved by a tool that does not maintain the field. The work item is a separate record, which is what an audit trail has to be. Reading a bean back as the trail . A work item is a usable trail when a wrong claim is left in place, with the correction appended beside it rather than replacing it. Read back, the work item shows the premise, the disproof, and the re-scoped work in order, so an agent resuming can see that the original framing was abandoned and why, which is what it needs to avoid re-deriving the same mistake. A work item tidied to show only the correct conclusion reads as though the work had always been aimed there. That is why bean-coordination.md has unwanted work scrapped with its reasons rather than deleted: a record that shows only outcomes cannot distinguish a dead end somebody ruled out from one nobody tried.

3043.title: Public comment channels and intake
3043.content: Skill public-comment-channels: Set up the channels a public-comment release goes out on (an offline Excel sheet, a Google Form, a GitHub issue form, and the review sheet), each limited to the release’s fixed references, with the editor’s instructions and the announcement, and bring every channel back in through one intake path that ends in agent triage into thematic change-sets. Use when a draft is released for public comment, when a channel is added to a running review, or when returned comments arrive from any channel. Named by: Release a draft for public comment . Process: folio-assistant-core/processes/content/public-comment-release.bpmn (Process_PublicCommentRelease): Task_SetUpChannels and Task_WriteAnnouncement. Intake lands in public-comment.bpmn (Process_PublicComment): StartEvent_CommentsReturned, then Task_Ingest, Task_Triage and Task_ProposeChangeSets. Tool: folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts. The comment store, the importer and change-sets are the public-comment skill’s. The review sheet’s script is review-sheet-script. A public-comment release is a frozen, line-numbered draft with an id, for example “Draft for Public Comment Release v0.9” (dpi-h-pc-v0.9). Every comment cites that draft, and nothing else, so every channel offers only the release’s own references: its numbered sections, its printed pages, and its captioned tables and figures. A channel that lets a reviewer type any section number brings back comments that cannot be placed.

3044.title: 1. The release’s fixed references
3044.content: Once the release is built (Task_BuildPcRelease), make the one list every channel is generated from: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts refs folio/<document>/review-anchors.json \ --release <release id> --title "<release title>" --draft-url <the release's draft link> \ --out review/public-comment/release-references.json . release-references.json holds the release id and title, the sha256 of the frozen PDF and .docx, and three lists: sections as a reader cites them (“3.4.5 Governance”, “Appendix C: Glossary”), printed pages in reading order, and table and figure captions. Commit it beside the comment store. It does not change while the release is open. A new release gets a new file and new channels.

3045.title: 2. The editor sets up the channels, before anything is announced
3045.content: The editor chooses which channels the review uses, and sets every one of them up before the announcement goes out, so the instructions can link to each one. Each is generated from release-references.json. Nobody edits a list by hand. | channel | make it | what the reviewer sees | limited to the release by | . | Offline Excel sheet | … xlsx release-references.json --out <release id>-comments.xlsx | Instructions, a Comments tab (their details at the top, one row per comment), a locked References tab | drop-down lists on Section, Page and Comment type that refuse anything else; the Release row | . | Google Form | … google-form release-references.json --out CreatePublicCommentForm.gs, paste into Apps Script, run createPublicCommentForm | “About you”, then one comment per response, with Submit another response | list questions for Section and Page; the release in the title | . | GitHub issue form | … issue-form release-references.json --out .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/public-comment.yml in the folio’s repository | one issue per comment, titled [<release id>] …, labelled public-comment | drop-downs for Section, Page and Comment type; the title prefix | . | Review sheet (committee, not the public) | the review-sheet-script skill, from the release’s template | Review Public Comments and Review Change Sets | the script’s Sections, Pages and Lines links, built from the same review anchors | . Line numbers stay free text in every channel: a line range or “Table 3.1” is one field, and a list of every line would be useless. The importer resolves them against the frozen draft and reports a miss. The editor’s set-up checklist. Done in this order, and every link is recorded for the announcement: . | The release is published: the line-numbered PDF and the comment-period site (its address says it is the public comment release, not branches/, and it is kept, not deleted on merge to main). Record both links. | release-references.json is made and committed. | Each chosen channel is made from it, as above. Record each channel’s link: the Excel sheet’s download link, the Form’s published link, the issue form’s …/issues/new?template=public-comment.yml link. | The review sheet is copied from its template, its Config set for this release, and an agent is asked to watch it (skill review-sheet-script). | Each channel is tried once by someone other than the editor: one comment in, then the check below run on what came back. Delete the trial comment. | The submitter records are ready (§4). The announcement is written last. | .

3046.title: 3. The announcement (Task_WriteAnnouncement)
3046.content: A short communication for the public. It names the release, says what is asked and by when, and links to everything. Keep the process description to a few sentences and link to the published process for the rest. Subject: Public comment: <document title>, <release title> <Organisation> invites comments on <document title>, <release title>, from <open date> to <close date>. Read the draft (line-numbered PDF): <PDF link> Read it online: <comment-period site link> Comment in whichever way suits you: - Online form: <Google Form link> - Offline: download <Excel sheet link>, fill in the Comments tab, and email it to <address> - On GitHub: <issue form link> (comments there are public) Please cite the section, page and line numbers of this draft. Your email is used only to contact you about your comments. Your name is published in the acknowledgements only if you say yes. What happens next: each comment is placed on the text it is about, grouped with related comments into proposed changes, and reviewed by <committee>. The editor decides each one, with a reason. How the review works: <link to the published public-comment process>. Only the channels the editor set up are listed. The links are the ones recorded in §2. Nothing goes out until every link has been opened once.

3047.title: 4. Who submitted: the Public Comment Source tab
3047.content: Submitters are recorded in the review sheet’s Public Comment Source tab, one row per public comment. The columns are No., date received, channel, reviewer name, organisation, country / region, stakeholder type, email, and “Acknowledge by name (Yes/No)”. Every column is Grey: the tab is the external source, copied in mechanically. The tab is locked, and it is the only place a submitter’s name and email are kept (the public-comment skill, §”The live review sheet”). | Each channel asks for the details once per submission: at the top of the Excel sheet’s Comments tab, on the Form’s “About you” page, and from the GitHub login on an issue. At intake, the submission’s details are copied onto every one of its comments’ rows in Public Comment Source, with the comment’s No. and its channel. | A returning submitter is recognised by the importer’s pseudonymous id r-<hash>, which comes from the email or else the name (reviewerId in schemas/public-comment.ts). Someone who comments through two channels with the same email is therefore one reviewer. | The repository gets only that id, the organisation and the country. It gets the name only when the submitter answered Yes to “Acknowledge by name”, and never the email. The importer follows this rule (the public-comment skill, §”Privacy”). | Submitter details are not configuration, so they never go in the Config tab. That tab holds the script’s settings and is written by the agent. | .

3048.title: 5. Intake: each channel has one path back
3048.content: All four channels end in the same importer (public-comment.ts import), because each returns a table whose headers are the importer’s own. Before importing, check that every reference is in the release: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts check <returned file> --refs review/public-comment/release-references.json . check lists each row that cites a section or page outside the release, or whose Release row names another release, and exits non-zero. It changes nothing. A flagged row is still imported (it arrives unplaced and triage places it); the list tells the triager where to look. | channel | what comes back | command (from the folio’s repository) | . | Excel sheet | the reviewer’s .xlsx, by email | public-comment.ts import <file> --channel comment-matrix --batch <release id>-<reviewer org> | . | Google Form | the response sheet, downloaded as CSV | public-comment.ts import <responses.csv> --channel online-form --series <release id>-form | . | GitHub issues | issues titled [<release id>] | gh api 'repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues?labels=public-comment&state=all&per_page=100' --paginate > issues.json, then public-comment-channels.ts issues-csv issues.json --release <release id> --out gh.csv, then import gh.csv --series <release id>-github | . | Review sheet | committee feedback, not public comments | the sheet sync (skill public-comment, §”The live review sheet”) | . | A letter or email that used no channel | prose | public-comment.ts import-narrative <file> --reviewer … | . Re-importing is safe: a file already imported is recognised by its sha256, and a form or issue export re-downloaded later adds only the rows (No.) it has not seen, because each carries a --series. Keep the returned files in the review owner’s private store, never in the repository: they hold emails.

3049.title: 6. Triage into thematic change-sets
3049.content: After each intake batch, the intake agent proposes change-sets (Task_ProposeChangeSets, the public-comment skill, §”The agent proposes; nobody is notified”): . | public-comment-changesets.ts seed lists the comments in no change-set, bucketed by section. A bucket is a starting point, not a change-set. | The agent groups comments by theme: comments that ask for the same change, or for changes that must land together, wherever they are in the document. A cross-cutting theme (a term, consent, normative keywords) is one change-set across sections. | Each change-set gets a title, requirements (what the text must do, not the new text), and its linked public comments (refs). Record them with propose --file proposals.json. They are proposed: no issue is opened and nobody is notified. | A comment that fits no theme stays out, on the dashboard’s open, in no change-set tile, for a person to place. | . The review sheet then shows the new change-sets on its next sync, and the committee reviews them there or on GitHub.

3050.title: 7. Closing
3050.content: At the agreed close: run closePublicCommentForm in the Form’s script, and remove the issue form (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/public-comment.yml) from main, so nobody is offered a closed release. The kept release site and PDF are not touched. Do a last intake from every channel. A comment that arrives after the close is imported like any other, and the editor decides whether it is considered.

3051.title: What not to do
3051.content: . | Do not type a list of sections into a form by hand, or edit the generated questions or headers: they are the importer’s column headers, and a renamed question is a column the importer cannot read. Regenerate instead. | Do not reuse one release’s channels for the next release. Its references are different. | Do not announce a channel before it has been tried once and check passed. | Do not put an email, or a name without consent, in the repository, an issue body the agent writes, or the Config tab. | .
