3109.title: Remote-mount a harness
3109.content: Skill remote-mount: Bring a harness, and every instance it depends on, into a checkout that does not hold it, from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories with a lock: a source.remote entry in the downstream’s root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration) and mountDefaults on the harness. Covers when to mount and when to subscribe instead, why there are no submodules and no .deps/, the transitive closure through needs and gitlinks, overrides by id, the lock, and the three states. Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Human Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . How a downstream folio gets the layers it is built on: . | no git submodules, ever; | no .deps/, because a dot directory collides with GitHub’s conventions and with this repository’s own dot-prefix guard; | a remote mount is a declared directory with a remote source, pinned to a full 40-character SHA; | the defaults live in the harness’s own declaration, so a downstream never restates the paths; | a downstream may override them by id, never by path; | mounts are resolved transitively across the dependency closure; | code arrives through the mounted code directories. | . |   | where | . | the process | mount-dependency.bpmn; the per-subgraph view is the remote and npm flows of mount-subgraph.bpmn | . | the schema | cat-harness/schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts, plus the remote, npm and hydrated members of SubgraphSource (schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts); the per-pin index package is subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts | . | the tool | bun run cat mount:remote (--plan to resolve without writing), and bun run cat mount:remote:check (offline) | . | the entry point | bun run cat state:mount, which the session-start hook already runs | .

3110.title: Mount, subscribe or associate: choose first
3110.content: | you want | relation | what arrives | . | to build on a harness: run its scripts, import its schemas, read its skills as your own | remote mount (source.remote in index.config.json) | the harness’s declared directories and those of everything it needs, at one pin | . | to read another graph and hold chosen parts of it | subscription (subscriptions): the kg-subscription skill | a snapshot of its declaration, then parts you materialise one at a time through the five gates | . | to know of a harness and link to it | association (associatedHarnesses): the associate-harness skill | nothing | . | to retrieve or distribute as a package | npm distribution (kg-retrieve-npm, source.npm): the npm-kg-distribution skill | an npm .tgz tarball (unhydrated source or hydrated view) | . The test is whether your code imports theirs. If it does, mount. If you only read their content, subscribe: a subscription gates every part through copyright and purpose, and a mount does not, because the code it brings is the platform you are built on.

3111.title: The two halves of the declaration
3111.content: The harness side goes in the harness’s own <name>.json and is written once by the harness’s owner: . "mountDefaults": { "path": "cat-harness", "directories": ["schemas", "scripts", "skills"] } . What arrives is what the declaration NAMES: the declaration itself, the chosen directories, and the instance-scoped files in its assets (its README and AGENTS.md). A file the declaration does not name, such as a platform.ts beside it, never arrives. Code the mounted graphs import has to sit in a declared directory. Both fields are optional, and each absence has a meaning: . | path absent means the instance’s home path (livesAt.path, else its directory in its own repository). | directories absent means every declared directory whose content is in the checkout. A branch, family or remote source is somebody’s state, not part of the harness. | . The downstream side goes in the checkout’s root index.config.json, as the source.remote of the instance it brings in. Which instances a checkout instantiates, where each comes from, and the fallback for a folio with no index are index-config’s rule. This skill covers only what a remote source means once it is declared: . { "name": "<harness>", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "<owner>/<repo>", "ref": "<40-character sha>", "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "directories": ["schemas", "skills"] }, "bootstrap": { "skip": true } } } } } . The fields are a remoteMounts entry without its harness, because the instance’s name is the harness (RemoteSourceSchema in schemas/kg/index-config.ts). A folio with no index still reads remoteMounts on its declaration. Declaring a mount in both places is an error: readDeclaredMounts throws and names both files. bun run cat index-config:migrate --write moves the entries across. Every tool that writes mounts writes through writeDeclaredMounts, into index.config.json, and none writes remoteMounts. overrides is keyed by instance name, then by directory id: . | path moves an instance. | directories replaces its default list. An id may be one the instance declares in its <name>.json or from within one of those directories (a "subgraph": true entry of skills/skills.json, such as voices); both are resolved at the pin through instanceDirectories, the resolver every on-disk reader uses. A nested id mounts its own path alone. An id declared in neither place is refused, not dropped, and the refusal says where it looked. The same holds for the harness’s own mountDefaults.directories. An id may also be a concern name, a code from code-lists/concern-group.json such as sdlc. It expands to every kind-first member the instance declares, such as sdlc/processes/ and sdlc/skills/, read from each grouping kind’s own declaration file at the pin. Each member is locked as <directory id>/<code>. A code that none of the instance’s kinds declares is refused like any other unknown id. | After a review of hydrated metadata, `mount:remote –choose [:] --directories a,b --tools x,y` writes the choice into `overrides.` (the choice, never the state), so a fresh clone replays it. It ends the review: that instance mounts as files, so its `hydrated` is dropped. The pin and consent do not move. | skip leaves it unmounted, and the lock records it as an answer. | tools names Tools this instance declares, by id, and mounts each one runnable: its definition, its implementation and their import closure. The next section but one says what that brings. | hydrated: true (here, or on the entry for its harness) mounts each chosen directory as one file: its published index.hydrated.jsonld at the pin, a hydrated source. Read what is there, then choose what to mount as files. No declaration is laid down, and needs is not followed. Where that file comes from is the next section. With no directories, a hydrated mount offers every top-level in-checkout subgraph and ignores mountDefaults.directories on purpose: that list chooses which FILES a downstream gets, and a hydrated mount is the step before choosing. Each top-level file already carries its nested subgraphs inline (hasSubgraph), so a nested one is named only when you want it on its own. | .

3112.title: Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package
3112.content: A pin’s subgraph index files (index.jsonld, index.hydrated.jsonld under <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/) are published per pin in a package, and a hydrated mount fetches them through the Tool its source names (the hydrated source’s tool, which is remote-mount unless it says otherwise). | Not committed in each repository. The files are builtAtPublish: they are computed over the checkout’s other instances, so no commit can hold them current, and a committed copy turns every re-pin’s check red. | Not generated at mount time. The downstream would need the whole index, kg-export and the framing toolchain to read one file of metadata, which is the cost a hydrated mount exists to avoid, and two downstreams could frame two different files for one pin. | . What that means in practice: . |   |   | . | the package | <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>: the index files at their published paths, and subgraph-index.json (folio-subgraph-index/v1) giving each file’s sha256 and the repository, pin and harness | . | where | assets of the GitHub release subgraph-index-<sha> in the instance’s repository, with the tarball’s folio-binary-release/v1 record beside it. Every name is computed (subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts) | . | who publishes | the subgraph-index-package Tool, run on every push to main by the reusable workflow layer-publish-subgraph-index.yml (the tools layer); a harness opts in with one uses: line | . | what a mount checks | the pin’s git tree first (a commit that does carry the file still works); otherwise the package: the tarball against its record (size, sha256), the manifest against the repository, pin and harness asked for, each file against its sha256, then the same schema and subgraph-IRI check a tree file gets | . | the lock | a directory that came from the package records the tarball’s URL and sha256 and the file’s path in it (package), so mount:lock fetches the same bytes and refuses any others | . No release for the pin is missing, and the detail says the package was looked for. A package that fails a check is missing; one that could not be fetched is could-not-determine. Neither is ever an empty mount. The record travels with the tarball, so its digest proves the transfer, not the publisher: who may publish is the repository’s write access, the same trust the git tree at the pin already rests on.

3113.title: Tools: choose by id, mount runnable
3113.content: The workflow: load the Tools’ metadata, review it, then materialise a chosen set. The first step is a hydrated mount of the declaring instance’s tools directory. Its index.hydrated.jsonld holds every Tool whole, and each Tool is its own tools/<id>/ subgraph. The last step is tools on that instance’s override: . "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "tools": ["bean-query", "bpmn-checklist", "agent-memory"] } } . Three rules govern this step: . | A Tool brings both halves. Its definition is <tools dir>/<id>/<id>.ts in the instance that declares it, by the folder convention in schemas/tools/tool-folders.ts. Its implementation is what its invoke names: . | inProcess.module, found in the declarer or in an instance whose needs names it (resolveImplementingPath’s rule; two holders is refused); | the script a bun run cat <key> command resolves to through the instances’ checkoutScripts. | . A bare runtime command (gh, beans) or manual brings no code. Both halves arrive with their import closure. A definition without its code is not a Tool you can run, and code without the modules it imports does not load: either way the checkout is half-working. | One closure walker. The closure is bootstrap-tools’ importClosure (scripts/check-closure.ts). check:tools-closure and the staging cone use the same walk. Do not write a second walker: two of them give two answers to “what does this code load”. | Directory granularity. The mount brings every declared directory the closure touches, whole. It takes the most specific declared directory (a nested one such as skills/voices mounts alone) and never a single file, so the lock schema is unchanged. A closure file in no declared directory, and an import that resolves to nothing, are refused with the file named. Neither is ever dropped. | . With tools named anywhere in a mount entry, each instance of that entry mounts the directories the closure touches, plus any its override names in directories. It does not mount its default list. A whole instance stays whole. A Tool id the instance does not declare at the pin is refused at plan time. tools together with hydrated is refused, because metadata brings no code. What it costs. A Tool folder is not a declared directory: tools/ is, and most definitions import its lib.ts. So a definition arrives with the whole tools directory, which holds every Tool’s definition. The cost that matters falls on the implementation side, which brings the directories its closure touches (in the tools layer, typically scripts and src). Without tools, the tools layer mounts every in-checkout directory it declares. The end-to-end check is the remote-mount test “load tools metadata, choose three Tools, materialise them” in the tools layer.

3114.title: Why the default path is the home path
3114.content: At its home path, a mounted instance keeps its position relative to its siblings. Two things then follow with no extra machinery: . | instanceRootsIn scans one level deep, so it finds every mounted sibling and needs resolves exactly as it does in the monorepo. | A relative import such as ../../cat-harness/schemas/… finds the file it names. | . Moving an instance by override is allowed, and the overlay still finds it through the lock (mountedInstanceRoots, mountScopeFor). The override is then responsible for any import that climbs out of the moved instance.

3115.title: The closure
3115.content: . | The harness’s declaration is read from the pinned tree, not from this checkout. | Each needs name is looked for in the same tree. | If it is not there, the planner looks for a gitlink at that tree’s root. A submodule entry is itself a pin, so a need on bootstrap resolves to litlfred/bootstrap at the gitlink’s SHA. The downstream gets the bytes and never a submodule. | A need the downstream already holds as a local instance is local: it is supplied by the checkout and never mounted over. | A need found nowhere is missing. It is never dropped. | .

3116.title: The lock, and the three states
3116.content: index.lock.json sits beside the downstream’s index.config.json and is committed. It is generated by mount:remote and never hand-edited, which is why it is a separate file rather than part of the index. Readers also accept the legacy name <name>.mount-lock.json, and both present is an error. It records: . | the pins it was written for; | for each instance: the repository, the SHA, how the pin was found (declared / same-tree / gitlink), the declaration’s digest, each directory’s tree digest, and declared instance assets (such as package.json); | what was not mounted, and why. | . The mounted bytes are not committed. With an index, each mount path is ignored by a generated block in the root .gitignore, written from the index (check:index-ignores is the gate). A path that block does not cover is reported as missing, never patched locally, because a local exclude is invisible to every other clone. In a folio with no index, a path its rules do not ignore goes into the worktree’s info/exclude. Mount path and route collisions. A mount with no path override lands at <name>/ in the downstream root, beside the downstream’s own directories, and its site routes sit beside the site-wide ones. To prevent collisions on disk and in route space: . | Reserved names: RESERVED_ROOT_AND_ROUTE_NAMES in schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts declares the one authoritative list of reserved root directories and site route names: ["skills", "tools", "docs", "assets", "glossary", "api", "payload", "branches/", "beans", "todos", "fsh-guts", "uploads", "test", "build", "_site", "_docs", "_kg"]. | Mount path check: checkMountPathCollisions (run during planning in mount:remote and by bun run cat check:mount-collisions) rejects any remote mount whose effective path (path or <name>/) collides with: . | a directory the downstream declares in its own configuration; | a reserved root or site route name; | another mount’s path. When a collision occurs, the error states how to fix it: “set path” (on the instance’s overrides.<name>.path in index.config.json or source.remote.overrides). | . | Route rules: . | Canonical: every visualiser is reachable at <base>/<harness>/<visualizer>/. Every generated link uses that form unless an alias is declared. | Alias: <base>/<visualizer>/ exists only when a declaration opts in via alias: true or alias: "<alias>" in its Visualisation declaration (coverage.visualiser). The site build refuses an alias that collides with another alias, a harness route, or a reserved site route, and names both claimants. | The route rule itself is in schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes”. | . | . Every instance ends in exactly one state: . | state | means | exit | . | mounted | on disk, hashing to the lock | 0 | . | unverified-approver | mounted, on consent no mountApprovers list checked | 0, reported apart | . | missing | not on disk, edited since mounting, not in the tree, refused, or the lock is for other pins | 1 | . | could-not-determine | the fetch failed, a declaration or lock is unreadable, or an instance is reached at two pins | 2 | . Could-not-determine outranks missing, and missing outranks mounted. A fetch that failed is never an empty layer. Re-pinning: from a checkout mounted from the lock . A re-pin is mount:remote --seed <name>=<owner/repo>@<sha> (it writes the pin and its consent into index.config.json), then mount:remote (it lays the bytes down and rewrites the lock). Do it in a checkout whose mounts match the lock: a fresh one, or one replayed by .github/mount-from-lock.sh. A mount with local edits is left untouched by the next mount, at its old commit, while the lock’s top-level pin moves, so CI would keep testing the old layer. --seed refuses while a mount it moves has such edits, and mount:check reports an instance entry behind its pin as missing. After the re-pin, check that the moved instance’s sha in index.lock.json is the new pin. The committer re-pins, locally, and CI only verifies. The person or agent who moves a pin does the whole re-pin in their own checkout: --seed, a fresh mount:remote, the regenerated agent surface (skill:commands, agent-memory, index:render), and the local checks. That same mount:remote then publishes the new lock’s layers cache ref (below) alongside the branch, with whatever credential pushes the branch. bun run cat layers:publish retries it, and --no-layers-publish skips it. CI never builds the ref when it exists: it fetches it and verifies it against the lock. Two writers are only fallbacks: . | the re-pin train, for layers nobody re-pinned; | main’s post-merge workflow, which rebuilds the ref for every push that changes index.lock.json. | . The layers cache: one fetch, every byte still verified . Replaying a lock fetches each pinned instance from its own repository. The layers cache is one git commit in the INDEX repository whose tree is the composed overlay a replay lays down: each locked directory at its mount path, each declaration and asset, and nothing an install, a state mount or a publish build wrote. | Ref: refs/cat/layers/<key>, where the key is the sha256 of the lock’s instances. refs/cat/layers/main moves with main’s lock. | Reader: mount:lock, and through it .github/mount-from-lock.sh, the session-start hook and every CI job, first tries ONE shallow fetch of the key’s ref, then of main. A layer whose copy verifies is laid down from it. A layer that does not verify, or a ref that is missing, is fetched from its own repository as before. --no-layers-cache (or CAT_LAYERS_CACHE=0) skips it, and CAT_LAYERS_URL points it at another remote. | Writer: the committer, through mount:remote or layers:publish. It refuses unless every mount reads current, then pushes the overlay. --main also moves main. --prune <n> keeps the newest n lock refs, main, and each --keep <key>, for example the lock of every open PR. | . The lock stays the sole authority. The cache is untrusted. Every byte taken from it is checked against the lock: the declaration’s and each asset’s sha256, and each directory’s treeDigest. These are the same checks a fetched byte passes. So a stale main still serves every layer that did not move, and a tampered ref costs time, never correctness. Trust is unchanged: consent was checked when the lock was written, and the cache cannot add an instance the lock does not name. A replay that fails is reported loudly, not swallowed: a stale mount makes local checks pass falsely.

3117.title: A changed lock re-renders the agent surface
3117.content: A mount is not done when the bytes are on disk. A newly pinned layer can bring new skills, renamed skills and new agent-memory entries, but an agent does not read the layer: it reads what is generated from it. | surface | generated by | from | . | .claude/commands/<name>.md | skill:commands | every user_invocable skill in the mounted kg graphs | . | .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md, .agents/skills/, .agents/rules/ | agent-memory | the memory directories the mounted instances declare | . So when a mount:remote run changes the lock, it runs both generators from the checkout root before it exits, and a generator that fails fails the run. A re-pin commit then carries the new layers and the surface rendered from them. --no-agent-surface opts out; --check, --plan and --staging never run it, since they change no lock a commit would carry. The list lives in one place, AGENT_SURFACE_GENERATORS in cat-harness-tools/scripts/remote-mount.ts. A new generator of something an agent reads (a rule file, a settings hook) is added there, not to a checklist: a step a person has to remember is the step that gets skipped. The process step is Task_RenderAgentSurface in mount-dependency.bpmn, between writing the lock and checking against it.

3118.title: Trust: what lets a mount proceed (H8)
3118.content: A real mount needs a person’s consent for that pin (trust.consent); a --staging mount needs none. schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts has the rules. Four things to know: . | The lock records the basis for each instance: staging, or consent with who and when. mount:remote:check re-runs the trust check against the current declaration, so consent withdrawn later reads refused. | A gitlink needs consent of its own. An instance reached through a gitlink is another repository at another commit. Give its consent on overrides.<name>.trust, for the gitlink’s SHA. | Who may consent. Declare mountApprovers and a consent.by not on the list is refused. Without the list, mounts report unverified-approver: exit 0, but never shown as clean. A checkout whose mounts index.config.json lists declares the list there, as its top-level mountApprovers; declaring it on the instance declaration as well is an error. | A refused mount is not current. Its old bytes stay on disk (an agent does not delete them). The lock records them under unmounted as leftOnDisk, and the check reports them as not mounted. | . Standing consent: a site keeps itself on an upstream branch . Pins stay per site. A site may declare, on one instance’s trust.standing, that a named person consents to following a branch — {follows: "main", consentBy, consentAt, require?: "green"}. The repin tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/repin-standing.ts, run by its standing-repin.yml workflow) then moves that pin to the branch’s newest (green) commit and writes trust.consent for the new pin, by that person and marked standing. The mount accepts it only while the same rule is still declared: withdraw or edit it and those pins ask again. A pin moved by hand still asks again, rule or not.

3119.title: Publishing a remote-mounted downstream — provision gh-pages first
3119.content: A mount brings layers into a checkout; it provisions nothing on the downstream’s remote. A downstream that publishes a site needs a gh-pages branch before GitHub Pages can be switched on, exactly as a new repository does. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in the getting-started process (getting-started §5), with the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision (idempotent, never forced; without the flag it only reports unprovisioned and the exact command), then set Pages to “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)”. A worked example is in repo-conversion §5.

3120.title: Never
3120.content: . | Never add a submodule to get a dependency, and never clone into .deps/. | Never pin a branch or an abbreviated SHA. The schema refuses both. | Never edit a mounted directory and expect a re-mount to keep the edit, or to throw it away. A re-mount leaves edited bytes untouched and reports them as missing. Move the edit upstream, or delete the directory and re-mount. | Never mount over tracked files, or over a directory that no lock says this mount made. Both are refused. | Never read missing or could-not-determine as “that layer has nothing in it”. A layer that is not mounted is absent from every overlay. | .

3122.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
3122.content: Skill render-kg-to-cdn: Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a publication root URL, and report a status and one message. The same step for a staging preview and for a release — only the root URL and the target differ. Names the target’s Tool, never its steps: GitHub Pages (gh-pages) is one Tool, and it carries its own subprocess. Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Human Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Render the content of a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a given publication root URL, independent of staging or release, and report the status of the push with a message. GitHub Pages is one Tool for this general step. Drawn as render-kg-to-cdn.bpmn.

3123.title: Inputs and output
3123.content: | input | what | . | Knowledge Graph | an instance root — or a tree the caller has already rendered and verified | . | Subgraphs | optional: declared directory ids; absent means the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | . | CDN target | which Tool performs the push — a Tool that satisfies: ["render-kg-to-cdn"] | . | output | what | . | status | pushed, not-pushed, or could-not-determine — a check that could not look is never pushed | . | message | one line, postable as it stands: what is live (a commit), where, and the QA result | .

3124.title: Staging and release are the same step
3124.content: A preview is this with a root under the release root; a release is this with the release root. What differs belongs to the caller: who may start it, what must be reviewed or verified first, what else lives on the same host and must survive the push. That is why feature-staging and docs-site-publish both call this process rather than restating it, and keep their own steps — the slug, the render log, restoring the open previews, the publication-manager alert — around the call.

3125.title: Name the Tool, not its steps
3125.content: The general process has one call activity, bound by the Tool: the activity names this skill, the Tool for the chosen target satisfies it, and the Tool lists its own subprocesses — the diagram of its steps (skills-and-tools, bpmn-processes). The general skill never lists them. | target | Tool | its subprocess | its message | . | GitHub Pages | gh-pages | bootstrap-tools processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn | the commit merged onto gh-pages + the QA of what is staged and what is served | . A target may need provisioning before it accepts a push; the Tool’s subprocess owns that. For GitHub Pages a gh-pages branch has to exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it, so the gh-pages subprocess creates it first — the general step does not. Another CDN is another Tool with its own subprocess, and nothing here changes. A CDN in front of an origin is a layer, not a publication host (kg-to-portal): the publication root URL stays the origin’s canonical one even when a CDN serves it.

3126.title: What this is not
3126.content: Not the verification of what a build produced — that is publish-verification, and it runs before a caller hands its tree over. Not the decision to release — content-publish and release-lifecycle. This step renders, pushes, and says whether the push landed.

3134.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages
3134.content: Skill render-kg-to-github-pages: Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, to GitHub Pages at a publication root URL, and report the push: a status (pushed, not pushed, could not determine) and one message carrying the deployed commit and the QA result. The same steps for a staging preview and for a release; only the root URL differs. Named by: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages . Inputs, each named by whoever starts the process: . | input | what | default | . | the Knowledge Graph | an instance root, the directory holding its <name>.json | none; required | . | Subgraphs | a list of directory ids from that declaration | the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | the declaration’s iriBase, else https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/ | . Output: a status and a message, and nothing else a caller must read. | status | when | . | pushed | the staged tree had no problem, the root URL answers, its README page (README.html) answers, and every document address answers | . | not-pushed | a check ran and failed: a staging problem, or a 404 at the root or at a document address | . | could-not-determine | nothing failed, but an answer was about the way here (403, 407, 5xx, no network) | . The message is one line a caller posts as it stands: pushed 1a2b3c4 to <root> — QA: staged ok (N files, M documents); root 200; README.html 200; documents M/M answer. The commit is which bytes are live: the commit on the gh-pages branch the site is served from. Staging and release are not two processes. A preview is this process with a root under the release root (…/branches/<slug>/, say) and a release is it with the release root. Anything that differs between them (who may start it, what must be reviewed first) belongs to the process that calls this one, never in here.

3135.title: The steps
3135.content: Drawn in processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Every command below is run from bootstrap-tools, with the instance as --root. | Resolve the inputs. Read the declaration; check every Subgraph id is one it declares; settle the root URL. An unknown id is refused, never rendered as a smaller site. | Make sure gh-pages exists and Pages serves it. Pages cannot be switched on to serve a branch that does not exist, so in order: . | git ls-remote --heads origin gh-pages; if absent, push an orphan placeholder (index.html + .nojekyll); | Pages on, Source = branch gh-pages, folder /: gh api -X POST repos/<o>/<r>/pages -f 'source[branch]=gh-pages' -f 'source[path]=/' when gh is signed in, otherwise the manual step (Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages, / (root)). bun run scripts/init.ts --root <instance> runs both as site:branch and site:enabled. This provisioning belongs to this process, not to the publication step that calls it. | . | Stage the rendering. bun run scripts/site.ts --root <instance> --out <dir> [--subgraph <id>]…: every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document at the IRI it names, the files as they sit, the README page as README.md — served at <root>/README.html — and index.html, a redirect to it. The redirect is only the default: an instance that carries its own index.html or index.md at its root gets that as its landing page instead. Every generated page opens with a notice naming bootstrap-tools and the script that wrote it, and its footer links the generator and its source rather than GitHub’s editor, which would edit the gh-pages copy the next publish overwrites. | Check what was staged. site.ts --check and bun run scripts/readme-book.ts --root <instance> --check. Any problem stops here: the report says not-pushed and names the problem, and nothing is deployed. A push of a tree known to be broken is not a push to report. | Deploy. Commit the staged tree onto gh-pages as a full replace with bun run scripts/publish-site.ts --site <dir> --remote <git url>: the instance’s Pages workflow runs it on a push to main, and an agent runs it with its own git credentials for an instance that carries no workflow (bootstrap). GitHub Pages builds the branch (Jekyll, unless .nojekyll). A rejected push is rebuilt and retried, never rebased. The gh-pages commit is the one the message names. | Check what is served, and report. bun run scripts/pages-status.ts --root <instance> [--url <root>] [--sha <commit>] [--subgraph <id>]… asks the root URL and every document address, and prints the message; --json gives the whole record. Exit 0 pushed, 1 not-pushed, 3 could-not-determine. | .

3136.title: What this is not
3136.content: It is one target. A harness above these tools may have several ways of putting a rendering in front of readers, and treat GitHub Pages as one of them; nothing here needs to know that, and nothing here names it. It does not decide who may publish, whether review has happened, or what happens to other previews on the same host: those are the calling process’s.

3144.title: Render logging — the publish branch keeps its own history
3144.content: Skill render-logging: Log every render to the publish branch — what was published, removed, restored or deliberately retained — to an append-only log that lives beside what it describes. Use when adding or removing anything on gh-pages, when asking “what happened to this preview”, or before writing a workflow step that deletes a published artefact. Named by: Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history .

3145.title: The question it exists to answer
3145.content: What happened to branches/<slug>, and why? . A preview can be cleaned up because its pull request closed, removed by a dispatch somebody confirmed, or deleted by an unrelated merge to main. Without a record on the publish branch itself, which one happened is not recoverable.

3146.title: Append-only, and never anything else
3146.content: A removal is a new entry, not the erasure of an old one. The pair — the rendered and the removed that follows it — IS the history. scripts/render-log.ts offers no verb that could lose an entry: no --remove, no --edit, no id to overwrite. The never-delete property is a shape of the tool, so a caller cannot be written wrongly. Emptying a log is a person’s decision, taken deliberately, with the confirmation every durable artefact here requires (deletion-requires-confirmation). No tool and no workflow does it.

3147.title: The four events, and why retained earns its place
3147.content: | event | what it records | . | rendered | published, or re-published over itself — so “when was this last built” needs no commit archaeology | . | removed | taken down. Requires a reason, refused without one | . | restored | carried across a full-replace deploy by restore-staging. Its own event, because “somebody pushed this branch” and “an unrelated merge nearly deleted it” are different facts | . | retained | a removal was considered and refused. Also requires a reason | . retained answers “why is this still up”: a preview still standing because a liveness signal fired leaves no trace otherwise.

3148.title: Where it lives, and why that is structural
3148.content: _render-log/<YYYY-MM-DD>.jsonl, at the root of the publish branch. Outside branches/, deliberately. The cleanup runs rm -rf "branches/$SLUG", and a branch named to collide with a directory under branches/ slugifies to exactly that name. A store outside branches/ is unreachable by that command whatever the slug says; a guard you have to remember is weaker than a location that cannot be reached. One file per UTC day, not one growing file and not one per entry. Six workflows publish to this branch; a read-modify-write of a single file loses whatever landed in between, and the tool appends a line rather than rewriting. One file per entry would make “what happened this week” a directory walk.

3149.title: It does NOT survive a deploy on its own — this is the part to get right
3149.content: docs-site.yml is a full replace: git rm -r --ignore-unmatch '*' over the whole branch, then copies _site in. It is the only one of this repository’s six gh-pages publishers without keep_files: true, and it is the one that fires on every push to main. So the log is carried across that deploy by restore-staging.ts, unconditionally — not gated on open pull requests the way previews are. A preview belongs to an open PR; a log entry about a closed one is exactly what nothing would carry, and exactly what a reader needs most. A log a deploy truncates is worse than no log, because a reader will believe its entries persisted. docs-site.yml runs restore-staging.ts from main, so a change to what the restore carries is not in force until it merges. --verify checks the carried prefixes as well as branches/, because a verifier blind to half of what the restore carried reports a clean run over the loss it exists to catch. A lost prefix is reported as not recoverable by re-running anything: a preview can be rebuilt from its workflow, and a record of what was already removed cannot. Only the prefixes the restore reported as carried are verified. A determined absent was never there to lose, and asserting on it would fail every deploy before the first entry is ever written. CARRIED_PREFIXES is where that is declared; it is a list, so another carried store is a new row, not a new code path. The carry runs before the preview check, so the log is carried even when there are no previews. A carry that could not be determined is not a warning. It collapses into the restore’s own unknown, exit 2, which fails the deploy step: continuing would run the full replace and delete the record. A determined absence — the branch is readable and has no log yet — is reported rather than omitted, because “there is no log yet” and “the carry never ran” look identical in a silent report and only the second is a defect.

3150.title: Who writes an entry
3150.content: Every path that can change branches/ writes one, and scripts/tests/workflow-yaml.test.ts asserts that by job rather than leaving it to be remembered: . | path | event | how it lands | . | feature-staging.yml → stage | rendered | the same commit as the deploy. The entry goes to the root _render-log/, never into _site, which would land it at branches/<slug>/_render-log/ — inside the directory a cleanup removes | . | feature-staging.yml → stage, preview cap | removed, one per rotated preview | the same commit as the deploy, written by staging-rotate.ts; the reason names the size budget, and the summary gives slug, age and size | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, confirmed | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, refused | retained | its own commit | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup-dispatch | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | docs-site.yml → restore | carried, not written | restore-staging.ts | . The reason is the gate’s own, never a restatement of one branch of it. cleanup emits merged | labelled | closed-unmerged-and-unlabelled and the entry carries that value. A hardcoded reason would name the wrong rule for some of them, and a wrong reason reads as evidence. A removal and its record are one commit. A separate log push can fail on its own and leave a preview that vanished with nothing saying why. The rendered and retained entries are continue-on-error. A preview that deployed and whose entry did not is a gap in the record, not a failed deploy, and failing the job there would turn a logging problem into a lost review surface. The step goes red in the run, so the gap is visible. A removed entry has no such fallback and needs none: it cannot fail separately from the removal it describes.

3151.title: Writing an entry
3151.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/render-log.ts --dir <gh-pages-checkout> \ --event rendered --kind staging-preview --path branches/<slug> --slug <slug> \ --summary "preview published" --branch "$BRANCH" --commit "$SHA" --run "$RUN_URL" . The tool writes into a directory and never pushes. The workflows that call it already hold a gh-pages checkout with their own retry and concurrency handling; a second pusher racing those is a new way to lose a deploy. One job knows how to push, this one knows what to write. Reading back: --read [--day YYYY-MM-DD]. It exits 1 when any line could not be read, and prints which — a short count must be visible as short, never passed off as complete. Same rule as ci-health: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean.

3152.title: A path is checked by VALUE, never trusted by provenance
3152.content: --path is refused unless it is / or a sequence of plain segments — no .., no leading /, no backslash. The staging slug sanitiser can emit .. (input .. gives output ..), and is safe only because git rejects every ref name containing it. That invariant holds for a slug taken from a ref and does not hold for one taken from a dispatch input — and cleanup-dispatch takes exactly that. So the check is on the value, not on where it came from.

3153.title: It is a specialisation of folio-log/v1, not a rival
3153.content: schemas/sdlc/log-entry.ts already answers “what does an entry look like”, and a render entry reuses those spellings: id, at, summary, detail, references, capture. Three things differ, each deliberately: . |   | activity log | render log | . | subject | what an agent did | what was published | . | store | fsh-guts/logs/, in the repo | the publish branch | . | published | no | yes | . An agent’s audit trail is not published; a record of what is on the publish branch belongs where its subject’s absence can be seen.

3156.title: /repo-conversion — folio-assistant over a repo that already has a life
3156.content: Skill repo-conversion: Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn, Task_ScanRepo, Task_ChooseHarnessed and Task_ConfirmImport (both non-relaxable). Scanner: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts.

3157.title: 0. The one rule
3157.content: Scan, show, ask, then move — and never in any other order. The author’s repository is the thing of value; the scaffolding is replaceable. A wrong import is not fixed by a git checkout, because the author has to work out what the agent did. Task_ConfirmImport is marked relaxable="false" in the BPMN, and a content package may not declare it away.

3158.title: 1. Scan — read-only, and honest about its limits
3158.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts # human-readable report bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts --json # same, as facts . It walks the working tree (respecting .gitignore) and sorts what it finds into three buckets: . | bucket | means | typical | . | library | external source material — something somebody else wrote, that the folio will cite or ingest | PDFs, papers, scans, datasets, references/, papers/, sources/ | . | content | material authored here, that could become folio blocks | Markdown prose, docs/, notes/, drafts/, .tex | . | unclassified | it could not tell | everything else, and it is reported, not hidden | . unclassified is reported, never forced. A two-bucket scanner’s mistakes arrive as moved files; this one reports what it could not place, and the author disposes of it. The classification is by path convention and extension only. It does not read file contents or call a model, so the author can disagree with any row of it in one word. Outside-content candidate scanning — preserving evidence and refutations . In repositories with formal, analytical, or domain-specific content, crucial verification scripts, macros, and counterexamples often live outside the primary content tree (content/ or folio/); a conversion that carries only that tree drops the evidence that some claims are false. scan-repo-content.ts scans outside the content tree and classifies these artifacts into read-only candidate classifications (defined by the content-type layer’s conversion refinement skill), reporting source location, rationale, and linkStatus (linked when referenced by at least one content block, or unlinked when orphaned). Like the general scan, candidate scanning never writes, moves, or modifies files; it presents the candidates to the author and agent so decisions can be made before importing.

3159.title: 2. Show, then ask — three questions, all as selections
3159.content: Present the scan as counts and a handful of examples per bucket, never as a 1,400-line file list. Then three questions, each answerable by picking. Load interaction-modality first. Q1 — import at all? . | Import everything the scan found (recommended) | Import only the library bucket — sources now, prose later | Import nothing; just set up folio-assistant | Let me pick bucket by bucket | . Q2 — where does each group go? Only for groups the scan was not confident about, and only when Q1 was not “nothing”. Offer library/ vs content/ per directory, not per file (a per-file interrogation is the accessibility failure in interaction-modality §0). Q3 — leave in place, or reorganise? . | Leave everything where it is (recommended) — the folio references the files at their current paths. Nothing moves, every existing link still works, and the decision stays open. | Reorganise into library/ and content/ — tidier, and it rewrites paths. Offer this only on a clean working tree, do it in its own commit, and use git mv so history follows. | . Recommend leave in place by default: a broken relative link in somebody’s README is a defect.

3160.title: 2a. Markers — choose what the harness reads (declare, don’t slurp)
3160.content: A harness declares what it reads in a repository; it does not take all of its content. The principle is directory-conventions §”A marker declares what is read, and nothing else is”. The scan’s fourth section, markers, lists the content a harness COULD be told to read: a sushi-config.yaml (an IG: contentTypes.ig), a legacy dak.json (contentTypes.dak), .bpmn processes, a work items store, library/, uploads/, Lean (contentType: paper) and folio manifests (contentType: document). For each it gives the paths, whether it is already declared — declared, not-declared, or unknown when there is no readable index.config.json to ask — and the snippet that would declare it, with where it goes (index.config.json#contentTypes, or a local instance’s <name>.json#directories). Content types come from the registry (defaultContentTypes; an { indexSection } type is checked against contentTypes.<id>), directory facets are checked against the registered graph typologies, and only the evidence the registries cannot state is a short table in cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/content-markers.ts. Where each kind of content lives is directory-conventions. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers # the list bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers --json # same, as facts . A plain command: any agent host (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot) or a person at a shell runs it, with no MCP server. It writes nothing. Q0 — which of these should the harness read? (Task_ChooseHarnessed, non-relaxable). Ask it the interaction-modality way — the full question in the chat, then a tap card where the host has one, otherwise a numbered pick-list with its default stated. Never a typed reply. Offer only the markers that are not-declared (or unknown), one option each: . | None of these for now (the default) — nothing is declared; the scan can be run again any time | contentTypes.ig — sushi-config.yaml, input/fsh/, … (the FHIR IG) | directories: processes — processes/ (7 BPMN files) | Let me pick several — the same options as a multi-select | . The default declares nothing, and the agent never declares a marker the person did not pick. Declare exactly the picks — the scan’s suggestion snippet, at its suggestion.at — in the scaffolding commit, or in its own commit on an instance that already exists. After setup, too. The same question fits any instance at any time: “what else could this harness declare?” is --markers on the instance’s repository, then Q0. Rows already declared are shown for context and are not offered. A content type registered by a higher harness layer appears as a hint when that layer is not loaded, with a note saying where the type lives. Declaring a scoped content type is not a boolean flag: its include list states everything that layer’s readers will read, so confirm the list with the person and consult that layer’s build-pipeline skill for how additional paths are added later.

3161.title: 3. Dispatch the ingestion
3161.content: Ingestion proper is processes/library/document-ingestion.bpmn (and the content layer’s document-intake refinement skill when converting into a content folio). What this skill decides is how much parallelism, and it is a question for the author because it spends their tokens: . | scale | when | how | . | inline | under ~10 documents | do it here, no subagents | . | one agent | tens of documents, one kind | a single background agent, reporting per document | . | small swarm | hundreds, or several distinct kinds | dispatch-agent — 2–4 agents partitioned by directory, never by file count | . Partition by directory because a per-file partition puts two agents in the same manifest, and the conflicts cost more than the parallelism saves. Open one work item per ingestion front before dispatching — running the existence check in todo-manager.md §”Check before you create” first — so a session that dies mid-import leaves a plan behind rather than a half-full library/.

3162.title: 4. The conversion itself
3162.content: Once Q1–Q3 are answered, folio_init against the existing directory. It refuses rather than overwrites where a file is already present, which on this branch is the common case (README.md, .gitignore, a docs/). Read its report rather than assuming; the files it declined to write are the ones you now merge by hand: . | AGENTS.md — if one exists, merge; do not replace. It is the most valuable file in the repository for the next agent. | README.md — never replaced. readme-sections.ts only writes inside marker pairs the author has opted into, so offer to add markers rather than content. | .gitignore — append the folio entries; keep theirs. | . If the remote is empty, push main first. A repository with work locally can still have an empty remote, and GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default. Run init-folio or push main before any feature branch. If main has no harness yet, land a setup-only PR first. A fork or an existing repository whose main has no index.config.json and index.lock.json gives the full PR checks nothing to compare against: the base side fails before any test runs, and the PR’s own gates are skipped. So open one small PR with only what folio_init writes and the pins, merge it, and only then branch for content. Draft-tier checks never build the base, so this does not show until the content PR leaves draft. The setup-only PR has a Tool: instantiate-harness. It pins the harness and every layer it needs, mounts them, commits the setup on harness/<harness>, opens that PR, and renders the branch’s preview at gh-pages:branches/<branch>/. On a repository with nothing mounted yet, run it from a fresh clone of the tools layer: . git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools /tmp/cht echo "<where the author consented>" | bun run /tmp/cht/scripts/instantiate-harness.ts \ --repo . --harness <owner/repo> --consent-by <who> [--plan | --local] . --plan prints the closure and every step and writes nothing; --local commits on the branch and pushes nothing. The harness’s own adoption steps are its checkout scripts instantiate:<harness> (files it declares, committed with the setup) and prepare:<harness> (what the site is built from, never committed). For an IG on a FHIR harness these declare contentTypes.ig and build the IG’s first AST. A harness built on this platform may add adoption steps of its own for its kind of repository, for example about CI that already publishes a site on every push. Ask skill_list for the skill governing that kind before calling the conversion done.

3163.title: 5. Publishing — provision gh-pages first; an overlay needs it too
3163.content: An overlay never reaches getting-started §5 by itself, so this section repeats the one step a publishing route cannot skip: provision gh-pages before GitHub Pages is switched on. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in getting-started.bpmn, on the shared path after scaffolding and before the Pages build, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. The tool is pages-bootstrap: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts # reports `unprovisioned` (exit 3) and the exact command when gh-pages is absent bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision # pushes an orphan gh-pages: placeholder index.html + .nojekyll . --provision is idempotent and never forces a push, and nothing creates a remote branch without it. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — the script prints the source it expects. When the repository’s publish workflow pushes gh-pages, “GitHub Actions” is the wrong source: the workflow would push a branch Pages was never told to serve. The same holds for an overlay that remote-mounts its dependencies. A mount brings layers in; it does not provision anything on the downstream’s remote.

3164.title: 6. Anti-patterns
3164.content: . | Moving a file before Q3 is answered. | Reporting a two-bucket classification. If unclassified is empty on a real repository, suspect the scanner rather than celebrate it. | A per-file confirmation loop. See §2. | Swarming a 12-document import. The dispatch overhead exceeds the work. | Replacing an existing AGENTS.md or README.md. Merge, or leave. | Treating the scan as ingestion. It reads; it never writes. Ingestion is a separate process with its own diagram and its own gate. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. See §5. | Dropping outside-content math artifacts or unlinked audit refutations. Carrying only the primary content tree (content/ or folio/) drops outside proofs, computations, and refutations showing that some paper claims are false. See §1. | .

3172.title: Review comments — from a PR comment to a structured todo
3172.content: Skill review-comments: Reviewer comments on a folio’s edit-set, from a tagged pull-request comment to a structured todo on the review page. Covers the tag a reviewer types, how the comments are ingested into review-comment/1.0.0 todos, where the published review-comments.json comes from and when it refreshes, how a comment follows a renamed block and survives a removed one, who may change a comment’s status, and how to change this process. Use when a reviewer asks how to comment on a block, when the review page shows no comments or a wrong one, when editing the ingestion, or when a folio’s staging workflow is set up. Named by: Committee review of a content change, Data sharing agreement document life cycle . Skill id: review-comments · Package: content-lifecycle-ext Tools: folio-review-comments (ingest), folio-review-comment-move (record a decision) . A reviewer comments on one block of a folio by writing an ordinary comment on the edit-set’s pull request, starting with a tag that names the block. The review process turns each tagged comment into a todo of a special kind, review-comment/1.0.0. The review page lists those todos beside the blocks they are about.

3173.title: Design
3173.content: | rule | why | . | The channel is a PR conversation comment tagged with the block label | Needs nothing installed, sits beside the approve, and is anchored by LABEL, so it survives a block moving. A line review comment is anchored to a file line and is lost when the block moves. | . | The record is a todo subtype declared by core, in the dynamic KG | A board, heat map or reader that understands todos reads a review comment without knowing about review. | . | The preview gets comments from a file the workflow writes | Works for private and public repositories, and no token ever reaches a browser. | . | A status change is committed to the folio’s todos/ on the edit-set’s feature branch | Reviewed with the edit it is about, lands on main only when that branch merges, and is part of the KG. | . The PR comment is the write channel; the todo is the canonical record.

3174.title: Writing a comment: the tag
3174.content: Start a conversation comment on the pull request with header lines, then a blank line, then what you want to say: . block: prose:overview kind: defect role: clinical-sme The dose in the second sentence contradicts table 3. | header | required | values | default | . | block: | yes | the block’s label, exactly as the review page shows it | — | . | kind: | no | question, defect, suggestion, editorial | question, which asserts least | . | role: | no | the lane you are reviewing in, a role id from roles.json | reviewer | . | The headers must be the very first lines. The first line that is not key: value ends the header. | block: takes the rest of the line, because labels contain colons (prose:overview). It must be ONE label. | A comment without block: is conversation, not a review comment, and is left alone. A PR thread is also where people talk. | A malformed tag is reported, never dropped. An unknown kind, or two words after block:, appears in malformed with the comment’s link, so the reviewer can fix it. | . The review page shows the exact block: <label> line for every changed block, ready to copy, and links to the pull request. GitHub cannot pre-fill a comment box, so copying the line is the one manual step.

3175.title: What a review comment IS
3175.content: review-comment/1.0.0, in folio-assistant-core/schemas/review-comment.ts. It is declared with nodeKind and its one parent is the harness todo, which itself is carried-note + themed. So it IS a todo: . | targetLabel is required. A general todo may float free; a review comment is always about one block. | status is closed: open, addressed, resolved, adjudicated, withdrawn. | Everything review-specific sits under one field, review: the repository, PR, comment id and URL, reviewer, role, kind, the block’s content hash and the commit when ingested, orphaned, anchoredFrom, and the decision that closed it. | . Keeping the review fields under one key means no field here can collide with one a parent adds later, which is the collision nodeKind refuses at load.

3176.title: Who may change a status: only the process
3176.content: A status moves only through transition(comment, to, {process, task}), and only along a row of REVIEW_TRANSITIONS. Anything else throws. | move | from | to | by (BPMN task) | needs a Decision | . | ingest | — | open | Process_ContentChangeReviewCommittee#Task_IngestComments |   | . | address | open | addressed | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides |   | . | send back | addressed | open | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides |   | . | resolve | addressed | resolved | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides | yes | . | adjudicate | open, addressed | adjudicated | Process_Adjudication#A_RecordEntry | yes | . | withdraw | open, addressed | withdrawn | Process_ContentChangeReviewCommittee#Task_WithdrawComment |   | . A comment’s status is what the coverage gate counts, so a comment closed outside the process would count as reviewed when nobody decided anything. A test holds every row to a task that exists in its .bpmn. Ingestion is the review coordinator’s first step in content-change-review.bpmn’s committee phase, content-change-review-committee.bpmn; withdrawal is the reviewer’s step there after the slices come back.

3177.title: Ingestion: the Tool
3177.content: bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comments.ts \ --repo owner/name --pr 7 --out _site/review-comments.json \ --folio folio --blocks-out _site/blocks.json \ --existing <previous review-comments.json> . Declared as the Tool folio-review-comments in folio-assistant-core/tools/folio-review-comments/, whose satisfies names this skill. | Read the comments. All pages of the PR’s conversation comments, with GITHUB_TOKEN when set. --comments <file> reads them from a file instead, for offline runs and tests. | Know the blocks. Either --folio <dir>, which reads the manifests as text and executes nothing, or --blocks <blocks.json> from an earlier run. | Keep everything already ingested. Every comment in --existing is kept, status included. A comment’s id is review-pr<N>-c<commentId>, so a re-run finds it rather than adding a second one. | Add the new ones. Each tagged comment not yet ingested becomes an open todo. A defect gets priority high; the others get medium. | Re-anchor every comment against the head’s blocks (reanchorToBlocks): . | the label is present: anchored; | a block lists the label in its renamedFrom: the comment moves to that block, and the old label goes into review.anchoredFrom; | neither: orphaned: true. Kept and shown, never dropped. | . | Write review-comments.json, folio-review-comments/v1. Its comments ARE the todo kind, each validated as one. The envelope adds only what one node cannot: provenance (repo, pr, commit, generatedAt), the malformed list, and the untagged count. So “no comments” and “comments nobody could parse” can be told apart. | . Why re-anchor against renamedFrom and not the ChangeSet. A ChangeSet compares against main. A block ADDED in the pull request and then renamed inside it is “added” both times, so the comment made on its first label would be orphaned. The block’s own renamedFrom (guarded by id-stable) says where it came from whatever the base. reanchor() over a ChangeSet also exists, for a caller that has only that.

3178.title: Recording a decision: commit to the feature branch
3178.content: When an editor or adjudicator decides what happens to a comment, the decision is committed to the feature branch that carries the edit-set, the same branch the edits are on: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comment-move.ts \ --id review-pr7-c1 --to addressed \ --process Process_Review --task Task_EditorDecides \ --published _site/review-comments.json --commit . | The move goes through transition(), so --process and --task must be a task allowed to make it, and resolved / adjudicated need --decision. The command is not a back door around the table above. | A new folio already has the directory. init-folio writes todos/todos.json declaring items and feedback (todo-feedback), and creates both. An older folio that lacks it gets an error naming the remedy. | The file goes where the graph says. That is the todos graph’s directory of kind todo-feedback (“todos raised against a specific block, carrying the submitter’s identity”), read from todos/todos.json. A graph that declares none gets an error naming the remedy. | The file IS the node: <feedback dir>/<id>.json, one review-comment/1.0.0, the same object the published file carries. It is JSON, not Markdown, because the todo reader’s front matter is flat and a review comment has a nested review field. | --commit refuses the base branch (default main, change it with --base) and a detached HEAD. The check runs before anything is written, so a refused commit leaves nothing behind. A status committed straight to main would record a review outcome that no merge ever accepted. | The first move reads the published file, where a comment first exists after ingestion. Every later move reads the committed file, which is the reviewed record. | . How it reaches the page. The commit is a push to the feature branch, which rebuilds the preview. That build’s ingestion reads the committed comments (--todos) and a committed comment wins over the previously published copy. The comment-triggered refresh checks out no branch code, so it cannot read them and keeps what the last build published. Nothing is lost between the two. What it costs. One extra commit on the edit-set’s branch per decision, and a PR from a fork cannot be written to by anyone but its author.

3179.title: Verdicts: “I read this version”
3179.content: A comment asks for something. A verdict records that a reviewer read a block, and what they judged. The coverage gate needs verdicts, because comments cannot say whether a block with none was read. The channel is the same tagged PR comment, with a verdict: or waive: line instead of kind:. block: prose:dose prose:schedule verdict: ok role: clinical-sme . | line | means | . | verdict: ok | read, no objection | . | verdict: changes | read, and it needs changing. The reasons go in review COMMENTS; the verdict only records the reading | . | waive: <reason> | the block needs no review (a pure rename, say). The reason is required and kept | . | block: may name several labels, so one comment can close a slice. One verdict is recorded per label. | A comment is a verdict or a review comment, never both. A tag with kind: as well is refused and shown as malformed, so nothing is counted twice under two meanings. The comment parser passes every verdict tag over. | A verdict is pinned to the block’s hash. It counts only while the block is at that version. An edit after review reopens exactly the blocks it touched. The old verdict is kept and shown as “on an earlier version”. | A verdict on a label the head does not carry is malformed, not recorded. | . Pages and inputs no block reaches. A page changed by a manifest or media file, the comment pages and every FHIR IG page have no block to give a verdict on, and an input no renderer could place may have changed any page. The same tag takes them, beside or instead of block:: . page: en/dpi-h-ra/index.html verdict: ok . input: sushi-config.yaml waive: only the version string changed . page: names a path in the preview’s rendered-impact.json, or a page the build measured and the prediction missed; input: names one of its undetermined inputs. Each is pinned to that file’s hash there, so it reopens when an input that reaches it is edited. A page or input the build does not list, or a build that published no rendered impact, is reported malformed with the reason. See rendered-impact. The folio-review-comments Tool ingests verdicts into the same review-comments.json, as its verdicts array (folio-review-verdict/v1, folio-assistant-core/schemas/review-verdict.ts). Coverage. The folio-review-coverage Tool computes every fact GW_Covered reads (uncoveredBlocks, openDefects, and, with --rendered and --measured, the page counts with their rendered and measured statuses) and prints them as JSON on stdout, ready for workflow_complete. Every fact is always printed, because the engine refuses a missing one. With --todos <root> --commit it writes the verdicts into the todos graph’s declared review-verdicts directory and commits them to the feature branch, as comment statuses are, and it refuses the base branch and a detached HEAD. init-folio declares that directory (todos/verdicts/) for every new folio.

3180.title: Publication: where the file comes from, and when
3180.content: folio-staging.yml (the reusable workflow a folio calls) has two jobs: . | job | runs on | blocks from | what it writes | . | stage | the folio’s pull request (including a push that records a decision) | --folio, the checked-out feature branch; statuses from --todos | the site, changeset.json, blocks.json, review-comments.json | . | comments | a new or edited PR comment containing block: | the published blocks.json | review-comments.json only | . The comments job never checks out or runs the pull request’s code. It is started by anyone who can comment, and it holds a token that can write to the publish branch. Checking out a PR’s code in such a job is the well-known way to hand that token to a stranger. So it checks out only: . | the platform, at platform_ref (never a copy the PR carries); | the publish branch, which holds only what earlier trusted builds wrote. | . A comment body is parsed as data and never reaches a shell. The job also skips bot comments, so the preview comment the workflow itself posts cannot start it. Freshness. A new comment appears on the page about a minute later, after the comments job runs. A push rebuilds everything and keeps every comment. Nothing refreshes on a comment when there is no preview yet (no blocks.json), and the job says so rather than failing. The caller must opt in. A folio’s own workflow has to list issue_comment among its triggers for the comments job ever to run. init-folio writes that for a document folio.

3181.title: The review page
3181.content: en/review/index.html in the preview reads review-comments.json beside changeset.json, at the preview’s root, when it is opened: . | each changed block lists its comments: kind, status, reviewer and role, the first line, a link to the PR comment, the resolve: <id> tag for an open or addressed comment, and the recorded decision for a closed one; | a comment filter (Show comments) filters the listed comments by status (open, addressed, resolved, adjudicated, withdrawn, or open and addressed) or kind (defect, question, suggestion, editorial); | a comment on a block this PR did not change is listed separately, since a review of a whole document comments on unchanged text too; | orphaned comments are listed under their own heading, with the label they were made on; | malformed tags are listed with their links, so the reviewer can fix them; | every changed block shows its block: <label> line and a link to the PR, for writing a new comment; | no review-comments.json means the page SAYS it has no comment data. An empty list would read as “nobody commented”. | .

3182.title: Changing this process
3182.content: The process is a Skill and a Tool rather than YAML steps, so it can be changed here: . | to change | edit | and | . | the tag grammar | parseReviewTag in schemas/review-comment.ts | this skill’s tag table; the tests | . | a status or who may move it | REVIEW_COMMENT_STATUSES / REVIEW_TRANSITIONS | the BPMN task it names; this skill’s table | . | where a decision is recorded | folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comment-move.ts | the folio-review-comment-move Tool node | . | a field on the record | ReviewFieldsSchema | the page, if it shows it | . | what the ingestion does | folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comments.ts | the Tool node’s io if a flag changes | . | when it runs | folio-staging.yml and init-folio’s caller template | the trust notes above | .

3183.title: Deciding from the review page: a resolve: comment
3183.content: The page decides through the same channel it comments through. Under each open or addressed comment it shows the tag to post as a pull-request conversation comment, with the words that comment’s status allows: . resolve: review-pr7-c123 decision: resolved The dose now matches table 3. | The words are transitions of the table above: addressed (address), reopened (send-back), resolved (resolve), adjudicated (adjudicate), withdrawn (withdraw). Anything the table refuses is refused here too. | Who. A repository owner, member or collaborator (GitHub’s author_association) decides; the comment’s own author may withdraw it. Anyone else’s tag is refused, because a PR conversation is open to every GitHub user and a status is what the coverage gate counts. | The Decision that closes a comment is the decision comment’s URL. | Once. Each applied decision’s comment id is kept in review.decisions, so a rebuild, or a committed copy that already carries it, applies nothing twice. | Never dropped. A tag that cannot be read or applied is listed under “Tags that could not be read or applied”, with its reason. | . The build (folio-review-comments, and stage-local for a site.build folio) applies the tags after ingestion, so the published file and the page show the decided status. With --write-decided the Tool also writes each newly decided comment into the todos graph’s feedback directory, as folio-review-comment-move writes it; stage-local passes it and then runs state:push for a todos graph kept on its own state branch (dth-hrh’s cat/dth-hrh/todos), so the decision is recorded without anyone running a command. A todos graph in the feature branch’s tree is left for the editor to commit.

3184.title: Not yet decided
3184.content: . | Committing a page decision to an in-tree todos graph automatically. | A reviewer who edits a comment after ingest. The edit is not re-read, so a record an editor has already acted on is not silently rewritten. Whether an edit should reopen the comment is open. | Line review comments are not read. A reviewer who uses one gets no todo. | .
