3535.title: uses[] Editorial Review
3535.content: Skill uses-editorial-review: Adjudicate uses-editorial-completeness — read a block as a reader would and judge whether its uses[] is complete and genuinely expository. The human/agent half of the uses QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-uses.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review, Committee review of a content change .

3536.title: The relation you are auditing
3536.content: uses[] is the editorial dependency relation: what must a reader have read to follow this block? It is authored content — a deliberate judgement about narrative order — and it is maintained by agents and humans, not generated. The same relation exists at term scale: a glossary term’s requires, and a schema term’s uses in bootstrap’s graph.schema.json, say what a reader must know before the definition. Same discipline — AUTHORED, never inferred, with a text matcher kept only as a guard that list and prose agree (see the glossary ordering discipline, §”Ordered glossaries”). It is not any machine-derived dependency graph. A content type with a formal layer also derives a formal relation, from what its proofs actually invoke, and the two relations answer different questions and diverge in both directions, correctly. The layer that ships such a content type holds that comparison and names this skill from its side (for a paper folio, the science layer).

3537.title: interprets is the same relation under a second field name
3537.content: uses[] is the curated list. interprets states the same reader-facing fact for a remark or example about one specific block, and the content graph counts both. Each editorial edge carries editorialField so a tool proposing an edit can still tell which field an author wrote: they are interchangeable to a reader and not to a writer, and collapsing them would make an automated edit rewrite the wrong field. Two caveats, both of which change what a number means: . | detangler-no-forward-ref builds its own uses-only adjacency and does not consume the shared graph, so forward-pointing interprets edges are outside what it counts. | The editorial graph is not acyclic. Counting both fields reveals genuine editorial cycles. Do not “fix” one without reading whether it is real. | . Do not quote a count from prose — run the check against the corpus in front of you. A number in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. For impact questions — what breaks if this changes? — use the union, via the content graph’s accessors, which default to it.

3538.title: The prime directive
3538.content: Never populate uses[] from a machine-derived dependency graph. Copying derived dependencies in destroys the editorial signal and inflates every ordering metric computed from it (graph energy, forward refs, cone size, PageRank). Never “sync” the two. When reviewing, do not open a block’s formal or generated sibling to decide what belongs in uses[]. The question is about the reader.

3539.title: Workflow
3539.content: . | Read the .md as a reader. Cold. Do not read the .ts first — you want your own sense of what the block presumes before you see what the author declared. | List what the narrative actually leans on. Note every point where the prose: . | uses notation it does not introduce, | names an object (“the canonical $X$”) defined elsewhere, | argues against or refines a prior result, | presumes a construction the reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. | . | Now read uses[] in the .ts manifest and compare both ways. | Judge completeness. Anything from step 2 missing from uses[] that a reader would genuinely stumble over ⇒ fail (major). A reader who could carry on unbothered ⇒ at most warn. | Judge editorial fitness. For each listed entry, ask: would a reader be worse off having not read this first? . | Yes ⇒ fine. | No, and it looks like a derived artefact (an entry the prose never mentions, copied from a generated dependency list) ⇒ fail (major). This is the pollution case. | No, but it is defensible context ⇒ warn. | . | Write the sidecar entry under uses-editorial-completeness with reviewer.kind: "agent" (or "human"), citing file:line and a verbatim quote for every finding — the block-QA evidence contract. | .

3540.title: Verdict rubric
3540.content: | Verdict | When | . | pass | List reads as a deliberate editorial judgement; nothing a reader needs is missing; nothing present is dead weight. | . | warn | A marginal entry, or a missing dependency a reader could shrug off. | . | fail | A missing dependency a reader would stumble over, or an entry that is plainly a copied-in derived dependency. | .

3541.title: Forward references and foreshadows[]
3541.content: A uses[] entry pointing at a block that appears later in the chapter is a detangler-no-forward-ref finding. Sometimes that is right — the exposition really does defer — and foreshadows[] records it. foreshadows[] is independent of uses[], so a chapter overview can name results it previews without asserting a dependency that is not real. It covers two cases you must keep apart: . | case | in uses[]? | who records it | cost | . | Pure forward pointer — the prose names something coming later and does not depend on it | no | derived from the .md, not authored | zero by construction: it never enters the dependency graph | . | Deferred prerequisite — a real dependency the paper states later on purpose | yes | declared by the author, and only the author | exempt from ordering cost; still counted for cycles, cones and depth | . Do not hand-author the first case. deriveForeshadows reads the block’s own markdown links and backticked labels, keeps those that resolve to a real block sitting later in reading order and are not already in uses[], and loadChapterGraph re-derives on every load. Writing them into the manifest duplicates the prose into metadata, where it goes stale. The derivation never reads deferral language; it matches links and labels only (phrasing detection misreads e.g. “Below $n^*$”, a numeric comparison).

3542.title: Declaring the second case
3542.content: Only a deferred prerequisite needs your judgement: it exempts a real uses[] edge from the ordering metrics, hiding a genuine defect behind an authored claim that the disorder was intended, and nothing downstream re-opens it. The contract in BlockBase.foreshadows is strict — the prose must frame the reference as deferred (“we will need X, proved in chapter 9”). The bar is a first-person authorial hand-off that says the treatment happens elsewhere: “we establish this in X”, “we work this out separately”, “the derivation is recorded in X”. | Looks like a deferral | Actually | . | Bare cross-reference — “See [X] in Chapter 7” | ordering. Says nothing about direction. | . | Organizational pointer — “these tables are projections of this master table” | ordering. About structure, not sequence. | . | Block asserts the target’s conclusion as background, then reasons onward from it | ordering. Consuming a result is the opposite of deferring it. | . | Target listed under “## Rigorous results” / “## Consumers / downstream” | ordering — and check the direction; these often run target→source. | . | A forward-looking word (“below”, “later”, “we must show”) | ordering unless the sentence is about this target’s placement. “Below $n^*$” is a numeric comparison; “we must show” is usually about research, not chapter order. | . Two failure modes survive a verbatim quote, so check both before declaring: . | False locator. “the functor of the next subsection” where the target is 21 sections and ~300 blocks away. The prose defers; it does not defer this far, and the edge is a real defect. | Mis-aimed deferral. The quoted sentence hands off to a different block than the edge under review. A deferral pointed elsewhere cannot exempt this one. | . Both are about the declared case only. A derived pointer is aimed by the link itself, so it cannot be mis-aimed, and it carries no exemption to abuse. Two rules police the field: foreshadows-resolve (every target must exist) and foreshadows-not-self. The foreshadows-point-forward criterion catches a target the reader has already passed, which is either a prerequisite filed in the wrong field or an inert back-reference.

3543.title: A block’s uses[] may be carrying the whole family
3543.content: Never judge an entry from the block’s own .md alone. A block is the head of a family — X-proof, X-interpretation, X-tableN-data — and the dependency you are looking for is often in a child while the declaration sits on the parent. | Table children. Pointer-style blocks (“See Table 3”) keep their substance in tbl:…-data. A name-and-notation search of the parent’s .md reports an absence that is not real. | Proof children. A proof cites what the statement assumes. The parent’s prose may never name a target its proof child cites by label; if the proof declares no uses[] of its own, the parent’s entry is the sole record of the dependency, and deleting it as “unsupported by the prose” erases the edge entirely. | . So before removing an entry, check whether any child leans on the target, and whether that child declares anything itself. An entry that looks like dead weight on the parent may be the family’s only declaration. Searching for the target’s words also misses a lean on the target’s object — a source writing “the canonical $\tilde w_\lambda$” depends on whatever defines the undeformed $w_\lambda$, whether or not it ever says so.

3544.title: Sibling parity is evidence only until a bulk edit touched the family
3544.content: “All the siblings declare nothing, so declaring it here would be the anomaly” is evidence only if no bulk operation has run over the family: a bulk edit (for example a transitive-prune pass) produces parity by construction, so parity cannot distinguish a shared convention from shared damage. Before resting on it, check the family’s history, not just the block’s: . git log --oneline -- <chapter>/<sibling>.ts # for two or three siblings . A convention shows up as blocks that were authored empty. Damage shows up as one commit emptying all of them on the same day. If the emptiness has a single commit behind it, parity tells you nothing about intent. The same caution applies to any evidence drawn from what “the corpus does”: a corpus that has been swept is a record of the sweep as much as of the authors.

3545.title: One reading is not the standard
3545.content: A single careful pass is not enough: on re-review, destructive uses[] verdicts and foreshadow declarations are overturned often, and keyword search over the .md alone misses real dependencies. Use two readers who cannot see each other’s verdicts for anything that edits the graph, and treat agreement as the signal. Where they disagree, or where either is unsure, leave the edge alone: a wrongly deleted editorial edge silently corrupts every ordering metric computed from the graph. A retarget carries both burdens. It asserts this edge is wrong and that one is right, so it needs evidence for each half separately. When only the second half holds, it is an addition, not a swap.

3546.title: Reading the mechanical findings first
3546.content: Run the script half before adjudicating — it is cheap and it changes what you should look at: . bun run pipeline/qa-checkers-uses.ts # via qa-sweep --axis uses . | Mechanical finding | What it means for your review | . | uses-editorial-hygiene fail — unresolvable label | A dangling reference. Fix the label or add the missing block before judging completeness; the graph is wrong until you do. | . | uses-editorial-hygiene warn — transitive redundancy | Tidiness only. The graph is correct, just not minimal. Do not let it distract from the completeness question. | . A content type with a formal layer adds its own advisory finding here; the layer that ships it says how to read it.

3547.title: Interaction with other skills
3547.content: | Skill | Interaction | . | content-graph | Owns the graph the mechanical checks read | . | prepare-merge | Runs the uses axis as part of the content gates | . A content type’s own skills that consume or extend this relation are named by the layer that ships the type, which links down to this skill.

3549.title: Visualizer loading — the page is layout, the graph is fetched
3549.content: Skill visualizer-loading: The general strategy for a complex visualizer: the generated page carries identity, layout and a pointer, and its bulky or repeated content is fetched from the Knowledge Graph in the browser rather than baked into every page. What must stay server-side, how to fetch, how to stay equivalent to the render being replaced, and how to verify a page whose content is not in its HTML. Read before generating any page that shows a KG node’s data at length: an IG artefact view, a graph viewer, a schema or sidecar view. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Skill id: visualizer-loading · Package: ui-core .

3550.title: The rule
3550.content: A generated page for a complex visualizer holds three things: . | Identity: the title, description and front matter that navigation, search and a link preview read. | Layout: headings, tabs and links, arranged by a template (liquid-templates). | A pointer: the KG file the content comes from, resolved by the generator. | . The content (a sidecar file, a node’s properties at length, a table derived from the graph) is fetched by the browser from the committed KG artefact. It is never copied into the page. Each copy is a second answer, free to drift from the first, and copied into a thousand pages it is most of the site’s bytes. kg-viewer is an instance of the pattern: one page that fetches its sibling graph document and computes back-links at load.

3551.title: What stays server-side
3551.content: Moving content client-side has costs: a reader without JavaScript loses it, a search index loses it, and so does the first paint. So these stay in the page: . | What navigation and search need: title, description, headings, and the link labels a reader scans for. | The way to reach the data without JavaScript: a link to the raw file, under <noscript> if nowhere else. A view that renders nothing without scripts must still say where its content is. | Anything short and unique to the page. A one-line value is not bloat, and fetching it costs a request to save a few bytes. | . Move a block when it is large or repeated and already a KG file. A block that would need a new file published just to be fetched is a design question for the owner, not a default.

3552.title: Where the data is served from — served: true
3552.content: The fetched file is the KG’s own, published verbatim. A directory declares served: true in its instance’s <instance>.json, and mount-instance-docs copies its bytes to /<instance>/<path> after Jekyll: no Liquid, no layout, no index page. Pages under the instance’s composed docs then reach it with a relative path. Never copy the file into docs/ beside the page instead — a gate flags it as an unknown file family in a docs directory. A generator whose data is not served writes no page that would fetch it, and says why.

3553.title: How to fetch
3553.content: . | Relative to the page’s own location, never via a configured base URL, so the same bytes work in production and in a staging preview (kg-viewer §”The page is generated, not committed”). | One shared loader per visualizer kind, published once and referenced by every page, never inlined in each page. | No dependencies: no CDN or framework. Same reason as kg-viewer: the data is this repository’s, and a third party in its trust boundary is at odds with that. | Three states on the page: loading, loaded, and could not load, which names the file and the error. A failed fetch that leaves a blank or a permanent “Loading…” is the silent-gap defect in another form. | .

3554.title: Stay equivalent to the render you replace
3554.content: When the page replaces another renderer’s page (for example the IG Publisher’s, which every phase must render equivalent to), compute the display the same way that renderer does, and then check it. For example, a page that shows a file as JSON.stringify(parsed, null, 2) differs from the file’s own bytes whenever the file has integer-like keys, which JavaScript orders first; showing the raw bytes would look right and be wrong.

3555.title: Printing and PDFs
3555.content: A browser prints the page as it is at that moment, so fetched content prints once it has loaded and not before: a PDF taken at domcontentloaded holds “Loading…”. | Every loader signals completion. Each counts itself in and out of window.__kgLoads, and the last one to finish sets <html data-kg-loaded>, on success or failure. A failed fetch still ends the wait, and its message is what prints. | Anything that prints or renders a PDF waits for that attribute, never for a fixed delay. That includes a Playwright page.pdf(), a PDF build step and a screenshot test. A page with no loader never sets it, so a tool that waits must first check whether the page loads one of the loader scripts. | A reader pressing Ctrl+P gets the page as loaded. The loaders are fast, but a print from a cold cache can still catch “Loading…”. That is a visible, honest state, not a blank. | .

3556.title: Verify in a browser, not in the HTML
3556.content: A static check cannot see fetched content: the built HTML holds only “Loading…”. Verification therefore means loading each page in a browser (Playwright, with the pre-installed Chromium) and comparing what it displays against the reference, as rendered-verification requires of any rendered artefact.

3557.title: Finding what to move
3557.content: A QA review over a built site: . | The mechanical half measures per-page bytes, blocks repeated across pages, and blocks matching a committed KG file, and writes a QA sidecar. | The agentic half judges each candidate against §”What stays server-side”. | . Repetition is a measurement, but whether a block may leave the page is a judgement.

3558.title: Do not
3558.content: . | Bake a KG file’s text into a page “for now”. That copy is what the next person will have to find and remove. | Move navigation or search terms client-side to save bytes. The saving is small and the loss is the page being findable. | Add a framework to fetch a JSON file. fetch and textContent are the whole loader. | .

3560.title: Voice authoring guidance
3560.content: Skill voice-authoring-guidance: Load the active voices’ rules BEFORE writing, so a block is drafted in the register it will be reviewed against. The authoring half of the voice overlay; voice-overlay-review is the half that runs after. Named by: Review task, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: place a note .

3561.title: Read the voices before the first sentence, not after the first review
3561.content: A voice is an editorial register — spelling, punctuation, terminology, how a normative statement is phrased. Get it right while drafting; correcting it afterwards means rewriting prose somebody has already reviewed. bun run cat check:voices # what this instance ships, and how many rules each carries . The active set is in the instance’s config, its index.config.json entry: . { "voices": { "active": ["milnor"] } } . An empty or absent list means no voice, and that is a real answer. The platform’s own documentation activates none. Do not add one because a voice exists.

3562.title: What to load, and what to do with it
3562.content: Each voice’s rules carry three things you need while writing: . | terminology — preferred/deprecated pairs. Apply these as you type; a terminology change ripples into every sentence built around the old word. | patterns — what the mechanical check will look for, i.e. which constructions will be questioned. | judgementOnly: true — no lexical check can decide it, so nobody will catch it for you. These are the rules to hold in mind rather than fix on a later pass. | .

3563.title: The rules most often broken by drafting on instinct
3563.content: The rules worth knowing in advance are the ones where instinct is wrong. For example, under the science layer’s milnor voice, “clearly” is fine in a mathematical block when it routes the reader away from a routine verification; do not write around it to appease the checker. This skill restates no voice’s rules: each rule belongs to the instance that derived it, with the publication, page and verbatim quote it was read from, and a copy here would lose that citation — and the uncited copy is the one a reader meets first and nothing can check. To learn which of your voices’ rules are counterintuitive, open the voices.

3564.title: When two active voices disagree
3564.content: Rules are unioned, not merged, and both stand. If honouring one would break the other, that is a finding for the author and not something to resolve silently in the prose — say which two rules and which voices, and let the editor decide. A silent choice hides a genuine conflict between two documents the folio has adopted.

3565.title: Do not
3565.content: . | Do not apply a voice the folio has not activated. An unasked-for register produces confident findings against prose never written to it. | Do not treat a voice as a substitute for the base house voice. Voices overlay one-voice-style-guide.md; they do not replace it. | Do not add a rule to a voice while drafting. A voice rule needs a citation that resolves (check:voices enforces it) — a rule you inferred from the prose you are writing is circular. | .

3567.title: Voice editorial review
3567.content: Skill voice-editorial-review: Adjudicate a voice-* finding — read the flagged passage as a reader of THAT genre would and decide whether the register is wrong, the criterion is out of scope, or the block is a stated exception. The human/agent half of the voice QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-voice.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review .

3568.title: The axis you are adjudicating
3568.content: Six criteria in pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts describe one house voice: . | criterion | what it matches | severity | . | voice-status-leak | status markers and derivation-status speech in body prose | critical | . | voice-scholarly-default | second-person address, lecturer-cadence openers, paper-past-tense narration | major | . | voice-author-notes-pollution | status banners, PR/commit refs, agent names, ISO dates | major | . | voice-emoji-content | emoji as content outside tables | major | . | voice-first-person-work | first-person work tone — “we’ll add”, “let me”, “needs more work” | major | . | voice-editorializing | “surprisingly”, “it is worth noting that”, “rather than merely …” | minor | . They are heuristics over phrase lists. A match is a question, not a verdict; a reviewer entry on the same sidecar confirms or overrules it.

3569.title: The scoping question comes first, and it is usually the answer
3569.content: Every criterion above was written for a paper: a scholarly artefact in third person, where a status marker really is a leak of the work tracker into the published text. A criterion without profiles scoping also runs over documentation, whose register addresses the reader: “you need bun, latexmk and Lean” is a correct sentence in a prerequisites page and a voice-scholarly-default match. Ask which is true before touching the prose: . | The register is wrong for this genre. Fix the passage. | The criterion does not belong in this genre. Add profiles: ["paper"] to it in the registry. One edit clears the finding for every document folio and records why. | The criterion belongs and this block is an exception. Record a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached, and nothing is silently rewritten. | . Many instances of one criterion across many guide pages is evidence about the criterion’s scope, not about the authors.

3570.title: What the criterion cannot know
3570.content: The checkers match text. They do not know what the page is about. Typical false positives: . | voice-status-leak on a page that is a deliberate inventory of gaps (**Not yet implemented:** is its subject, not a leak). | voice-status-leak on prose about a work-plan lane: prose about a to-do store contains the words of a to-do store. | voice-emoji-content inside a transcript of an agent session, quoted as data. | . Each is a criterion reading a quotation as an assertion, and the reviewer entry says so in those words.

3571.title: Adjudicating one finding
3571.content: . | Open the block, not just the evidence line. The sidecar quotes one line; the register is a property of the passage around it. | Name the genre. Paper, guide, reference, transcript. That decides which of the three outcomes applies before you read another word. | Record the outcome where the next reader will find it — a prose edit, a registry edit with profiles, or a reviewer entry. A finding left open comes back on the next sweep. | Re-run the sweep — bun run pipeline/qa-sweep.ts --root docs/source — so the sidecar, the icon and the panel agree with what you decided. | .

3572.title: Where the open findings are
3572.content: Tracked in the work plan, one item per criterion, each carrying its blocks with file, line and the matched text: . beans list | grep "Voice axis" . The evidence itself lives in <block>.qa.json beside each block, and is published per block on the docs site: the QA icon opens the criterion, and the criterion opens the witness that ruled on it — which checker, at which script_hash, and whether the verdict still matches the file on disk.

3573.title: Do not
3573.content: . | Do not edit prose to silence a criterion you believe is out of scope. That hides the scoping defect and costs the next folio the same argument. | Do not mass-apply one finding’s resolution across its siblings without reading them; one criterion can fire for different causes. | Do not treat critical as “fix first”. Severity ranks the criterion’s authors’ concern, not the confidence of this match. | Do not delete a finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one comes back with no record that anyone looked. | .

3576.title: What you are reviewing, and against what
3576.content: One block, against the rules of the voices the folio has activated — not every voice it ships. The instance’s config (its index.config.json entry) holds the list; an empty list means there is nothing for this skill to do and that is a pass, not a gap. bun run cat check:voices # the voices, their rule counts, and that every citation resolves .

3577.title: The rule’s citation is the argument, so open it
3577.content: Every voice rule carries a source that resolves to a real file — a library/<doc>/sections/<section>.md for a rule read from an ingested document, or a path for a house standard. It also carries the quote the rule was read from. Open the citation before upholding a finding. | A reviewer who has read the source can say why the rule applies to this block. | The rule may be wrong. A rule derived from a document can misread it. If the quote does not support the rule, the rule is the defect and the work item goes against the voice, not against the block. | .

3578.title: Three outcomes, as with the house voice axis
3578.content: Identical to voice-editorial-review: . | The finding stands — the register is wrong for this block. Fix the prose. | The rule does not apply to this content — record it, and consider whether the rule needs appliesTo scoping on the voice. One scoping edit beats many per-block overrules. | The rule applies and this block is an exception — a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached and nothing is silently rewritten. | .

3579.title: A mechanical match is a question
3579.content: A pattern is a regex over text; it does not know what the block is about. Examples of non-defects it matches: . | voice-scholarly-default on documentation pages whose register is correctly second-person. | voice-editorializing on merely inside a comparative, where the contrast is the block’s claim. | voice-editorializing on clearly used as proof economy. | . Verify before upholding, and when a rule fires repeatedly across a corpus on the same non-defect, that is evidence about the RULE.

3580.title: Recording the verdict
3580.content: Voice findings go on the block’s QA sidecar like any other, through the same writer, so the icon and the published witness agree with what you decided: . bun run pipeline/qa-merge-findings.ts --file findings.json . insertAdjudication places your entry ahead of the script entry, because list[0] is a criterion’s effective verdict. The script’s entry is kept beneath yours, because the disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.

3581.title: Do not
3581.content: . | Do not uphold a finding you have not traced to its quote. A rule that misreads its source is the failure this design exists to prevent. | Do not review against a voice the folio has not activated. | Do not delete a script finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one returns with no record that anyone looked. | Do not resolve a conflict between two active voices in the prose. Both rules stand: name them and let the editor decide. | .

3583.title: Voice overlay review
3583.content: Process_VoiceReview · advisory · 6 step(s) . The voice axis: load whichever editorial voices are active, run each rule’s mechanical half, and decide — for each finding — whether the prose is wrong, the rule does not apply to this content, or this block is a stated exception. You are in this process after the base voice has been adjudicated, and only if a voice is active at all: the first gateway ends the process honestly when none is, rather than reporting a clean review of nothing. Three outcomes, all legitimate, and the third is the one that needs recording: an exception without a reviewer entry is indistinguishable from a rule nobody ran. There is also a fourth path the diagram draws deliberately — if the rule’s own citation does not support it, the RULE is the defect, and that becomes a bean rather than a finding against the prose. i i i i i i

3591.title: Input and output
3591.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: the use (design or as-is), the topic (for CRDM, the proposal slug), the surface, and, from CRDM, the requirements that change it, the proposal path, the humanReviewer (requester or BA), the channels the candidates are shown in, and the branch. | Out — the renderings: assetDir, intent, and one candidates[] entry per candidate: its source HTML path, its screenshots.web and screenshots.mobile paths (from wireframe-check), their staging deep links, its per-criterion entries, and its outcome with the reason. chosen names the candidate, who chose it and the comment that records it; it is absent until a person chooses. | Out — as changed assets: changedAssets[] lists every wireframe file the branch adds, changes or removes (candidate HTML, screenshots, intent, reviews) in the record shape a staging preview’s graph carries (change, kind, title, before, after, source, pages or pagesUnknown; ChangedAsset in cat-harness-tools scripts/kg-changed-assets.ts). 3592.title: Two uses
3592.content: | use | candidates | review | . | Design: a new or changed UI | at least two, compared blind | per-criterion, then adjudication, then options analysis | . | As-is: an existing visualiser, drawn as it renders on main | exactly one, marked as-is | the same criteria. A finding becomes a work item against the visualiser, not a redesign | .

3593.title: 1. Intent
3593.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

3594.title: 2. Candidates
3594.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

3595.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
3595.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

3596.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
3596.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

3597.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
3597.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and a dispensation needs its reason. | The choice between surviving candidates is Process_OptionsAnalysis. Rejected candidates stay, each with the reason it lost. | .

3598.title: Staging links
3598.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: staging-review §”The deep-link rule”.

3599.title: Showing it to the requester
3599.content: Design use from CRDM ends in a person’s choice, so the candidates must be in front of that person before implementation starts: . | Commit the candidates, intent.md, checks/ (screenshots) and reviews/ under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, so feature-staging publishes them with the rest of the branch. | Show them where the requester will look, chosen from context: the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or more than one of these. Where it goes is a judgement (staging-review, the deep-link rule, point 5); every place chosen carries the same content: a short narrative of what each candidate does differently; branches/ deep links to each candidate’s HTML (not the site root); and its web and mobile screenshots shown as images, not only linked. Say which could not be linked or rendered, and why. | Ask the requester or BA to choose, with the comparison (one row per candidate, from A_CompareOptions) and a recommendation, per interaction-modality where it applies. | Record their choice in the proposal and in the output’s chosen. An agent never chooses on their behalf. Implementation (CRDM Phase 6) builds against the chosen candidate, and the delivery summary links it beside the after-screenshot. | .

3608.title: State in a running process
3608.content: Skill workflow-state: Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what <cat-harness.processes:bean op> actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A process instance is not self-contained. It walks a diagram that lives somewhere else, records its position somewhere else again, and reads facts it must not change. Five stores; confusing any two of them is how a work plan comes to disagree with itself.

3609.title: Which store answers which question
3609.content: | question | store | graph typology | layer | . | what does this process DO? | processes/**/*.bpmn | cat-harness | content | . | where did this instance GET TO? | the workflow-state node of the work item graph | workflow-state | state | . | what is being worked on? | the bean-defs node of the work item graph | bean-defs | state | . | what does a PERSON still owe? | todos/ | todo-items | state | . | what do I already know? | agent memory | memory | context | . The layer column says what a step may do. A step may write to a state graph; that is what state is for. A step that writes to context is a defect, not an update: memory changes when a human directs an authoring act, outside any instance. content-context-and-state-graphs carries the axis; processMayWrite() is the predicate.

3610.title: The diagram is content and the instance is state, and that is the whole model
3610.content: A .bpmn is authored, reviewed, versioned and read by anyone — it stands on its own. An instance is a token position in that diagram plus a history: it means nothing detached from the file it walks. That is why the two live in different graphs and why an instance names its process rather than embedding it. Two consequences: . An instance is never edited by hand. It carries "$schema": "folio-workflow-instance/v1" and the interpreter owns it. Hand- editing a token is asserting a step happened, which is precisely what the gate exists to refuse. A diagram change does not rewrite history. An instance records where it got to under the diagram as it stood. If a step is renamed, the honest answer is that the old instance names a node that no longer exists — not that it retroactively took a different path.

3611.title: Beans and instances are ONE answer, not two
3611.content: bean-defs says what is being worked on; workflow-state says where it got to. Those must be one answer or they diverge, and a work plan that disagrees with itself is worse than one that is merely coarse. The loop is closed by <cat-harness.processes:bean op="…"> on an activity. A bean-marked step is not a step about the work plan — it IS the work-plan operation, so completing the step performs it: . | op | on completing the step | . | claim | status → in-progress, idempotent | . | note | append the caller’s note to the body | . | resolve | status → completed, only if the instance itself finished (or only archive steps are left) | . | archive | move a completed or scrapped work item into the archive, only once the instance finished | . claim is drawn only in Process_BeanOpen, and resolve and archive only in Process_BeanClose; every process that works on a work item calls both (check:bean-calls). note is drawn where the work happens. resolve is the careful one. A work item is never closed on somebody else’s judgement, so it does not fire on the caller’s say-so: the work item completes only when the instance tracking it has completed, which is a fact derived from the process rather than asserted by the agent calling it. A still-running instance gets a note. An op the build does not implement fails at process load. A step that says it resolves a work item and quietly does nothing is exactly the divergence the extension exists to close.

3612.title: What state does NOT buy you
3612.content: Ordering is not quality. A completed instance means the gates ran in order and a person saw the findings. Whether the content is correct is what the QA axes, the build and the validators are for. A green process must never be read as a reviewed artefact, and any dashboard built on this has to say so. A position is not a claim. An instance at Task_Commit says the token arrived, not that the commit is good.

3613.title: Where running instances live — the state graph on the branch store
3613.content: Running instances are part of the work-plan store (workflow-state graph typology; positions in work-plan-store). Where the deployment uses the git state-branch Tool, the store is mounted and pushed as described in work-plan-store-git-branch. The container is ephemeral and a work plan only one agent can see is not a work plan. Instance state lives in the shared work-plan store for the same reason work item definitions do: a sibling session, or the same session resumed in a fresh container, reads the store to find the position that exists rather than starting a second one beside it. When an instance advances, its state is written through the store’s Tool (bun run cat state:push when backed by the git state branch). This keeps instance state globally visible without cluttering code PR diffs on main. Instance ids are derived from the subject rather than random, so re-entering a step finds the instance that is already there: beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing, so an id you can recompute is what prevents duplicates.

3614.title: Reading the state you did not write
3614.content: Before acting on an instance you did not start, ask what it is waiting on. A work item’s status defaults to non-blocking; a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff — because a block with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work. bean-blocking carries that, and bean-coordination carries the rule that a claim announces rather than reserves until your PR exists.
